items.title: UAEF: A framework-agnostic system for closed-loop evaluation of AI agents
items.description: Teams building AI agents on AWS use a range of frameworks, including LangGraph, LangChain, Strands Agents, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Each framework records agent execution in its own way, so the structure of messages, tool calls, and handoffs between agents differs from one to the next. Evaluation tooling tends to follow the same boundaries: teams build metrics, scoring logic, and result storage against a single framework’s trace format, and they must rebuild them when they switch frameworks or run agents on more than one. This coupling makes a basic development question harder to answer: did a change to the prompt, model, or tools improve the agent? Answering it requires consistent metrics across versions of an agent and a shared record of past results to compare against. Agent quality also spans several dimensions that a single accuracy score does not capture: tool calling, response quality, responsible AI, performance, multi-turn conversation, multi-agent coordination, and reasoning. In this post, we introduce the Universal Agent Evaluation Framework (UAEF). Customers across 12 organizations in the telecom, healthcare, and financial services industries used UAEF to evaluate their AI agents with one consistent set of metrics and compare agent versions before release. UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system: it uses adapters to convert traces from each framework into a common format, then scores those traces with 36 built-in metrics across 7 dimensions. It stores the results in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and generates reports and insights that inform the next iteration of the agent. This post describes how UAEF works, provides a playbook for choosing metrics and preparing datasets, and points to runnable notebooks for each supported framework. UAEF: One evaluation layer for agent frameworks UAEF is a framework-agnostic evaluation system for AI agents. It takes the agent a team already has and scores it the same way across supported frameworks and runtimes. UAEF takes two inputs: the agent under test and a dataset to run it on. The dataset provides the inputs for each test case, and it can also include ground-truth answers, the expected output for each input. Ground truth is optional, and only metrics that compare the agent’s response against a reference use it. To evaluate tool calling, the ground truth must also include the expected tool calls for each test case: which tools the agent should call, in what order, and with what arguments. Everything after that happens inside the UAEF. Figure 1 shows the path a single evaluation takes, from the inputs to the reports and insights. First, an adapter reads the agent’s native execution, its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs, and normalizes it into one canonical trace, so that the steps that follow are identical no matter which framework produced the agent. Next, UAEF screens the trace for personally identifiable information (PII), such as email addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers, before data is stored. The evaluation engine then scores the trace on a selection from 36 built-in metrics across 7 quality dimensions. When you persist a run, UAEF records it as an experiment in Amazon DynamoDB and Amazon S3: Amazon DynamoDB holds the per-experiment metadata used for listing and comparison, and Amazon S3 holds the full results. With runs stored, a team can compare an agent version against a baseline to detect regressions and generate reports and insights that explain what changed and why. Those reports close the loop: the team evaluates the agent, learns what regressed or improved, changes the prompt, model, or tools, and evaluates again. Figure 1: UAEF closed-loop evaluation data flow The rest of this section follows that flow in order: the adapters that make UAEF framework-agnostic, the evaluation engine and its metrics, PII detection, experiment storage and comparison, and the reports that close the loop. Canonical trace and adapters Adapters are what make UAEF framework-agnostic. An adapter reads the record of an agent’s run, including its messages, tool calls, and agent-to-agent handoffs. It converts that record into one canonical representation called the AgentTrace , which is the only thing the rest of UAEF scores. Because of that conversion, UAEF works with the agent, whatever SDK it was built with (such as LangGraph, LangChain, or Strands Agents). It can run locally, behind an HTTP endpoint, or on a managed runtime such as Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with traces in Langfuse or not captured at all. UAEF provides an adapter for each of these, and they produce the same AgentTrace , so metrics, scores, and comparisons stay consistent across every one of them. A trace reaches UAEF two ways. If one already exists, from a past run, a log, or an observability store, it is handed to UAEF and the matching adapter normalizes it. If not, UAEF invokes the agent for you: given a runtime Amazon Resource Name (ARN) or an HTTP endpoint, it calls the agent on each dataset input, collects the response, and adapts it in one step. Either way, the output is the same AgentTrace . Because every metric, mode, and report operates on the AgentTrace rather than on a framework native format, the scoring that follows is identical no matter where the trace came from. That separation, normalization first and scoring second, is what lets a team compare an agent built on one framework against an agent built on another on a single scale. Evaluation engine The evaluation engine scores a canonical trace across 7 quality dimensions, each capturing a distinct aspect of agent behavior that a single accuracy number would hide. items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.description: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works. The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs. I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below: We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...] As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention . Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...] The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units. Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself , allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster. We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues , where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments. items.title: Introducing usage-based pricing for Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming
items.description: Usage-based metering for bidirectional streaming solves a software billing problem for real-time speech AI. Customers deploying streaming models on Amazon SageMaker AI bidirectional streaming pay for the endpoint infrastructure that hosts the model. Separately, model providers listing on AWS Marketplace need a way to charge for what customers consume during a live stream. Today, we’re announcing usage-based metering for Amazon SageMaker bidirectional (bidi) streaming inference, so model providers can report actual usage for the AWS Marketplace software charge. Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Deepgram , the real-time speech AI company, is the launch partner for this capability, bringing usage-based Speech-to-Text (STT) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) billing to AWS Marketplace. This post builds on a series of innovations between Deepgram and AWS. First, we introduced bidirectional streaming for real-time inference on Amazon SageMaker AI , which supports long-lived bidirectional streams between clients and model servers. Then, Deepgram enhanced Amazon SageMaker AI support with AWS Identity and Access Management (AWS IAM) temporary delegation , simplifying secure authentication for enterprise deployments, and expanded observability with enhanced metrics . Now, with usage-based metering, we further strengthen the foundation for production real-time AI, aligning billing with how customers consume streaming and real-time AI workloads. Why streaming broke the existing billing model With AWS Marketplace software metering for SageMaker AI real-time request-response inference, model providers can report a unit count in an HTTP response header. AWS Marketplace uses that quantity for the software charge. This works for request-response APIs where the billable quantity is known when the response is sent. Bidirectional streaming is different. A client streams audio and receives transcriptions through the SageMaker AI API using an HTTP/2 event stream. SageMaker AI connects to the model server over WebSockets. A session can last 30 seconds or 30 minutes. Usage accumulates as the session runs, and the final total isn’t known until it ends. A response header alone can’t report periodic usage during that live session. Hourly software pricing can charge customers while a model is available, including quiet periods. With usage-based metering, providers can align the AWS Marketplace software charge with reported usage. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges remain separate and continue to apply while the endpoint is provisioned. How companion metadata streaming works The solution introduces a second WebSocket connection alongside the existing inference stream. When a bidirectional streaming session starts, SageMaker AI establishes two connections to the model server: Data connection : carries inference request and response data, the existing bidirectional stream. Metadata connection : a companion WebSocket dedicated to metering data. Model servers opt in by returning one header on the WebSocket upgrade response: X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Supported: true SageMaker AI then opens a companion WebSocket to the model server at /invocations-bidirectional-stream-metadata . Both connections carry the same X-Amzn-SageMaker-Request-Id header, which the model server uses to correlate metering records with the active inference session. The model server sends metering data as JSON text frames on the metadata connection. Send records at a frequency that matches the billing model: incrementally as usage accrues (recommended), either as each unit is consumed or as periodic batches of units consumed since the previous record. Send any final record as soon as the session ends. Each frame contains exactly one metering record, rather than an array of records. The metadata stream has a rate quota of one message per second per connection, with a maximum message size of 512 bytes. We recommend sending metering records incrementally as usage accrues. This reduces the amount of usage left unreported if a session ends unexpectedly. Transport delivery alone does not establish that usage has been billed. Validate reported units against AWS Marketplace reports and buyer charges. { "Metering": { "Dimension": "inference.count", "ConsumedUnits": 720, "ClientToken": "a3f2b1c0-unique-uuid" } } Metering messages use the inference.count dimension, and ConsumedUnits supplies the quantity for that dimension. If the product charges per second of audio, a record reporting 12 minutes of metered audio carries 720 seconds as ConsumedUnits: 720 . The dimension name doesn’t mean one unit per request. The provider defines which audio counts as metered usage, and the AWS Marketplace offer maps the unit to its price. The listing shows one price per unit, labeled per request, with up to three decimal places. The ClientToken field supports idempotency. If a duplicate token arrives on the same connection, SageMaker AI drops the duplicate message silently. The metadata connection runs over TCP, which provides ordered, reliable delivery at the transport layer. If it fails to establish or drops mid-session, inference continues by default because X-Amzn-SageMaker-Metadata-Stream-Required defaults to false . Set this header to true when the provider must stop inference if the metadata stream becomes unavailable. This choice trades inference availability for metering continuity. It doesn’t guarantee that malformed or dropped records are billed. What this means for customers If you deploy real-time AI models for transcription, contact centers, voice agents, or captioning, the new metering model changes how the AWS Marketplace software charge is calculated. SageMaker AI endpoint infrastructure charges still apply. Transparent, per-unit billing through AWS Marketplace means usage flows directly into your AWS bill. items.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
items.description: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities. items.title: When Does It Actually Make Sense to Put AI Into Products?
items.description: Over the past few years, the tech industry has rushed to plug a new microchip into every device on the assumption that if you can add AI, you should. Smart-vision toothbrushes , mood-reading household robots , and a host of physical products are invading consumers’ daily lives, reliant on artificial intelligence to learn, predict, and adjust our behavior. But as anyone who’s struggled to update the firmware in their fridge knows, AI doesn’t improve every product. Some product designers are asking where the line is between genuine innovation and a solution looking for a problem. Savannah Kunovsky leads a team of industrial product designers at Ideo , a design consultancy based in San Francisco focused on helping clients unpack when AI becomes a barrier rather than a breakthrough. Kunovsky spoke with IEEE Spectrum about the pressure to integrate AI in everything, where that integration goes wrong, and what companies can do to determine when an AI integration is—and isn’t—a smart choice. When AI makes products worse How much of the current wave of AI integration into physical products is driven by pressure from investors and shareholders to keep up with industry trends? Savannah Kunovsky : Some of it. Teams come to us feeling pressured to show they’re doing something with AI, sometimes because a CEO has promised the board an “AI story” before the next earnings call, or a competitor has just launched an AI-powered version of their product. In all cases, the first thing we do is step back and ask who the product is for and what they’re trying to do. Once that’s clear, the role AI should play, whether large, small, or invisible, usually becomes obvious. There is an appetite for this kind of grounding in the industry right now. People want to cut through the hype and see what works in practice. How do you distinguish between a genuinely helpful AI feature and a gimmick? Kunovsky : The test for an AI gimmick is the same test we’d apply to any product experience: Does it help someone do what they’re trying to do? Answering that means understanding how people would use the product in the real context they’ll be using it. Many companies look straight to large language models (LLMs) because that’s top of their mind, but there is a whole AI toolbox to draw from: computer vision, sensor fusion, on-device models, et cetera. Picking the right capability for the task matters as much as deciding whether to use AI in the first place. As a new interaction paradigm, AI is asking people to change their behavior, so it needs to be simple. When IDEO’s predecessor firm worked on Apple’s first mouse in the early 1980s , the team gave it only one button because people were learning a completely unfamiliar system and the interaction mechanism needed to be effortless. The wearable Humane AI pin used projection instead of a screen-based display, making a dramatic shift from the smartphone interface users already know. Angel Garcia/Bloomberg/Getty Images In which products has AI made the user experience worse? Kunovsky : The clearest examples are products where AI replaced something that already worked. I have a lot of respect for Humane’s AI Pin as a provocation, but the technology [a screenless, wearable smartphone alternative that uses an AI assistant instead of apps] wasn’t ready . The Pin asked people to give up an interface they knew well for one that was slower and less reliable, which is a hard trade-off to ask of anyone. You see versions of this problem everywhere—a voice assistant that mishears a simple command and turns off the wrong light, a customer service bot that keeps you in a loop when you just want a person. In cars, climate and volume controls moved onto touchscreens and voice menus, so something you used to do by feel now takes your eyes off the road. Euro NCAP , Europe’s car safety rating program, now rewards physical controls for that reason. People love certain products precisely mainly because they are analog. Part of the value of a film camera, a good kitchen knife, or a notebook is the craft and the feeling of being fully in control. But it doesn’t have to be either/or. In a smart home you can ask a voice assistant to turn off the lights, use an app, or hit the switch on the wall. Having more than one way to reach the same goal is a good thing, as long as it doesn’t add complexity for its own sake. Can you share an example where you convinced a client to ditch an AI implementation? Kunovsky : A client wanted a cooktop with no knobs: You tell an AI what you are cooking and it manages the heat. When we tested it, the pan started smoking and the user reached for a knob that wasn’t there. They said “turn it down” twice and pulled the pan off the burner, all before the AI responded. Needless to say, we ended up keeping the knobs. Anything you need to do instantly, by feel, or under stress is usually best kept physical : a volume knob, a light switch, a stove burner, an emergency stop. In those moments, a mechanical control is faster and more trustworthy than a system that has to interpret what you mean. Toward better AI product design What does “good” AI integration look like? Kunovsky : Companies often start by considering the technical feasibility of AI because the technology is so exciting. But understanding what people need is the key, followed by technical feasibility and what makes sense for the business. From there, the question is, what role should AI play? Sometimes it is the core of the experience, like a voice interface that allows you to talk to a product naturally. Sometimes it works in the background, learning your preferences so you stop repeating yourself. Either way, the measure is whether it helps someone do what they set out to. items.title: US data brokers are selling half a billion dollars in RL training environments to Chinese AI labs

items.title: NSF’s X-Labs Program Draws Support From Charities and Investors
items.description: When the U.S. National Science Foundation began its X-Labs program in May, the agency said the higher-risk, higher-funded awards would create new kinds of partnerships that would confront urgent scientific and technological challenges. Now the NSF is doubling down on the idea, with an announcement in October that charities, companies, and investment funds would provide X-Lab winners practical support such as laboratory space, software, shared equipment, and access to key data and expert guidance. The help provided by these organizations, which the NSF is calling “ consortium partners ,” will not give them ownership stakes in the X-Labs projects. The addition of the consortium partners may help the initial winners—who will be announced later in November or December and receive US $1.5 million for a 9-month planning phase—reach the aggressive targets needed to compete for much larger $50 million multiyear grants. “It’s a way of telling X-Labs applicants you don’t need to reinvent the wheel, so you’re not spending half of your X-Labs money to go build or buy basic infrastructure,” says Matt Cimaglia , an investor in consortium partners Occam Foundry and Florida Quantum Center . NSF X-Labs Focus on AI, Computing, and More The NSF initially announced two focus areas for the X-Labs program: scientific instruments for sensing and imaging and photonic microchips for quantum systems . In September, the agency followed up with three additional areas in AI for physical devices , decoding biological sequences , and pushing the physical limits of computing . The NSF requires potential X-Labs award recipients to eventually demonstrate autonomy : Leaders for projects must be focused on the work full-time, for example, and must be able to make hiring and spending decisions independently from any university or commercial owners. That agility sets X-Labs apart, along with the risk appetite. Consortium partners saw the potential to provide infrastructure and operations support to allow X-Labs recipients to focus on research. “[We’re] very interested in the enabling structures of R&D,” says Joshua M. Greenberg , program director at the Sloan Foundation, one of the participating partners. Greenberg says that the foundation has supported multiple focused research organizations, or FROs, already. FROs are independent entities in the same vein as what the X-Labs program hopes to create. Unlike university laboratories or larger tech companies, FROs are founded with a time-limited purpose of advancing research in a well-defined area. Because they start with a clean slate, FROs may lack the infrastructure that university or corporate research groups might inherit. To address that lack of infrastructure, bioengineering service firm Ginkgo Bioworks , in Boston, is offering X-Lab winners up to $5 million worth of access to its “cloud lab,” says Jason Kelly , the firm’s CEO and founder. Ginkgo’s cloud lab can conduct complex and flexible laboratory work, and the company will also offer laboratory space and internal datasets that could be useful for training AI models. Kelly is enthusiastic about the potential for X-Labs, which he says have the potential to “pull platforms into existence” like the federal Human Genome Project once did, which enabled a lot of subsequent innovation. As scientific and technology companies become more powerful, Kelly says, it’s natural that governments should revisit how to involve them in government-led science. “The scale of companies is not like it was in the Vannevar Bush era [in the 1940s],” he says, “so how should the United States leverage those [much larger, more capable] companies? It’s silly to leave them on the sidelines.” In 1945, Vannevar Bush wrote an influential report that helped shape the modern NSF and U.S. federal science funding. A July report by Michael Kratsios, director of the Office of Science and Technology Policy, offered the current administration’s vision for an update to the Bush report, including the role of X-Labs. Arthur Daemmrich , a historian of U.S. technology policy at Arizona State University (ASU), says he welcomes the administration’s willingness to experiment with science funding. “The field had gotten very staid…this administration has a certain energy that I haven’t seen in past administrations.” He also points out that the X-Labs approach to scientific work is “like gig work for science,” so while it may work for some people and some problems, it may not work for others. The contribution these larger projects make to society is also worth studying, says Zachary Pirtle , a former NASA program manager and now a colleague of Daemmrich’s at ASU, though it’s an open question just how to do so. “If you’re funding these amazing teams and you want them to benefit society, you can’t just have engineers and scientists. Do you need to have economists on some of these teams? Or a variety of different social scientists?” Academics Embrace X-Labs AI Model Some academics are leaning into the X-Labs model. Nathalie Risso , an electrical engineer at the University of Arizona in Tucson, does applied research on automating mining equipment. Risso is applying under the AI for physical systems topic, aiming to test self-learning AI operation of heavy mining equipment. “X-Labs lets us explore things that are bigger than we can do in a lab, or that we might have done in a mine, but they won’t let us use their concentrators because they cost so much,” she says. The costs of getting it right exceed a typical university grant and the cost of getting it wrong is more than any industry partner wants to risk. These kinds of missed opportunities justify an X-Labs–size program, say supporters. items.title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
items.description: I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets: Empirical alignment research : design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for) Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it) Direct alignment work : making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data) In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment [1] ), etc. Automating empirical alignment research This is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of. Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots. The capabilities that are needed for automating empirical alignment research very heavily overlap with the capabilities needed for automating AI capabilities research. Therefore, it doesn’t seem like a priority to try to accelerate this type of automation. However, the prospect of getting a lot of automated empirical alignment work before we have good versions of other types of automated alignment work increases the priority of work which complements it. Significantly, that may mean better specification of the kind of numbers we would like measured/targeted. Automating conceptual alignment research What about automating the type of metric choice/construction that we’ve just said would be a good complement to automating empirical alignment work? Or more generally improving our understanding of how to think about alignment, what we’re even aiming for, etc.? This is essentially theoretical research. Automating it is trickier than automating empirical work because of the lack of verifiable signal about what constitutes progress. Accelerating the automation of conceptual research is somewhat fraught (feeding into some dangerous technologies), but seems helpful for a number of high-priority areas, including macrostrategy as well as conceptual alignment work. Overall it seems likely good to do, if we can. Methods for helping to automate conceptual research broadly might include: Curating training data for finetuning Building scaffolds to try to elicit more research progress from current or future models Building methods to extract more signal from existing conceptual research data Building benchmarks for conceptual research capabilities, that can be targeted by AI researchers (or potentially by automated capabilities researchers) Or just identifying good ideas for benchmarks, even if they aren’t fully implemented Automating direct alignment work As well as learning more about what it takes to make systems more aligned , sometimes we want to just make our actual systems as aligned as possible . This overlaps with empirical alignment work, but the emphasis is different: Empirical alignment work is science Direct alignment work is engineering Automating direct alignment work could include a lot of activities which leverage scalable cognition for alignment-relevant purposes. This could include careful auditing of particular RL environments or training data, or direct monitoring/supervision of systems during training. RLAIF for alignment properties is a form of automated direct alignment work; Claude 3 Opus’s apparent self-alignment was another (albeit accidental in that case; but if we knew how to reproduce or generalize the behaviour perhaps it could happen deliberately). I think that the limit of automating direct alignment work would be a form of system 2 learning , where updates are not made blindly towards a training objective, but reflectively by an AI system that was already sufficiently aligned (not necessarily having robustly good values already — just enough genuine care about being aligned, and honesty with itself, that its reflective updates tend to move it further in that direction), and wished to become more so — whatever the deep true version of aligned should mean [2] . Embarking on such a path could be fraught (because of difficulty in being confident that the starting conditions were in the right basin of attraction), but compared to other alignment approaches, it has the benefit that it might leverage the full strength of the AI’s cognition to help, so that its “self-improvement” in an alignment direction is a closer analogue to meditation than to self-performed neurosurgery. So, accelerating the automation of direct alignment work could include: Designing (and analysing) setups that can deploy AI labour to help with direct alignment work Designing paradigms (that could then be tested empirically) that allow AI to be a more active participant in its own alignment Producing data (or scaffolds) to help improve AI taste at the alignment-relevant tasks necessary for this Interactions These categories blur and interac

FindLink: Learning to Assess Scientific Connections from Source-Grounded Premises
items.description: arXiv:2611.02545v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific discovery from the literature requires assessing connections among findings obtained under different study conditions. Source attribution makes individual findings traceable, but does not determine what they jointly support. We introduce GI-TraceBench, a benchmark of 10,282 questions in gastrointestinal oncology that unifies provenance question answering, knowledge discovery, and hypothesis evaluation through shared Paper, Claim, and Evidence Span records. We further propose FindLink, a two-stage framework for provenance-grounded scientific reasoning. Premise Grounding constructs source-bound premises with explicit study context and support status. Structured Reasoning organizes these premises into support plans that represent both supported relations and unresolved conditions, then generates evidence-conditioned answers using deterministic compiler feedback. The compiler verifies structural and source-binding consistency, but does not assess scientific entailment. On the 1,545-question fixed-evidence test set, FindLink improves the balanced family macro score from 67.95 to 87.25 over direct supervised fine-tuning of the same backbone. A retrained variant without Structured Reasoning achieves slightly higher premise-identifier F1, but substantially lower relation and evidence-sufficiency F1. These results indicate that scientific reasoning requires not only identifying grounded premises, but also assessing what connections those premises support.

items.title: PathXAI: Evidence-guided structured pathology reporting by transferable tissue segmentation
items.description: arXiv:2611.09117v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Pathology reporting translates tissue observations across regions and slides into diagnoses and supporting morphological descriptions, yet explicit tissue-composition measurements are rarely used to guide H&E-based report generation. We developed PathXAI, which pairs transferable tissue segmentation with a pretrained vision-language model. Because supplying tissue information directly with H&E images gave limited benefit, PathXAI-Report uses segmentation overlays and tissue statistics in separate steps, selects between candidate diagnoses by fixed rules, acquires further images when evidence is insufficient and records every step for review, without updating model weights. Its segmentation component exceeded baselines in mean Dice on internal and external tests. In automated evaluation on 1,200 public and 151 private cases, PathXAI achieved higher agreement with reference diagnoses and documented morphology than H&E-based comparators. On the public cohort, it exceeded Qwen+H&E by 4.4 percentage points in cancer family match rate and 5.7 percentage points in finding F1.

items.title: BEiTScore++: Reference-free Image Captioning Evaluation with BEiT-3 and Conformalized Quantile Regression
items.description: arXiv:2611.09505v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Reliable uncertainty estimation is important for deploying evaluation metrics in real-world settings, where both input ambiguity and domain shifts are common. In this work, we propose an uncertainty-aware extension of the BEiTScore image captioning metric, producing conformally calibrated confidence intervals alongside alignment scores. Our approach models predictive distributions over human judgments, enabling both accurate scoring and principled uncertainty quantification in a single forward pass. We evaluate our BEiTScore++ metric across multiple benchmarks with human-annotated ratings, showing that it preserves the ranking correlation of BEiTScore, while producing intervals whose width tracks the prediction error more closely than Monte Carlo dropout on most benchmarks. The estimated uncertainty also grows under image degradation and on out-of-domain artwork images, making BEiTScore++ a practical tool for uncertainty-aware evaluation of image-caption alignment.

items.title: Reasoning Before Translation: Enhancing Legal Machine Translation with Structured Reasoning
items.description: arXiv:2607.19181v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) in the legal domain is a linguistically and conceptually demanding task, primarily due to the complexity of legal language and the high level of precision it requires. The recent emergence of reasoning-capable language models opens new possibilities for tackling such challenges. They add to a set of other previously proposed techniques to enhance the translation quality, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. In this work, we perform a comparison between these various approaches. More particularly, we evaluate small language models such as Qwen3.5 4B, Qwen3.5 9B, and Gemma 3 12B enhanced with various re-training paradigms and compare their performances against frontier reasoning models. We focus on the Swiss legal system, which -- with its unique multilingual statutes -- offers a particularly challenging testbed for reasoning-augmented models. Our results show that the quality of small ``base'' models can be greatly enhanced, and that reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can be applied to NMT in the legal domain and surpasses the translation quality of supervised fine-tuning. The performance of enhanced small models is close to the one of state-of-the-art reasoning models yet remains inferior. We also note that re-training paradigms yield diminishing returns as model size increase. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/aixiuxiuxiu/Legal-MT-SFT-RL.

items.title: Integrate the Reward, Don't Sample It: Window Likelihood for Interruptions and Backchannels in Full-Duplex Speech Models
items.description: arXiv:2610.35581v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When a user talks over a full-duplex dialogue model, it must decide whether the user is interrupting (stop) or backchannelling (carry on). Post-training can improve this discrimination or change how readily it stops. In our GRPO runs the second dominates: no configuration lowers both error rates on more than one model, and two released checkpoints discriminate no better than their bases. We trace this partly to how the reward is estimated. The probability of stopping inside a short window is a known function of a few stop probabilities the policy emits, yet GRPO estimates it by sampling. A group of rollouts that all agree gives no gradient, even when all fail; the push on the stop threshold is strongest where the model is unsure, whichever outcome is right; and whole-rollout credit reaches decisions the reward never judges. Confining the credit to the window removes only that leakage. Window likelihood (WL) samples the words but integrates over the stop decisions, so the probability of the correct outcome is computed exactly and its logarithm maximised. On HumDial-FDBench, across four open models, WL gives the best F1 and lowers both error rates by more than their confidence intervals, without talking into silence.

items.title: Circe: Training-Free LLM Self-Evaluation via Component Interaction Consistency
items.description: arXiv:2611.07948v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, evaluating the correctness of their responses is crucial for reliable use. However, such evaluation is challenging because reference answers are rarely available in practice. Existing reference-free methods mainly rely on output signals, which may assign high scores to incorrect responses and thus do not necessarily reflect correctness. This motivates exploring the model's internal computation for complementary correctness signals. Recent studies exploit internal states, but they mainly analyze hidden-state trajectories across layers, which record only the combined updates of attention and feed-forward networks (FFNs) and overlook how these components interact. We therefore propose Circe, a training-free self-evaluation method that assesses a response using both internal and external signals, without reference answers or repeated sampling. For internal signals, we first introduce component interaction consistency (CIC), which measures the directional alignment between attention updates in earlier layers and attention-induced FFN output changes in later layers. We further incorporate representation geometry (RG) to characterize normalized displacement and angular changes along layerwise hidden-state trajectories. For the external signal, we convert the mean negative log-likelihood of generated tokens into a bounded likelihood confidence (LC) score. Finally, we fuse CIC, RG, and LC into a unified correctness score. Experiments on five LLMs and six benchmarks across four domains show that our method distinguishes correct from incorrect responses more effectively than existing baselines, and generalizes to multilingual, multimodal, and open-world settings.

items.title: Selective Retrieval Routing for Multi-Violation Knowledge Graph Repair
items.description: arXiv:2611.07342v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Knowledge graphs often contain missing or inconsistent facts that undermine the applications built on them. Schema validation detects such violations but does not identify which of several valid repairs recovers the intended graph. External corpora can supply the evidence needed to identify the intended repair, but retrieving from them is costly and not always successful. We propose a framework for selective retrieval in iterative graph repair. An LLM repair agent explores and edits the graph, while a router controls its access to a researcher agent that retrieves external evidence. We extend a violation-injection framework to generate cases with multiple compatible violations and known reference repairs. The agent's repair outcomes on these cases provide supervision for training the deployment-specific router. On two building-automation datasets, researcher access improves repairs for some violations and degrades them for others, with effects differing across deployments. The router uses fewer repair-time tokens than always enabling access in all six evaluation suites. It achieves higher repair $F_1$ than always disabling access in five of six suites.

items.title: Towards Scalable Diagnostic-Driven Whole-Slide Image Retrieval for Pathology Archives
items.description: arXiv:2611.07935v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The growing adoption of digital pathology has rapidly expanded collections of hematoxylin-and-eosin whole-slide images, yet efficient navigation through these archives remains challenging, as metadata is often inconsistent or unavailable. Content-based image retrieval addresses this challenge by identifying similar cases directly from visual representations instead of manual annotations or metadata. Existing retrieval systems have demonstrated promising performance but largely rely on handcrafted indexing pipelines and predefined sampling strategies, constraining scalability and generalization. Here, we present CLEAR-WSI (Constant-Length Embedding for Automatic Retrieval of Whole-Slide Images) as a scalable, diagnostic-driven slide-retrieval framework, validated on both public and clinical data. Using a fixed-length slide embedding, CLEAR-WSI refines retrieved candidates with either a predicted diagnostic label or the ground-truth label, depending on the retrieval setting. Newly processed cases are subsequently added to the expanding memory bank, allowing the retrieval archive to grow over time. On a comprehensive benchmark consisting of two public and one private clinical datasets representing four retrieval tasks, CLEAR-WSI improves Precision@5 over the strongest evaluated baseline, with gains on CAMELYON16 (3.10), BRACS-1 (2.75), BRACS-2 (1.95), and X-HER2 (3.75). Additional ablation and latency studies further examine the contribution of each component and highlight its potential for scalable deployment.

items.title: Self-Improving Training & Thinking
items.description: arXiv:2601.21343v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models are classically trained in stages: pretraining on raw text followed by post-training for instruction following and reasoning. However, this separation creates a fundamental limitation: many desirable behaviors such as safety, factuality, overall generation quality, and reasoning ability are only added at a late stage, even though the patterns learned earlier strongly shape a model's capabilities. To tackle this issue, we introduce a new way to pretrain and mid-train models that incorporates these behaviors earlier. We utilize an existing strong, post-trained model to both rewrite data and to judge policy model rollouts, thus introducing thinking and reinforcement earlier in training. We further improve reasoning at all stages by introducing the concept of self-improving post-thinking: improving the model's reasoning and self-judging ability by reasoning after generation. In our experiments, we show these approaches can give strong gains across multiple axes.

items.title: Towards Foundation Decision Models: Drex
items.description: arXiv:2611.07854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: https://github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

items.title: Projection-Free Evolution Strategies for Continuous Prompt Search
items.description: arXiv:2603.13786v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Continuous prompt search offers a computationally efficient alternative to conventional parameter tuning in natural language processing tasks. Nevertheless, its practical effectiveness can be significantly hindered by the black-box nature and the inherent high-dimensionality of the objective landscapes. Existing methods typically mitigate these challenges by restricting the search to a randomly projected low-dimensional subspace. However, the effectiveness and underlying motivation of the projection mechanism remain ambiguous. In this paper, we first empirically demonstrate that despite the prompt space possessing a low-dimensional structure, random projections fail to adequately capture this essential structure. Motivated by this finding, we propose a projection-free prompt search method based on evolutionary strategies. By directly optimizing in the full prompt space with an adaptation mechanism calibrated to the intrinsic dimension, our method achieves competitive search capabilities without additional computational overhead. Furthermore, to bridge the generalization gap in few-shot scenarios, we introduce a confidence-based regularization mechanism that systematically enhances the model's confidence in the target verbalizers. Experimental results on seven natural language understanding tasks from the GLUE benchmark demonstrate that our proposed approach significantly outperforms existing baselines.

items.title: Volatility Heredity in Multivariate Time Series: A Statistically Guided Temporal Convolutional Approach to Variable Ordering
items.description: arXiv:2611.07746v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Volatility heredity concerns the information that past fluctuations in one series may carry about another after accounting for the target's own persistence. QS-TCN compares this dependence in both directions to estimate an order of temporal precedence. For each series, quasi-maximum likelihood estimation yields a persistence coefficient, and the matrix pencil method extracts temporal modes from the autocovariances of squared observations. These estimates define filters in a temporal convolutional network. The network models the target's squared observations from their own past and scores the association between the residuals and the filtered history of a candidate source. Differences between the two directional scores are aggregated into a global order. In an exploratory simulation with 100 systems in each of four volatility regimes, an ensemble of ten models trained with fixed seeds achieved higher mean ordering quality than CCF-AUC, a lead--lag method based on distance correlation, in every regime. Against CCF-AUC applied to squared standardized observations, the mean gains were 8.69 percentage points under positive linear coupling and 7.81 points when nonlinear coupling depended on the target's state. In the other two regimes, paired 95\% bootstrap intervals for the gains included zero. Mean agreement with reference constraints was 71.55\% across nine Finance systems and 54.02\% across 27 simulated functional magnetic resonance imaging systems, compared with 50\% expected under random ordering. In a panel of daily currency and gold returns, the estimated order placed the dollar--franc and dollar--yen exchange rates before gold.

items.title: ALTO: African and Levantine Tech-Facilitated Gender-Based Violence Corpus
items.description: arXiv:2611.06706v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Tech-facilitated gender based violence (TFGBV) is a pervasive online harm affecting women and gender minority groups through its many direct and covert forms. Current models and annotated datasets for gendered harm detection are dominated by data from, and models trained in, Global North languages. In collaboration with civil society organizations (CSOs) from Jordan, Francophone West Africa, and Kenya, we developed a community-led approach to crowdsource culturally and linguistically relevant instances of TFGBV in Levantine Arabic, African French, and Swahili. We annotated the crowdsourced data using active learning to develop a small but performant dataset (N=3022) called ALTO to improve TFGBV detection in the three languages. Through benchmarking and fine-tuning experiments, we show that existing harmful content detection models show poor TFGBV recall within ALTO and improve with fine-tuning. We found that models often miss covert harms across all languages, while error rates are markedly higher in Swahili. We report the experimental results and release the annotation taxonomy, dataset, and trained models.

items.title: Multi-User Large Language Model Agents
items.description: arXiv:2604.08567v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed as assistants in planning and decision making, yet most existing systems are implicitly optimized for a single-principal interaction paradigm, in which the model is designed to satisfy the objectives of one dominant user whose instructions are treated as the sole source of authority and utility. However, as they are integrated into team workflows and organizational tools, they are increasingly required to serve multiple users simultaneously, each with distinct roles, preferences, and authority levels, leading to multi-user, multi-principal settings with unavoidable conflicts, information asymmetry, and privacy constraints. In this work, we present the first systematic study of multi-user LLM agents. We begin by formalizing multi-user interaction with LLM agents as a multi-principal decision problem, where a single agent must account for multiple users with potentially conflicting interests and associated challenges. We then introduce a unified multi-user interaction protocol and design three targeted stress-testing scenarios to evaluate current LLMs' capabilities in instruction following, privacy preservation, and coordination. Our results reveal systematic gaps: frontier LLMs frequently fail to maintain stable prioritization under conflicting user objectives, exhibit increasing privacy violations over multi-turn interactions, and suffer from efficiency bottlenecks when coordination requires iterative information gathering.

items.title: Combining Relevant Expert Knowledge Using Mixtures of Feedback Fuzzy Cognitive Maps
items.description: arXiv:2611.05664v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A neuro-symbolic system should combine only relevant answers from expert agents or other knowledge sources. Using only relevant experts for a given input query becomes ever more important for accuracy and scalability as the knowledge network grows and connects ever more knowledge sources. We extend the standard definition of relevance from the legal theory of evidence: An answer is relevant if and only if it is both probative and material for the matter at hand given the knowledge available. We apply this relevancy scheme to mixing the feedback fuzzy cognitive maps (FCMs) of real or artificial experts. The expert FCM directed causal graphs mix or combine into a common knowledge network. We compare the equilibrium limit-cycle predictions or answers of the experts to the answers of the mixture FCM and then estimate the probative status of answers by their difference or variation. A new Bayes-like theorem de-mixes the knowledge mixture into corresponding posterior-like FCMs that also allow relevancy-based comparisons. The result is a final set of relevancy mixing weights that produces a relevancy-mixed FCM knowledge network for the given query. So different queries produce different relevancy-mixed FCMs. We demonstrate this relevancy approach using generated synthetic FCMs from an actual 13-node expert FCM that models the causes and feedbacks of ischemic-stroke risk.

items.title: CompressionBench: How can your coding agents compress LLMs?
items.description: arXiv:2611.06858v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recursive self-improvement requires AI systems to improve the models and infrastructure used by subsequent systems. LLM compression offers a concrete efficiency objective: retain a pretrained model's behavior within a smaller model storage budget. We study whether coding agents can carry out this step autonomously. We formulate compression as a terminal task in which an agent receives a source checkpoint, storage limit, inference environment, and time budget, then constructs compressed weights and executable inference code. The agent controls its algorithm and experiments; perplexity feedback guides search, and independent verification checks the final model. Across six agents and six model--size settings, 29 of 36 submissions pass verification. Selecting the lowest-perplexity agent design per task yields an average 3.4% perplexity increase over BF16 and 77.33% downstream accuracy, compared with 79.56% for BF16. Recorded experiments reveal how agents achieve these outcomes and where improvement breaks down. Agents lower PPL in 21 of 24 revisions at nearly fixed storage; complete-model feedback reverses 17 of 79 prior local rankings; and generation and inference tests expose failures that likelihood alone misses. The results identify representation design, experimental judgment, and capability validation as central to agent-driven model compression, a measurable component of efficiency-oriented self-improvement.

items.title: Recasting Visual Language Models as EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Neurodiagnostics
items.description: arXiv:2611.05538v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Historically automated electroencephalography (EEG) systems was done using task-specific supervised models trained on purposely annotated data. A more recent modeling paradigm relies on creating a unified representation, or a 'foundation model', for multiple modality-specific tasks through large-scale domain-specific pretraining on the unannotated EEG signal. The quality of this unified representation directly depends on the availability of the modality-specific datasets. At the same time, generalist Vision Language Models (VLMs) exhibit broad few-shot learning capacities as well as good fine-tuning adaptability to different visual and language tasks. Can VLMs learn how to read and interpret EEG visually, emulating to a degree the way human clinicians inspect the EEG patterns? In this work we make a case that they can: we show that generalist VLMs without large-scale EEG pretraining perform competitively across a collection of clinical neuro-diagnostic tasks, can adapt to different tasks in a few-shot learning setting better than specialist foundation models, and exhibit better performance with model scaling when modality-specific models fail to exhibit.

items.title: Distill to Think, Foresee to Act: Cognitive-Physical Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Driving
items.description: arXiv:2605.21139v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Current end-to-end autonomous driving models are fundamentally constrained by the behavioral cloning ceiling of imitation learning. While reinforcement learning offers a path to smarter autonomy, it demands two missing pieces of infrastructure: (1) a cognitive foundation that understands traffic semantics and driving intent, and (2) a foresighted physical environment that can anticipate the consequences of candidate actions. To this end, we propose CoPhy, a CognitivePhysical reinforcement learning framework for autonomous driving. To distill to think, we distill VLM knowledge into the BEV encoder and then discard the VLM entirely, retaining cognitive ability at zero inference cost while releasing the cognitive channel as a pluggable interface for optional human language commands. To foresee to act, we build an auto-regressive BEV world model that explicitly predicts future semantic maps conditioned on candidate actions, serving as an interpretable physical sandbox from which safety metrics are directly derived. Built upon this dual infrastructure, we optimize the driving policy via GRPO with a novel dual-reward mechanism: a physical reward derived from BEV rollouts enforces hard safety constraints, while a cognitive reward from a language-aligned scorer ensures intent compliance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoPhy not only achieves state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM v1 and v2 benchmarks, but also enables safer driving via cognitively informed scene compliance and flexible intent control through user-defined language instructions. Project page: https://wuyang98.github.io/CoPhy/.

items.title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
items.description: arXiv:2611.12933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.

items.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
items.description: arXiv:2611.12934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

items.title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
items.description: arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8

items.title: LandslideFM: A Foundation Model Towards Unified Landslide Perception and Understanding
items.description: arXiv:2611.12936v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.

items.title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
items.description: arXiv:2611.12937v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

items.title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
items.description: arXiv:2611.12938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
items.description: arXiv:2611.12940v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reinforcement Learning has achieved tremendous success in recent years. Extending its scope from the traditional complex games such as Atari, Go, Pokeman, and Chess, reinforcement learning has caught researchers' attention on modelling real-life scenarios. Personalized medicine and the dynamic treatment regimen are two such preliminary research fields; researchers are focusing their mindsets currently. Estimating the optimal dynamic treatment regimens from the observational real clinical data is being popularized among the researchers, widening its scope towards more advanced versions of reinforcement learning algorithms. This research is about a research study that focused on reinforcement learning techniques that have been approached in the context of cancer chemotherapy treatments. Primarily this thesis addresses the result of the study by means of the state-of-the-art on reinforcement learning techniques used in generating the optimal policy for sequential treatments, including the existing online reinforcement learning approaches. Thereby a simulation for cancer chemotherapy via traditional Q-learning would be presented. Secondly, the study will extend towards using offline reinforcement learning in the optimal policy generation. Thus, the proposed solution follows a data-driven approach, which works on the real human colon cancer clinical data. The novelty of the proposed solution resides in the implementation of an offline reinforcement learning approach by means of a model-based architecture using the conservative Q-learning and the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm. As per the experimental results and the evaluations, it was revealed that the proposed Chemo RL model caters well the problem of cancer chemotherapy treatment scheduling and serves as a supportive model for the junior oncologists in deciding their treatment decisions.

items.title: AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence
items.description: arXiv:2611.12941v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomously acting AI agents makes the governance of agentic systems urgent. We propose the competence circuit, summarized as IKC + KC + C, that decomposes an agent's real-world impact into three pathways: intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. Using the canonical fast-takeoff debate as a stress test, we formalize the conditions for intelligence-mediated fast takeoff as a conjunction jointly sufficient for fast catastrophic supremacy, showing that most rely on rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence alone. We operationalize epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and validate this framework via stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios spanning the conjunctive chain. An analytic bound supported by the simulations shows that intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty. The simulations also expose a fast-takeoff dilemma: a large intelligence-driven speedup multiplier materializes only when the hypothesis space is noisy, but the absolute timescale remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical tests, so a large multiplier need not imply rapid progress. Simulations also indicate that institutional chokepoints disproportionately slow down superintelligent agents when mandatory authorization delays are large relative to the negligible time these agents spend on unproductive search. We argue that the dominant safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone, and this applies to agentic systems at any capability level. Purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks, strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally "put physics in the loop."

items.title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
items.description: arXiv:2611.12942v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict from a labelled context in a single forward pass. A recent benchmark reported that they decisively outperform tree ensembles for customer churn, but it compared them with untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and scored only ranking metrics, while a retention campaign is judged in money. We re-evaluate TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast and TabICL v2 against Optuna-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits. We separate three questions: whether a model ranks churners well, whether that ranking earns more expected maximum profit (EMP), and whether its probabilities can drive a threshold policy. With a split-aware test and Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%), and these two gains also hold against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. On Orange it is ahead in all 10 splits (14.3%), but the gain is not significant after correction (Holm p = 0.155). The splits resample the same datasets, so these results do not stand for independent operators. TabICL v2, the earlier benchmark's leader, beats the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, not all three of them, and underpredicts Orange churn by 2.1 points on a 7.3% base rate. On the datasets and splits where we tested them, a substantially larger tuning budget and a duplicate-aware split leave the main conclusions unchanged. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it. The licence of the TabPFN-3.5 weights we used (License v1.0), not scoring cost, is what stands between its gains and production use.

items.title: SetPrint: Black-Box LLM Fingerprinting via Setwise Correspondence of Response Changes
items.description: arXiv:2611.12950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Black-box LLM fingerprinting aims to determine whether a target model was derived from a source model when only the output responses to input queries are observable. One way to reveal this relationship is to perturb each query and observe the resulting responses of both models, yielding two corresponding sets of response variations. These sets provide two complementary sources of information: the relations among response changes within each set, and the correspondence of response changes between the two sets. Existing approaches, however, have not fully exploited both. We introduce \textbf{SetPrint}, a training-free method that jointly captures both within-set relations and between-set correspondence. SetPrint expresses each response change relative to the mean change of its own set, and then compares changes from the two models that were induced by the same perturbation. On LeaFBench, SetPrint consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods. Further analyses attribute these gains to both within-set relations and between-set correspondence.

items.title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
items.description: arXiv:2611.12953v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).

items.title: Physics2Weight: Direct Neural Network Architecture and Weight Generation from Physical Laws Using Large Language Models
