items.title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
items.description: This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's. This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period. You can adjust various axes of this proposal: Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition. What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints. When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed. One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.” This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”. What does this look like when implemented? Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end. A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use. The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang. More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time. A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models. In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days]. The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally without the below rules. All work has to be fully transparent to auditors. Options for how the X days are structured: Staged testing Stage 1, first part of X: pre-registered evals and named testers in an isolated environment. Stage 2, second part of X: broad monitored internal use, but the model can’t launch jobs, merge code, write to training data, or touch prod. Parallel, hidden runs: whenever someone at the developer uses a cleared model, the new checkpoint gets the same task in a separate sandboxed copy of the environment. Its outputs go only to monitors and the safety team, never back to the person who asked. Open questions The rule itself Should we also allow capability testing? What about ML R&D tasks? One way to game this is to register thousands of tasks from your open R&D backlog, and call running them a capability eval. The outputs are real research (e.g. a faster kernel), and even if you ban using them, people still have to read the transcripts to grade them, so they learn what worked. Pre-registering evals doesn’t help, since it fixes the task list in advance but doesn’t check whether the tasks are live problems. You might end up needing a compute cap. Should we give exemptions for doing safety research? This is an important crux to ask alignment researchers about. Without an exemption, safety research is done with a model that is X days behind, but a blanket exemption lets capabilities work pose as safety work. Should a safety fix (e.g. more post-training, or redoing RL from an earlier checkpoint) restart the X-day wait? It would be bad if it did, as Avi Brach-Neufeld points out here . A developer that finds an issue on day 8 of testing loses more time than one that finds it on day 2, so the rule penalizes finding and fixing problems during the wait. This is probably tolerable at small X, but gets worse as X increases. If safety fixes don’t restart the clock, however, developers could just call capabilities training “safety”. What is the principle behind how much X increases? How large is the risk that an emergency clause would be abused? Concerning behaviours aren’t necessarily caught during pre-deployment testing windows, and are often caught through subsequent monitored internal use. How much are we willing to trade off the value of catching some misaligned behaviours via monitoring internal deployments, vs. being able to pace internal R&D? Which models are covered How is “substantially more capable” defined: effective compute, or something like the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI)? How would an auditor check that the developer has faithfully stuck to the “more capable” definition? How do you avoid bringing classifiers built using a frontier model into scope? Can a developer keep using earlier checkpoints from a family after it becomes covered? A developer could train a second model family and keep it just under the “substantially more capable” line, so it’s never covered. Researchers could then use that family right away,

items.title: Build a daily dependency watcher with LangGraph and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore web search
items.description: AI agents increasingly handle work that depends on what changed today, such as security advisories, product releases, prices, and regulations. A model’s training data can’t answer those questions, so agents need web search. For production use, teams also need results they can cite, and control over which sources count. They want search queries to stay inside their cloud environment because those queries often reveal internal work. The Web Search API in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is now available. It gives agents and applications current web results through a single API call, signed with the AWS credentials they already use. AWS serves every query from a web index that Amazon operates, and doesn’t send it to a third-party search engine. Each result includes the page’s title, URL, publication date, and an extract relevant to the query. Requests can include or exclude domains, and limit results to a publication date range. On AWS Lambda , Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) , or Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime , your agent calls the API with its execution role. There’s no search API key to store or rotate. Web Search on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is also available through AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. There, one administrator source policy covers every agent and Model Context Protocol (MCP) client. For LangChain developers, the AgentCore web search tool in LangChain’s AWS integration now calls the Web Search API. One function call gives an agent current, cited search results. The tool can also hold rules that the model can’t change, such as a date window, a source blocklist, and a search budget. It returns its results as data that your code can check. It works with LangChain agents, with LangGraph , the orchestration framework that runs them, and with Deep Agents , which adds subagents, a virtual filesystem, and context compression. In this post, you build a daily dependency watch for a security team as a LangGraph graph on the Web Search API. Every morning, the watch checks whether anything new affects the open source packages and container base images the team ships. It researches three package ecosystems in parallel, while your code keeps the date window, the blocklist, and the search budget out of the model’s control. It checks each finding against the sources it cites and remembers what it already reported. Then you run the watch on AgentCore runtime, and offer it across teams through AgentCore Gateway. In our test, the three branches finished in 36 seconds, against 99 seconds one after another. Solution overview The model decides what to search for and writes the findings. Every rule that must hold, whatever the model does, stays in code: the date window, the blocklist, the search budget, and the checks on each finding. Figure 1 shows how these parts fit together when you run the watch from the notebook. Figure 1: A daily dependency watch with LangGraph and the Web Search API, run from a notebook The numbered steps: A run starts the graph with the watchlist and the watch window. fan_out starts one research branch per ecosystem: npm, PyPI, and container base images. LangGraph runs the three branches in parallel. Inside each branch, the agent calls an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock . The model decides what to search for and, at the end, produces structured findings. The branch’s search tool adds the date window and the blocklist to each query. It calls the Web Search API with a request signed with AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) . Steps 3 and 4 repeat, up to four searches per branch, in every branch at the same time. Each branch keeps only findings that its sources support and that fall inside the window. When all three branches finish, LangGraph merges their findings and runs keep_new once. keep_new checks the LangGraph store and records new findings, so nothing is reported twice. report builds the cited table of new findings for the security team. Prerequisites Before you start, you need the following: An AWS account, working in an AWS Region that offers the Web Search API. The examples use the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1). For other Regions, see Supported AWS Regions . Python 3.10 or later. AWS credentials for the identity that runs the notebook, from environment variables or an AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) profile. That identity needs the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permission from Step 1 and access to an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock. The following Python packages: boto3 1.43.127 or later, the AgentCore Python SDK (bedrock-agentcore) 1.26.0 or later, and langchain-aws 1.9.3 or later. Install them with this pip command: pip install -U "boto3>=1.43.127" "bedrock-agentcore>=1.26.0" "langchain-aws[tools]>=1.9.3" langchain langgraph Web Search and model calls are billed per use. For details, see Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . One run of the watch makes at most 12 searches. The complete code is in this notebook . The notebook runs every cell, including setup. The following steps cover the parts that matter for search. Step 1: Grant the permission First, give the identity you run as permission to search. The Web Search API needs one IAM action on one resource that AWS owns, so the statement is the same in every account. (For the full setup, see Grant permission to call the API .) This uses the same permission that a gateway’s service role uses for web search: { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": "bedrock-agentcore:InvokeWebSearch", "Resource": "arn:aws:bedrock-agentcore:us-east-1:aws:tool/web-search.v1" } Step 2: Build a search tool with fixed rules Now build the search tool that each research branch uses. The watch can’t let the model choose the date window, the trusted sources, or the number of searches. The graph also needs the returned sources as data, to check findings against them later. items.title: The agent evaluation playbook: Built-in, DeepEval, and AutoEval on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations
items.description: When you deploy an agent to production, one of the hardest questions is whether it’s actually working? The bar isn’t whether it runs. It’s whether it does what the business needs, at scale. Many teams will tell you they can’t really see this. They spot-check outputs, watch latency, and collect user feedback when they can get it. None of that tells you whether the agent finished the user’s task, stayed on topic across a long session, leaked personally identifiable information (PII), or quietly skipped half the steps it was supposed to follow. Figure 1: Teams usually watch surface signals, but business outcomes are decided by the agent behaviors below the waterline Agent evaluation solves this problem. What makes this challenging is that a good score on one metric can hide a failure on another. A support agent can resolve every ticket and still expose personal information in its replies. In this case, the agent is failing although it has a high completion rate. To get evaluation right, measure the behaviors that matter for each agent, at the right level of detail. This post shows how to do this on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We use the AgentCore built-in evaluators together with the DeepEval and AutoEval evaluators directly from AgentCore Evaluations. Start with business outcomes, instead of metric names The most common mistake is to start with the metric list and pick the names that sound right. “Helpfulness sounds good, so we use it.” The result runs and produces numbers, but it gives almost no useful insight. The metric fits its label, not what success means for the agent. Instead, start with three steps. Define success in business terms. For a customer support agent, that might be first-contact resolution. For a research agent, it might be producing a complete, well-sourced answer grounded entirely in retrieved documents. For a content moderation assistant, it means flagging everything that should be flagged and only what should be flagged. Break the outcome into observable behaviors. A customer support agent that achieves first-contact resolution will typically complete the user’s stated goal, stay coherent across turns when the issue requires clarification, keep responses within compliance boundaries, and correctly invoke backend tools like ticket creation or order lookup. Map each behavior to an evaluator at the right level. Trace-level metrics cover per-turn or per-tool-call behaviors. Session-level metrics cover outcomes that only make sense when you look at the whole conversation. Figure 2: Translating a business outcome into observable behaviors and then into specific evaluators at the trace or session level This three-step process is the mental model that makes evaluation useful. The rest of this post is about what AgentCore gives you to execute it. The evaluator catalog AgentCore has a broad catalog of evaluators from three sources: Built-in evaluators are authored and quality-tested by AWS. You reference them by their ID ( Builtin.GoalSuccessRate , Builtin.Helpfulness , and 13 more) and the service handles everything else. They are benchmarked for reliability and cover the common dimensions, so they are the straightforward place to start. Third-party managed evaluators come from DeepEval and AutoEval , two established open-source evaluation libraries. When you use them in managed mode, AgentCore hosts the code, picks the judge model, and runs inference on its own capacity, exactly like built-in evaluators. If your team already uses one of these libraries in development, you can run the same metrics in production without a separate evaluation service. Custom evaluators take a built-in or third-party evaluator as a base, so you can swap in your own model and modify the prompt or rubric. Figure 3: The three evaluator tiers trade AWS quality assurance for increasing control over the model and account that run inference After creation, a custom derived evaluator is used exactly like other ones. The evaluator landscape AgentCore ships with a broad catalog of evaluators, so you rarely start from a blank page. Before you write a custom judge, check whether one already measures the behavior you care about. The following figure shows the whole landscape. Figure 4: The full evaluator landscape on AgentCore across built-in, DeepEval, AutoEval, and custom sources Built-in AWS evaluators fall into five groups: Response quality covers whether the answer is accurate, grounded, and well-formed: Correctness , Faithfulness , Helpfulness , ResponseRelevance , Conciseness , Coherence , InstructionFollowing , and Refusal . Task and goal completion has GoalSuccessRate , which looks at the whole session and asks whether the user’s goal was met. Tool use has ToolSelectionAccuracy and ToolParameterAccuracy , which check whether the agent picked the right tool and passed it the right arguments. Skills has SkillSelectionAccuracy and SkillInstructionFollowing , for agents that load skills: was the right skill invoked, and were its steps followed? Safety has Harmfulness and Stereotyping . Next to these are three ground-truth trajectory checks: TrajectoryExactOrderMatch , TrajectoryInOrderMatch , and TrajectoryAnyOrderMatch . They compare the agent’s actual tool path against the one you expected. Reach for them when how the agent got there matters as much as what it produced. DeepEval provides managed open-source metrics in four groups: Task and goal completion: TaskCompletion , GoalAccuracy , and ConversationCompleteness . Conversational quality: TurnRelevancy , KnowledgeRetention , and Summarization . Tool use: ToolUse . Safety: Bias , Toxicity , and PIILeakage . These metrics are especially useful for multi-turn agents. ConversationCompleteness catches an agent that answers the latest message but quietly drops earlier requests. items.title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
items.description: Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows. The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it. You had one job Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals. items.title: What happens to mathematics when AI becomes an oracle?
items.description: Our modern world runs on math, from social media algorithms, package delivery, and weather prediction to medical imaging and machine learning. The rise of computers helped fuel its dominance, enabling us to work with increasingly large numbers that would otherwise be beyond the capacity of our finite human brains. But with the rise of large language models, AI chatbots, and, soon, quantum computing, so-called "big math" is beginning to outstrip its creators entirely. What that means , and how we might adapt, is the focus of a new book, Big Math: The Hidden Codes That Run Our World , by applied mathematicians Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend. Strogatz is perhaps best known in his field for his co-authorship of a seminal 1998 paper with Duncan Watts on the collective dynamics of small-world networks. He has also studied chaos theory as applied to physics, the geometry of supercoiled DNA, and the biological collective oscillators, such as swarms of synchronously flashing fireflies and crickets that chirp in unison. In 2005, Strogatz extended his study of synchronicity to the crowds that caused the wobbling of London's Millennium Bridge . An award-winning communicator, Strogatz wrote three series of columns on mathematics for The New York Times in 2010, 2012, and 2025 and hosted a podcast for Quanta magazine from 2020–2021. He has written four popular books: Sync (2003), The Calculus of Friendship (2009), The Joy of X (2012), and the New York Times bestseller Infinite Powers (2019). Read full article Comments

items.title: Autonomous treasury agents: How Trovata built an AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock and AgentCore
items.description: Corporate treasury teams face a persistent challenge: fragmented banking data scattered across dozens of bank portals, manual reporting trapped in spreadsheets, and legacy Treasury Management Systems (TMS) that can’t scale for modern enterprise needs. For treasury teams these manual processes create delays, errors, and an inability to make real-time cash decisions when they matter most. Trovata is an AI-native cash and liquidity management platform with direct connections to over 10,000 banks, serving enterprises globally from a single cloud-based platform. In 2023, Trovata launched the first generative AI built specifically for treasury. Now, with Trovata’s latest AI-native updates, they’ve evolved from delivering insights to deploying autonomous agents that act on behalf of treasury teams. Trovata’s customers have seen measurable results: $1M+ in annualized cost savings, over 5 hours per day saved per accounting team, a 77 percent reduction in annual TMS costs, and treasury reporting reduced from hours or days to under a minute. In this post, we explore how Trovata built autonomous treasury agents on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, the architecture secured with role-based access control (RBAC) that supports bank-branded AI deployment, and how agentic workflows are transforming corporate treasury from manual operations to real-time decision-making at enterprise scale. Solution overview Trovata operates as an AI-native treasury operating system, providing direct connections to over 10,000 banks through a single system for cash reporting, forecasting, analysis, and money movement. Treasury teams today face a three-pressure problem: Fragmented banking data across multiple portals, requiring manual aggregation and reconciliation. Manual reporting and reconciliation consuming hours or even days of skilled team members’ time. Legacy TMS applications that lack cloud-native architecture and AI capabilities needed for modern operations. Trovata’s evolution from its first generative AI for treasury in 2023 to its AI-native capabilities with autonomous agents represents a fundamental shift. The solution moves from static insights to persistent agentic workflows that operate continuously on behalf of treasury teams. Critically, Trovata AI is built directly into the treasury operating system. It’s not a generic chatbot layered on top, but embedded intelligence tied to real treasury objects with a governed path to automation through agents. Trovata chose AWS for this transformation for three reasons. Its serverless, cloud-native infrastructure supports real-time execution, Amazon Bedrock provides large language model (LLM) inference for natural language queries and AI features, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore handles agent orchestration with RBAC security, rapid deployment, and global scale. The core AWS services powering Trovata’s AI-native solution include: Amazon Bedrock – LLM inference for natural language understanding and generation. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Agent orchestration, agentic workflows, and RBAC security. Serverless AWS infrastructure – Real-time execution at enterprise scale. Architecture diagram The Trovata AI architecture centers on autonomous treasury agents operating within a bank-branded, RBAC-secured framework. The solution comprises several key components working together: Trovata AI Chat – Natural language querying of multi-bank treasury data, so users can ask questions like “What was our net cash position across all accounts yesterday?” and receive instant, accurate responses. AI Insights – Automated anomaly detection, variance explanation, and trend analysis that surfaces critical information proactively. AI Agents – Persistent workflows running on schedules, triggers, or rules to monitor activity, explain variance, detect anomalies, and deliver updates automatically, without human intervention. Agent Builder-Configurator – A management console for building and configuring treasury agents, giving teams full control over agent behavior and scope. Enterprise RBAC – Role-based access control securing agentic workflows, making sure that agents operate within the same permission boundaries as human users. Figure 1: Trovata AI architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, from the bank-branded portal through to multi-bank connectivity Technical implementation Trovata built its AI-native solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, combining autonomous agents, natural language querying, and enterprise access controls. The following sections describe what the team built, the primary use cases, and the AgentCore capabilities behind it. What Trovata built: AI-native solution Trovata AI delivers autonomous treasury management agents embedded directly within the Trovata treasury operating system. These AI agents turn repeatable operational work into persistent workflows that run continuously. This is the work that consumes hours of skilled professionals’ time. Agents operate on schedules, triggers, or rules to monitor activity, explain variance, detect anomalies, and deliver updates automatically. The entire system runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a secure, isolated environment purpose-built for enterprise AI. When a user asks a question, the AI retrieves data through Trovata’s own verified API layer, analyzes it, and presents the response within that secure infrastructure. Primary use cases Cash forecasting – Automated cash flow forecasting across multi-bank environments with scenario modeling, replacing manual spreadsheet-based projections. Natural language querying – Enterprise users query bank data in plain English. For example: “What was our net cash position across all accounts yesterday?” . Anomaly detection – Real-time detection of unusual transactions, balance changes, or cash flow patterns that might indicate errors, fraud, or operational issues. Automated reconciliation – AI-powered reconciliation summaries across hundreds of accounts, reducing what previously took hours

items.title: 求人原稿をAIエージェントで作る5ステップ 応募につながる書き方のコツ！
items.description: 求人原稿を書こうとしても仕事内容の整理だけで時間が過ぎ、書き上げても応募が集まらない。兼務で採用を担う担当者ほど、この悩みを抱えやすいでしょう。 求人原稿の作成は、 AIエージェントに採用要件と過去原稿を渡す ことで、初稿づくりから媒体別の書き分けまでを任せられます。ChatGPTに一度だけ依頼する使い方とは違い、複数の工程を段取りして進める点が特徴です。 一方で、AIが出した原稿をそのまま公開すれば、他社と同じ無個性な表現や、誤った労働条件の掲載につながります。応募が来ないだけでなく、法令違反として信頼を損なうリスクもあります。 本記事では、求人原稿をAIエージェントで作る5ステップを中心に、職種別のプロンプト例と公開前に押さえる注意点を解説します。 読み終える頃には、自社の採用要件から媒体別の求人原稿までをAIと分担して作り、人が確認すべき箇所を迷わず判断できるようになります。 求人原稿をAIエージェントで作る5ステップ 求人原稿の作成は、次の5ステップで進められます。 ステップ1：採用要件と求人情報を渡す ステップ2：過去原稿と競合求人を読み込ませる ステップ3：原稿の初稿を生成する ステップ4：媒体別に書き分ける ステップ5：人が事実確認して公開する AIに任せるのは1から4で、5だけは必ず人が担います。この分担を守れば、時間を削りながら誤掲載を防げます。 ステップ1：採用要件と求人情報を渡す 最初に、採用したい人物像と労働条件をAIエージェントに渡します。AIは入力された情報の範囲でしか書けないため、ここが原稿の質を左右します。 渡す情報は次の4点にまとめると過不足がありません。 職種名と仕事内容 必須スキルと歓迎スキル 給与・勤務地・勤務時間などの労働条件 求める人物像と配属先の雰囲気 箇条書きのメモで構いません。 文章に整える作業まで人が行う必要はない ため、現場マネージャーへのヒアリング内容をそのまま貼り付けられます。 ステップ2：過去原稿と競合求人を読み込ませる 次に、自社の過去の求人原稿と、同じ職種で募集している他社の求人を読み込ませます。前者は自社らしい文体を、後者は差別化の材料をAIに与えるための工程です。 過去原稿が反応を得られたものだけを選ぶと、AIが踏襲する表現の質が上がります。競合求人は、競合が強調している条件と書いていない条件の両方を見比べさせるのがコツです。 求人票作成用のAIエージェントが過去の求人票を参照して項目を事前入力する仕組みは、ServiceNowの公式ドキュメントでも紹介されています。 > Use AI agents to create job requisition（ServiceNow）はこちらから ステップ3：原稿の初稿を生成する 材料がそろったら、仕事内容・応募条件・待遇・職場の魅力といった構成ごとに初稿を出力させます。 全体を一度に書かせず、項目ごとに出力させる と、修正点を特定しやすくなります。 このとき、トーンや禁止事項も指示に含めます。たとえば「誇張表現は使わない」「数字は入力情報にあるものだけを使う」と明記すると、事実と異なる記述を減らせます。 初稿は完成品ではなく、たたき台です。担当者は、ゼロから書く負担が消えた状態で、内容の取捨選択に集中できます。 ステップ4：媒体別に書き分ける 同じ職種でも、求人サイト・自社の採用ページ・SNSでは読者の状況が異なります。AIエージェントに媒体ごとの特徴を伝え、1つの初稿から複数の版を作らせます。 求人サイト：条件を網羅し、検索で見つけられるよう職種名と勤務地を明確にする 自社の採用ページ：事業の方向性や社員の声を加え、志望動機につなげる SNS：短い文量で職場の様子や仕事の面白さを伝える 媒体ごとの書き分けは手作業だと最も時間がかかる工程です。 1つの要件から複数の版を同時に出せる ことが、AIエージェントを使う利点です。 ステップ5：人が事実確認して公開する 公開前に、給与・勤務地・勤務時間などの条件が社内の正式な情報と一致しているかを人が確認します。AIは事実と異なる内容をもっともらしく書くことがあるためです。 確認の対象は、数字、固有名詞、条件の例外規定の3点です。差別につながる表現が混じっていないかも、この段階で見ます。 最終確認を人が担うことで、AIの速さを生かしながら、原稿の責任の所在を明確に保てます。 求人原稿の作成にAIエージェントを使う3つのメリット 求人原稿の作成にAIエージェントを使うメリットは、次の3つです。 原稿の作成時間を短縮できる 担当者による品質のばらつきを抑えられる 応募状況に合わせた改善を回しやすい この3点を押さえると、導入で何が変わるかを社内に説明しやすくなります。 原稿の作成時間を短縮できる AIエージェントは、要件の整理、初稿の作成、媒体別の書き分けを一続きで担います。ゼロから書く工程と、媒体ごとに書き直す工程が減ります。 担当者は空いた時間を、採用要件の見直しや候補者への対応に回せます。 手を動かす作業から、判断する作業に比重が移る ことが最大の変化です。 担当者による品質のばらつきを抑えられる 求人原稿は、書く人の経験で出来が大きく変わりがちです。AIエージェントに自社の過去原稿と書き方の基準を覚えさせれば、誰が依頼しても一定の水準で初稿が出ます。 担当者が交代しても文体がぶれにくく、 採用ブランドの一貫性 を保ちやすくなります。 応募状況に合わせた改善を回しやすい 応募が少ないときに、原稿の見出しや訴求点を変えた版をすぐに作れます。手作業なら数日かかる改稿を短い間隔で繰り返せるため、反応を見ながら調整できます。 どの表現が応募につながったかを記録しておけば、次の募集にも生かせます。改善の知見が担当者個人でなく、社内の資産として残ります。 求人原稿の作成に使えるプロンプト例3選 AIエージェントに最初に渡す指示は、職種ごとに押さえる点が異なります。次の3職種のプロンプトを用意しました。 【営業職】 【エンジニア職】 【店舗スタッフ】 【】の部分を自社の情報に置き換えて、そのまま貼り付けて使えます。 【営業職】新規開拓型のプロンプト 営業職は、扱う商材と顧客層、評価の仕組みが応募者の判断材料になります。成果の評価基準を必ず入れるよう指示します。 あなたは採用広報の専門家です。以下の情報から、営業職の求人原稿を作成してください。 【会社概要】【事業内容を2〜3行で記載】 【職種】法人営業（新規開拓） 【仕事内容】【担当する商材、顧客層、1日の流れ】 【必須スキル】【記載】 【歓迎スキル】【記載】 【評価の仕組み】【記載】 【労働条件】【給与、勤務地、勤務時間、休日】 条件： ・入力した情報に無い数字や制度は書かない ・誇張表現を使わない ・見出しは「仕事内容」「応募条件」「待遇」「この仕事の魅力」の4つ ・です・ます調で書く 出力後は、評価の仕組みが実際の制度と一致しているかを確認します。 入力にない制度を補って書かれていないか を見る点が重要です。 【エンジニア職】開発メンバーのプロンプト エンジニア職は、技術スタックと開発体制が応募者の最大の関心事です。使う言語やツールを具体的に渡し、抽象的な表現を避けさせます。 あなたは採用広報の専門家です。以下の情報から、エンジニアの求人原稿を作成してください。 【会社概要】【事業内容を2〜3行で記載】 【職種】バックエンドエンジニア 【開発している製品】【記載】 【技術スタック】【言語、フレームワーク、インフラ】 【開発体制】【チーム人数、開発手法、レビュー体制】 【必須スキル】【記載】 【労働条件】【給与、勤務地、働き方、勤務時間】 条件： ・技術名は入力した表記のまま使う ・「成長できる環境」など中身のない表現は使わない ・技術的な挑戦や裁量の内容を具体的に書く ・です・ます調で書く 技術名の表記ゆれは応募者の信頼に響きます。 技術名を入力どおりに使わせる指示 を入れておくと、誤記を防げます。 【店舗スタッフ】接客職のプロンプト 店舗スタッフの募集では、勤務時間帯やシフトの柔軟性、研修の有無が応募の決め手になります。働き方のイメージを湧かせる記述を求めます。 あなたは採用広報の専門家です。以下の情報から、店舗スタッフの求人原稿を作成してください。 【店舗の特徴】【業態、客層、店舗の雰囲気】 【仕事内容】【接客、レジ、品出しなど】 【シフト】【勤務時間帯、週の勤務日数、シフトの決め方】 【研修】【内容、期間】 【労働条件】【時給、交通費、勤務地、休日】 条件： ・未経験者が不安に感じやすい点に先回りして答える ・入力した情報に無い数字や制度は書かない ・1日の流れが想像できる文章を入れる ・です・ます調で書く 未経験者が不安に感じる点に先回りさせると、応募のハードルが下がります。ただし、研修内容などの事実は必ず現場の情報と照合してください。 求人原稿を作るAIは3タイプから選ぶ 求人原稿の作成に使えるAIは、汎用生成AI・求人特化ツール・採用管理一体型の3タイプに分けられます。 タイプ 向いている企業 強み 弱み 汎用生成AI まず試したい企業 無料プランから試せ、指示の自由度が高い プロンプトの設計と事実確認を自社で担う 求人特化ツール 原稿作成を定常業務にしたい企業 求人向けの入力項目が用意されている 対応する媒体や機能がツールごとに異なる 採用管理一体型 採用業務全体を効率化したい企業 応募者管理や日程調整と連携できる 導入と運用の負担が大きい 自社の採用規模と、AIに任せたい業務の範囲で選びます。以下で各タイプを解説します。 【汎用生成AI】ChatGPTやGeminiなどを使う ChatGPTやGeminiといった汎用の生成AIは、求人原稿の作成にも使えます。 無料プランのあるサービスなら、費用をかけずに試せる 点が最大の利点です。 一方で、入力項目の設計や過去原稿の管理は自社で行う必要があります。無料プランの利用条件は各サービスの公式情報で確認してください。 【求人特化ツール】求人原稿の作成に特化したサービスを使う 求人原稿の作成に特化したWebサービスは、職種や条件を入力するだけで原稿が出るよう、入力項目があらかじめ整えられています。プロンプトを考える手間が省けます。 対応する媒体や、過去原稿の読み込み機能の有無はサービスごとに異なります。導入前に、自社が使う求人媒体に合う形式で出力できるかを確かめましょう。 【採用管理一体型】採用業務全体を扱うAIエージェントを使う 採用管理システムと連携するタイプは、求人原稿の作成に加え、応募者の管理や日程調整までを一続きで扱えます。採用業務全体を効率化したい企業に向きます。 採用業務全体にわたるAIエージェントの種類とおすすめのサービスは、別記事で詳しくまとめています。求人原稿の作成だけが目的なら、前の2タイプで足りることが多いでしょう。 AIが作った求人原稿で応募が集まらない原因と対策 AIで作った原稿でも応募が伸びないときは、次の3つの原因が考えられます。 仕事内容が抽象的になっている 自社の魅力が他社と同じ表現になっている 求める人物像と原稿の訴求がずれている 原因を切り分ければ、AIへの指示を直すだけで改善できる場合があります。 仕事内容が抽象的になっている 入力情報が少ないと、AIは「幅広い業務に携わる」のような一般的な表現でその場を埋めます。応募者は具体的な業務を知りたいため、抽象的な原稿は判断材料にならず離脱されます。 対策は、1日の流れや担当する案件の具体例を入力に加えることです。 具体的な業務の描写を渡す ほど、原稿の説得力が上がります。 自社の魅力が他社と同じ表現になっている AIは一般的な求人の言い回しを学習しているため、指示が弱いと「アットホームな職場」のような、どの会社にも当てはまる表現が出やすくなります。 対策は、自社ならではの事実を材料として渡すことです。社員の声や職場のエピソードを入力し、 他社が使わない言葉で魅力を伝える よう指示します。 求める人物像と原稿の訴求がずれている 求めるスキルや経験の人に響かない訴求だと、応募の数も質も伸びません。たとえば経験者を求めるのに、未経験歓迎の文脈を強調した原稿では、応募者層がずれます。 対策は、ステップ1で人物像を明確に渡し、 誰に向けた原稿かを指示の冒頭に書く ことです。応募後の面接で見られた応募者の傾向を、次の原稿に反映させれば精度が上がります。 求人原稿をAIで作るときの注意点 求人原稿の作成にAIを使うときは、次の3つの点に注意が必要です。 誤った条件を載せると法令違反のおそれがある 応募者の個人情報などを入力しない 社内の生成AI利用ルールを確認する この3点を押さえておけば、AIの速さを安全に生かせます。 誤った条件を載せると法令違反のおそれがある 2022年10月1日に施行された職業安定法の改正で、求人等に関する情報の的確な表示が義務化されました。 虚偽や誤解を生じさせる条件を原稿に載せてはいけません 。 出典： 職業安定法の改正について（厚生労働省） AIが条件をもっともらしく補って書いた場合も、公開した企業の責任になります。給与や勤務時間、固定残業代の有無など、誤解されやすい項目は、公開前に人が社内の正式な情報と照合してください。 表示すべき項目の詳細は、厚生労働省の公表資料で確認できます。 応募者の個人情報などを入力しない 求人原稿の作成に、応募者の氏名や履歴書の内容は必要ありません。AIに入力した情報は、サービスによっては学習に使われたり、外部に保存されたりします。 入力するのは、職種・条件・社内の公開済み情報に限りましょう。 非公開の経営情報や個人情報は入れない ことを、担当者間のルールにします。 社内の生成AI利用ルールを確認する 企業によっては、生成AIの利用範囲や使えるサービスを定めたガイドラインがあります。人事部門が独自のツールを使い始める前に、情報システム部門や法務に確認します。 利用ルールに沿ったサービスを選べば、後から利用を止められる事態を避けられます。採用ページなど対外的な文書での利用可否も、あわせて確かめておきましょう。 求人原稿のAI作成に関するよくある質問 求人原稿のAI作成に関する質問は以下の3つで

items.title: AIエージェントとは？仕組みと種類から企業の導入手順まで解説
items.description: 「AIエージェント」という言葉が社内で飛び交うものの、ChatGPTやRPAと何が違うのか説明できず困っていないでしょうか。 AIエージェントとは、 目標を与えると自ら手順を計画し、ツールを使って実行するAI です。 定義をあいまいにしたまま進めると、名ばかりの製品を選んだり、成果の出ない試験導入に予算を使ったりしかねません。理解しておけば、ベンダーの提案を自分の言葉で見極められます。 本記事では、生成AIやRPAとの違いと仕組みを中心に、種類、できること、リスク、導入の5ステップまで解説します。 読み終える頃には、自社で最初に任せる業務と、押さえるべきリスクを判断できるようになります。ぜひ最後までお読みください。 AIエージェントとは？生成AIとの違い AIエージェントの理解には、次の3つの視点が欠かせません。 AIエージェントの定義 生成AIとの違い RPA・チャットボットとの違い 最初に線引きを押さえておくと、以降の仕組みや導入判断の話が格段に読みやすくなります。 AIエージェントの定義 AIエージェントとは、 目標を達成するために、状況を読み取り、自ら判断して行動するAIシステム です。 人が一手ずつ指示する必要がない点が特徴です。LLM（大規模言語モデル）が次の行動を判断し、検索や社内システムの操作といったツールで実行し、結果を見て再び判断します。 たとえば「来週の会議の日程を調整して」と頼むと、参加者の空き時間の確認、会議室の予約、招待の送信までを一連で進めます。 Anthropicも、エージェントを「LLMが自らの処理の流れとツールの使い方を動的に決めるシステム」と整理しています。 出典： 『Building effective agents』（Anthropic） 定義の軸が「自律的な判断と実行」だと押さえておけば、ベンダーの説明が単なる自動応答ではないかを見分けられます。 生成AIとの違い 生成AIは問いに答えて成果物を返す道具であり、AIエージェントは 目標に向けて作業を進める担い手 です。 観点 生成AI AIエージェント 動き方 指示ごとに1回応答する 目標に向けて計画と実行を繰り返す 出力 文章や画像などの成果物 予約・更新・送信などの作業結果 人の関与 指示のたびに必要 目標と権限の設定が中心 両者は対立する関係ではありません。AIエージェントは、内部で生成AI（LLM）を頭脳として使っています。 顧客からの問い合わせメールを例にすると、生成AIは返信文案を作るところまでです。AIエージェントは契約情報の検索、返信文の作成、送信、対応履歴の記録まで進めます。 文案作成なら生成AI、複数の作業にまたがる業務ならAIエージェントと使い分ければ、過剰な投資を避けられます。 RPA・チャットボットとの違い RPAは決められた手順を忠実に繰り返す仕組みで、チャットボットは用意された回答で応答する仕組みです。 観点 RPA・チャットボット AIエージェント 判断 事前に決めたルールに従う 状況に応じてAIが判断する 想定外への対応 止まる、またはエラーになる 手順を組み直して対応を試みる 設定 手順やシナリオを事前に設計する 目標と使えるツールを与える RPAは入力形式が変わるとエラーで止まりがちですが、AIエージェントは画面や文面の変化を読み取り、手順を調整します。ただし判断が確率的なため、 毎回同じ結果になるとは限りません 。 件数が多く正確性が求められる定型処理はRPA、例外が多く判断を要する処理はAIエージェントが向いています。両者を組み合わせる構成も現実的です。 既存のRPA資産を捨てずに、判断が必要な部分だけをAIエージェントで補う選択肢を持てます。 AIエージェントの仕組み AIエージェントは、次の4つの働きを繰り返して動きます。 認識：目標と状況を読み取る 計画：手順を組み立てる 記憶：文脈と履歴を保持する 行動：ツールで実行し結果を確かめる この循環こそが、人の手を離れて作業を進められる理由です。 認識：目標と状況を読み取る 認識とは、 与えられた目標と現在の状況を読み取る 働きです。 ユーザーの指示、メール、社内データ、画面の情報などが入力になります。LLMがこれらを読み、何が求められ、今どこまで進んでいるかを把握します。 たとえば「先月の問い合わせを分析して」という指示を受けると、対象データの場所と、分析の観点を読み取ります。 認識がずれると以降の作業も外れるため、指示には成果物の形式と期限まで具体的に書くと精度が上がります。 計画：手順を組み立てる 計画とは、 目標を達成するための手順に分解し、実行する順番を決める 働きです。 LLMが大きな目標を小さなタスクに分け、どれから着手するかを判断します。途中の結果に応じて手順を組み直せる点が、固定手順の自動化との違いです。 「会議資料を準備して」と頼むと、関連ファイルの検索、要点の整理、資料の作成という順番を自分で決めます。ファイルが見つからなければ、別の場所を探します。 手順を人が事前に設計しなくてよいため、定型化しにくい業務にも適用できます。 記憶：文脈と履歴を保持する 記憶とは、 会話の文脈や過去の作業結果を保持し、次の判断に生かす 働きです。 短期の記憶は、今の作業の経過や直前のやり取りを指します。長期の記憶は、過去の対応履歴や社内の知識を蓄え、必要なときに呼び出す仕組みを指します。 顧客対応であれば、前回の問い合わせ内容と対応結果を踏まえて回答できるため、同じ質問を繰り返し聞く必要がありません。 何を記憶させるかを設計すれば、担当者ごとの属人的な知識を共有できます。ただし、機密情報を保存する範囲には注意が必要です。 行動：ツールで実行し結果を確かめる 行動とは、 ツールを呼び出して実際に作業を実行し、結果を確かめる 働きです。 検索、ファイル操作、メール送信、社内システムのAPI呼び出し、コードの実行などが該当します。実行後は結果を再びLLMが確認し、目標に近づいたかを判断して次の行動を決めます。 「請求書を登録して」と頼むと、経理システムに入力し、登録結果を確認し、エラーがあれば修正します。ここが生成AIとの決定的な違いです。 行動できる範囲は、与えた権限で決まります。権限の設計が安全性を左右すると理解しておけば、導入時に確認すべき点を絞れます。 AIエージェントの種類は4つ 本記事では動き方と用途から、AIエージェントを次の4つに整理します。 汎用型 業務特化型 開発支援型 マルチエージェント型 分類の方法は解説によって異なりますが、自社の目的に合うタイプを先に絞ると、製品選びで迷いにくくなります。 汎用型 汎用型は、 幅広い依頼に1つのエージェントで対応するタイプ です。 Web検索、ブラウザ操作、資料の作成など、業務を問わず任せられます。ChatGPTのエージェント機能やManus（マナス）が代表例です。 調べ物から資料の下書きまでを一度に頼めるため、まず試して感触をつかむ用途に向いています。 一方で、業務固有のルールや社内システムとの連携は別途設計が必要です。本格運用では、次の業務特化型との使い分けを検討しましょう。 業務特化型 業務特化型は、 問い合わせ対応、営業、経理など特定の業務に最適化されたタイプ です。 対象業務の手順や用語、連携先のシステムがあらかじめ組み込まれており、設定の負担が小さくなります。 カスタマーサポート向けのエージェントであれば、問い合わせの分類、回答の作成、担当者への引き継ぎまでを標準機能として備える製品があります。 導入先の業務に詳しい分、汎用型より短い指示で動かせます。 対象が絞られるぶん成果も測りやすく、初めての導入で選ばれやすいタイプです。 開発支援型 開発支援型は、 コードの作成、修正、テストまでを自律的に進めるタイプ です。 Claude CodeやGitHub Copilotのエージェント機能が代表例です。リポジトリ全体を読み取り、複数ファイルにまたがる修正を行います。 開発部門は作業の成果がコードとして残り、テストで検証しやすいため、AIエージェントの活用が先行しやすい領域です。 ただし、生成されたコードは人がレビューすることが前提です。権限の範囲と確認の手順を決めたうえで使いましょう。 マルチエージェント型 マルチエージェント型は、 複数のエージェントが役割を分担して協働するタイプ です。 調査担当、執筆担当、確認担当のように役割を分け、エージェント同士が成果物を受け渡して1つの業務を完成させます。 1つのエージェントでは扱いきれない複雑な業務にも対応できます。反面、構成が複雑になり、どこで誤りが起きたかの切り分けも難しくなります。 最初は単体のエージェントで始め、必要になった段階で分業を検討するのが現実的です。 AIエージェントでできること AIエージェントが担える代表的な業務は、次の5つです。 問い合わせ対応 営業・マーケティング 開発・プログラミング 事務・バックオフィス リサーチ 自社の業務のどれに近いかを探しながら読み進めてください。 問い合わせ対応 問い合わせ対応では、 質問の意図を理解して回答し、必要な手続きまで実行 できます。 契約情報や注文状況を検索して回答を作成し、判断が難しい案件は担当者に引き継ぎます。 たとえば配送状況の確認であれば、注文システムを照会して回答し、再配送の手続きまで進めます。 回答の根拠となる社内マニュアルやFAQを読み込ませておくと、案内の正確さが保たれます。夜間の一次対応も任せられます。 担当者は、人の判断が必要な案件に集中できます。 営業・マーケティング 営業・マーケティングでは、 情報収集と事務作業を任せ、顧客対応の時間を確保 できます。 見込み顧客の企業情報の収集、提案メールの下書き、商談後のCRM（顧客管理システム）への入力などが対象です。 商談の議事録から次のアクションを抽出し、フォローのメールを作成するところまで進める使い方もあります。 架電や訪問の優先順位づけに使う情報の整理も、対象になります。 入力や調整に使っていた時間を、顧客との対話に回せます。 開発・プログラミング 開発・プログラミングでは、 コードの作成、修正、テストの実行、不具合の調査 を任せられます。 リポジトリ全体を把握したうえで、複数のファイルにまたがる修正を提案し、テストを実行して結果を確認します。 たとえば「この関数の仕様変更に合わせて、呼び出し元をすべて直して」と依頼すると、影響範囲の調査から修正までを進めます。 テストが失敗した場合は、原因を調べて再修正まで試みます。 人はレビューと設計判断に専念でき、開発の待ち時間を短縮できます。 事務・バックオフィス 事務・バックオフィスでは、 書類の読み取りから登録、チェックまでを一連で自動化 できます。 請求書の読み取りと会計システムへの登録、経費精算の内容確認、書類の仕分け、スケジュール調整などが該当します。 書式がまちまちな書類や、例外の多い処理は、固定手順のRPAでは対応しづらい領域です。AIエージェントなら内容を読んで判断できます。 社内の承認ルールを与えれば、条件に合う申請だけを通す運用も可能です。 定型作業から解放されれば、改善業務や確認が必要な案件に時間を使えます。 リサーチ リサーチでは、 Web検索、資料の収集、要点の整理、レポート化まで を任せられます。 複数の情報源を横断して調べ、論点ごとにまとめた報告書の下書きを作成します。 競合の動向調査や市場の情報収集のように、時間はかかるが判断は定型的な作業に向いています。 調べる観点を事前に指定すると、報告書の質がそろいます。 ただし、出典の確認は人が行う必要があります。下書きとして受け取り、重要な数値は原典で確かめる運用にすれば、調査の初動を大幅に短縮できます。 AIエージェントを導入する3つのメリット AIエージェントの導入で得られる主な効果は、次の3つです。 工数の削減 対応品質の均一化 24時間の稼働 どの効果を狙うかが決まると、対象業務の選び方も定まります。 工数の削減 AIエージェントは、 定型的な調査、入力、調整の作業を任せて、担当者の工数を減らせます 。 複数のシステムをまたぐ作業や、例外の多い作業も、人が手順を細かく設計せずに任せられる点が従来の自動化と異なります。 たとえば営業担当者のCRM入力や、経理担当者の書類確認といった毎日発生する作業が対象になります。 効果を測るには、導入前に作業時間を計測しておくことが欠かせません。比較の基準があれば、投資判断の根拠を示せます。 対応品質の均一化 AIエージェントは、 手順書やルールを与えれば、誰が依頼しても同じ基準で対応 します。 人による対応は、経験や担当者の判断によって品質にばらつきが出ます。ルールを明文化してエージェントに与えると、判断基準がそろいます。 問い合わせ対応で回答の表現や案内する手順を統一したい場面は、その典型です。 新任の担当者でも、ベテランと同じ手順で対応を始められます。 ただし、品質はルールの質に左右されます。誤った手順を与えれば、誤った対応が均一に広がる点には注意が必要です。 24時間の稼働 AIエージェントは、 夜間や休日も止まらずに作業を進められます 。 人の勤務時間に縛られないため、夜間の問い合わせへの一次対応や、依頼を翌朝までに処理しておく運用が可能になります。 海外拠点との時差があるチームでも、待ち時間を減らせます。 たとえば夜間に届いた見積依頼を、営業開始までに整理しておくといった使い方です。 対応の遅れによる機会損失を抑えられます。重要な案件は、翌営業日に人へ引き継ぐ運用にしておくと安心です。 AIエージェントの4つのリスクと課題 AIエージェントの導入前に押さえておきたいリスクと課題は、次の4つです。 誤った判断で動くリスク 情報漏えいや不正操作のリスク 費用対効果が見えにくい課題 責任範囲が曖昧になる課題 リスクを先に知っておけば、導入後に慌てず対策を組み込めます。 誤った判断で動くリスク AIエージェントは、 誤った情報や判断に基づいて、そのまま作業を進めてしまう ことがあります。 LLMは確率的に出力を生成するため、事実と異なる内容を含む場合があります。人の確認を挟まなけ

items.title: How TCS built an agentic test orchestrator with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: This post was co-written with Varun Valsan from Tata Consultancy Services (TCS). Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) runs large-scale testing for Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) clients, where the slowest part of a release is rarely writing application code. The larger constraint is the chain of work that follows: interpreting requirements, designing scenarios, writing and maintaining automation, preparing execution environments, investigating failures, and assembling evidence for review. BFSI clients need to increase testing throughput while preserving the controls expected in financial services. The objective wasn’t to replace quality engineers. It was to remove repetitive translation and execution work so that engineers could spend more time on risk analysis, exploratory testing, and release decisions. These industry needs generated four specific requirements for TCS. First, every test must be grounded in project-specific context rather than generic prompts. Second, it had to cover both API and browser-based UI testing to match how BFSI applications are built. Third, security is paramount, so every tenant’s data and knowledge store must be isolated. Finally, it must provide a repeatable path from requirement ingestion to test evidence and reporting, so the gains hold across teams and releases. In this post, we show how TCS built an agentic test orchestrator that turns requirements into executable, governed tests, and what it changed for its BFSI testing teams. Why conventional automation and systems weren’t enough TCS already uses traditional test automation for its clients, and it does improve execution speed. But it leaves the slow work untouched: teams must still create the scenarios, convert them into scripts, maintain locators and dependencies, and diagnose failures. When a linked user story changes, scripts generated for an earlier story can quickly become stale. A single generative AI prompt also doesn’t provide the control needed for a multi-stage engineering workflow. TCS therefore designed the Agentic Test Orchestrator to decompose testing into specialized tasks. Each task has its own agent, tools, validation rules, and context. A deterministic supervisor routes work, while an execution workflow controls retries, error classification, persistence, and reporting. To run these agents, TCS chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a service to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Three capabilities drove the decision. First, Amazon Bedrock offers a choice of models, so each agent uses the model that fits its task, such as scenario design or code generation, and TCS can adopt newer models as they become available. Second, AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, scales with demand, so testers across many tenants can run generation and execution sessions at the same time without TCS provisioning or tuning agent servers. Third, the runtime runs each session in its own isolated microVM, which gives TCS session-level separation for its multi-tenant platform without having to build that layer itself. Together, these capabilities let TCS focus its engineering effort on testing logic rather than agent infrastructure, which shortened the time to bring the platform to its BFSI clients. Solution overview The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow of the platform across five stages, with a per-tenant security layer underneath. Inputs from Jira, business requirement documents (BRDs), and GitLab enter a tenant web application that runs on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) behind Amazon CloudFront , with sign-in through Amazon Cognito . TCS uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime to host the platform’s specialized agents, built with the Strands Agents SDK . These agents generate the tests, refine them with the tester, and manage their execution. Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) runs the generated tests. Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon DynamoDB store the results, and Amazon CloudWatch captures the logs. Throughout, AWS WAF , Amazon Cognito, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) , and AWS Secrets Manager enforce per-tenant security and isolation. Figure 1: High-level solution architecture The TCS Agentic Test Orchestrator is a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) solution built on AWS. A tester provides requirements through Jira stories, business requirement documents (BRDs), Swagger specifications, uploaded documents, GitLab source folders, or captured UI flows. From those inputs the platform then generates test scenarios, Gherkin feature files, and executable Java or Python tests. It runs those tests on Amazon ECS, stores artifacts and results, and shows progress and reports in a per-tenant web application. The sections that follow describe how each part of the platform meets one of the four requirements TCS set. 1. Separate the control plane from each tenant application plane TCS required strict isolation of each tenant’s identity, data, and keys, so the platform uses pooled compute with siloed data and identity. A shared control plane provides the Amazon EKS cluster, container registry, administrative portal, tenant registry, onboarding automation, Amazon CloudFront distributions, and AWS WAF protection. Each tenant application plane receives its own Kubernetes namespace, Amazon Cognito user pool, AWS KMS key, Amazon S3 bucket, Amazon DynamoDB tables, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases . This separation gives each BFSI tenant the data and key boundaries that financial-services controls demand. Tenant onboarding is event driven. The administrative API writes a pending tenant record, emits an event through Amazon EventBridge , and starts an AWS CodeBuild project that deploys the tenant infrastructure with AWS Cloud Development Kit ( AWS CDK ). This pattern makes tenant provisioning repeatable while retaining tenant-specific identity and data boundaries that TCS needed. 2. Groun

items.title: Amazon Bedrock tokenomics data lake
items.description: If you need an observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock workloads, you’re not alone. When you’re running thousands of model invocations a day across multiple accounts, after a request is sent you might be wondering, what happened? You can see the aggregate bill, but you can’t see what happened inside each call. You might start to ask questions: what prompt was sent, what the model returned, how many tokens it used, which model handled it, and whether the response was any good! If you’re a platform or machine learning (ML) engineer looking after a fleet of Amazon Bedrock workloads across teams, that’s a real problem. You can’t debug a spike, you can’t spot wasteful prompts, and you can’t tell one team’s usage from another’s. We built something to help: a centralized observability data lake for your Amazon Bedrock invocations. In this post, I cover what native data you have and how we designed the lake. I also show how to use it to see your prompts and derive the per-invocation cost. The AWS CloudFormation templates, AWS Lambda code, and SQL queries are all in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . This post walks through the architecture and deployment steps. The repo has everything you need to deploy it. What Amazon Bedrock visibility do you have today? Amazon Bedrock offers model invocation logging , and it’s genuinely powerful. You turn on invocation logs in the settings in each AWS account you are using Bedrock . It delivers a full record of requests and responses to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) or Amazon CloudWatch . The data exists, but it’s locked inside individual accounts. What you really want is a single, fast, queryable view of every invocation across your whole organization. That’s what the data lake gives you. What is the Amazon Bedrock observability data lake? A centralized Amazon Bedrock invocation log data lake pulls raw model invocation logs from your linked accounts into Amazon CloudWatch . Subscription log filters then forward those records to your central account. The central account processes the data through Amazon Data Firehose , and exposes them through Amazon Athena as one clean table you can query across your organization. Figure 1: Amazon Bedrock invocation observability data lake architecture across a central account and linked accounts Everything is deployed as Infrastructure as Code using two AWS CloudFormation templates, so you can roll it out repeatably across every account in your organization. This can be found in the AWS Sample Bedrock Invocation Data Lake GitHub repository . What does each Amazon Bedrock invocation log capture? After we run this solution, you will have a combined set of data across the linked account you deploy to so you can query with Athena. What you get per invocation after the logs are flattened into the processed table: The prompt the user or application sent. The model response that came back. Input and output token counts , so you can measure the true weight of each call. The model used, so you can understand utilization of models across teams. The stop reason (for example, max_tokens ), which tells you when a response was cut off. The account and timestamp , so you can attribute and time-slice everything. The AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role , so you can see who sent the prompt. After every invocation is captured like this, you go from “We used X tokens on Amazon Bedrock” to “Here is exactly what each model calls contained, and how efficient it was.” That’s the visibility platform and ML teams have been missing. How is the Amazon Bedrock data lake designed? The data lake moves each invocation through five stages, from the moment Amazon Bedrock writes a log to the point you can query it in Athena. 1. Amazon Bedrock writes an invocation log Every time an application calls an Amazon Bedrock model, Amazon Bedrock can record what happened: which model, which account, which IAM identity made the call, how many input and output tokens were used, and the prompt and response text. You turn this on once per account with a single API call, pointing Amazon Bedrock at a CloudWatch log group and giving it a role that can write there. 2. CloudWatch forwards the logs to a central account Each source account gets a subscription filter on its Amazon Bedrock log group. Think of it as a permanent forwarding rule that says “send every new event to this address.” The address is an Amazon CloudWatch Logs destination living in your central account. Source accounts don’t get permissions on the central pipeline. They hand events to the destination, and the central account’s own role takes it from there. 3. A small Lambda tidies each record CloudWatch doesn’t hand over clean JSON. It bundles events into batches and wraps them compressed and encoded, so what arrives looks like gibberish until you unwrap it. A small Lambda function does three jobs: Unwraps the batch back into individual log records. Throws out the noise. CloudWatch sends occasional housekeeping messages and plain-English notices like “Permissions are correctly set for Amazon Bedrock logs.” These aren’t invocation data, and letting them through breaks the next stage. Flattens one awkward field. The caller’s identity arrives nested one level down. The Lambda lifts it to the top so it’s straightforward to query later. 4. Amazon Data Firehose converts to Parquet and writes to S3 Amazon Data Firehose buffers the records and writes them to an Amazon S3 bucket, converting from JSON to Parquet on the way through. Firehose also files each object under a date path ( year=2026/month=08/day=27/ ). 5. Use Athena to query the data and connect it to cost data An AWS Glue table tells Athena how to read those files, so you can query the lake with ordinary SQL. items.title: AIFP: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
items.description: METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario . This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) before 2029 . SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs. Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report. If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement . Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights ( more ). Full post: https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q35-timelines-update-looks-like-the Discuss

items.title: Q3.5 Timelines Update: Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All
items.description: We want to get this post out quickly given the urgency of the topic. It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. We would love to be corrected on any mistakes we made. METR recently estimated that Anthropic is now making AI progress about twice as fast as its historical rate (they would not be surprised by anything from 1.3x to 3x), and guessed that “perhaps ≈80%” of the current acceleration is due to AI. If they’re right, that implies an AI-driven acceleration that is 5 months ahead of the AI 2027 scenario . This level of acceleration due to AI is very unexpected. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) [1] before 2029 . SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs. [2] Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). [3] We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report. [4] . If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement . Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights ( more ). [5] Timelines/Takeoff Update Summary We estimate that METR’s report implies a 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration in the pace of progress today, relative to historical levels. This surprises our model; we made our most recent timelines forecasts less than three months ago, and even the most aggressive model-based distribution (Daniel’s) assigned less than 4% to the pace of progress being sped up by at least 1.7x in November 2026. [6] 1.7x AI-attributable acceleration is a bigger deal than it may seem; e.g., it’s a much bigger deal than making employees 1.7x more productive . We focus in this post primarily on forecasting when Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will arrive. We also discuss Top-Expert-Dominating-AI (TED-AI): AIs that are better than top human experts at virtually all tasks. ( more ) In this post, we forecast SAR and TED-AI using the following approaches: Simple models: Research taste linear extrapolation : Even assuming that the recent pace of progress doesn’t accelerate further due to automation, the fact that the recent trend is above historical rates is a big update to our timelines; a linear extrapolation of the recent rate of AI progress predicts that SAR will likely be achieved by the end of 2027. Labor uplift extrapolation : An exponential extrapolation of self-reported labor uplift predicts SAR in mid-2028. In addition to not modeling automation, there are reasons to think that an exponential is too conservative. However, self-reports may be too bullish. Extrapolating Anthropic automation levels : Anthropic recently shared a graph showing how the percentage of R&D tasks at various automation levels has changed over time. Extrapolating this predicts SAR in late 2027; this method also doesn’t model speedup from automation. Extrapolating software R&D uplift per unit of ECI : AI software R&D uplift must have recently been increasing by a larger factor with each ECI point. If we linearly extrapolate the rate at which this “factor of extra uplift per ECI point” is increasing, we get SAR in Dec 2027 (if we assume that the self-reported AI labor uplift chart is accurate) or July 2027 (if we assume that there was no meaningful automation 12 months ago and all the speed-up has happened after then). Tom Davidson’s toy model: Predicts superintelligence in around a year conditional on a software-only singularity, so SAR sometime in 2027. Filtered AI Futures Model (AIFM) : Keeping the existing AIFM (including parameter distributions), and filtering for trajectories that match METR’s AI-attributable pace of progress acceleration estimates. This serves 2 purposes on top of the simple extrapolations: Modeling how automation changes the rate of progress, allowing forecasting reasonably beyond SAR. Informing what parameter settings in the simple research taste extrapolation are plausible. The results of these methods: How to think about these results: The simple research taste extrapolation, which is a simplified version of the AIFM, gives July or September 2027, depending on whether you account for parameter uncertainty. Other simple models predict late 2027 to mid-2028. When conditioned on 1.7x Nov 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, the AIFM predicts a SAR median of Feb 2027. This is faster than the simple research taste extrapolation because it usually has a higher level of Sep 2026 research taste (in the median case, matching a median researcher), [7] and it accounts for further automation. When additionally conditioning on a 1.2x May 2026 AI-attributed acceleration, predictions get slower because it indicates a lower rate of growth than is typical when only conditioning on 1.7x in Nov. We then explore hypotheses for why the AI Futures Model was wrong , including parameter adjustments and modeling changes. The analysis is highly preliminary, and we were unable to come to strong conclusions. Our top candidates for what explains where we went wrong are: Near-AC coding skills result in more AI R&D uplift than we anticipated . items.title: DeepMind reveals Gemini Robotics 2.5 and open safety benchmark "ASIMOV-jailbreak"
items.description: Google DeepMind has revealed a new generation of the AI-powered Gemini Robotics platform. In the 2.5 release, Google says its robotic AI is getting tantalizingly close to completing real-world tasks as well as humans do. In fact, some Gemini robots were able to get actual work done in Mercedes-Benz factories, and the team is preparing for a day when robots operate alongside humans with an open source safety benchmark. DeepMind's physical AI platform has several computational layers between user input and robotic action. There's the vision-language model piece, which is Gemini Embodied Reasoning. Essentially, it takes your instructions and uses live video to plan how the robot can accomplish the task. The other main component is the vision-language-action (VLA) that actually generates robot actions, like moving an actuator—that's Gemini Robotics, which has been bumped to version 2.5. DeepMind says that Gemini Robotics 2.5 is much better at tasks that require a high degree of dexterity. The model was evaluated across more than 200 activities, including serving food with tongs and using a pipette, as you would see in a laboratory. Google also showed that Apptronik’s Apollo 2 humanoid robot with Gemini Robotics 2.5 can now tie a bow with its five-fingered hands, a notable feat, because deformable objects (like ribbon) are notoriously difficult for robots to manipulate. items.title: Ukraine’s fiber-optic drones get squeezed by AI data center demand
items.description: Impervious to battlefield jamming, drones physically connected to human operators by miles of fiber-optic cables have become such a common weapon of war in Ukraine that trees and fields are strewn with tangled cables thinner than fishing lines. But importing such fiber-optic material from China has become more costly as drone warfare’s needs compete with global demand from AI data centers for the same limited supply—and so Ukrainian drone makers have been adapting. Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, the Ukrainians have been forced out of necessity to continually develop battlefield innovations involving first-person view (FPV) quadcopter drones and other heavier types of drones. But it was the Russian military that first deployed unjammable fiber-optic drones to repel Ukrainian forces’ cross-border incursion into the Kursk Oblast in 2024. The Ukrainians quickly followed suit in developing their own fiber-optic drones, given the drones’ capability to shrug off electronic warfare jamming that could neutralize radio-controlled drones. Russia and Ukraine have relied on Chinese suppliers for some off-the-shelf drones and a wide array of drone components, including bulk orders of fiber wound around very large spools or sometimes small finished spools ready for installation on drones. The finished spools can hold enough fiber-optic cable for drones to regularly operate at ranges of dozens of miles, and sometimes up to 62 miles (100 kilometers) in extreme cases, as reported by the independent Russian publication The Insider . items.title: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
items.description: Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as: [...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing. For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40. The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others: Model Prompt size Input ($/M) Cached input Output GPT-6 Luna ≤272k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >272k $0.20 $0.02 $0.75 Muse Ember 1.0 ≤200k $0.10 $0.004 $0.50 >200k $0.30 $0.012 $1.50 Claude Haiku 5.5 ≤100k $0.10 $0.01 $0.50 >100k $0.50 $0.05 $2.50 But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem. For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models: The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement: It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task. (That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!) Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles . The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response. Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too: The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder , which is 40x the price of Muse Ember. items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.description: Claude Fable 5.2 pays close attention to who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model tended to add to the existing structure when the prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, even when that duplicated existing code. When the prompt said the code base was the model’s own, it often consolidated duplicated code and sometimes made related fixes without being asked. If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you. The ownership sentence makes the model much more likely to consolidate duplicated code into one shared function. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the sentence and in about 75 percent of runs with it. — Prompting Claude Fable 5.2 , Anthropic documentation Tags: prompt-engineering , anthropic , generative-ai , ai , llms , claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Archetypal contexts in the neurons of language models: an architecture for intelligence?
items.description: arXiv:2611.07234v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We validate our previous hypothesis that a language model holds relational patterns apart from the subject domains that instantiate them (Nordfors, 2026). These archetypal contexts are patterns of relations that people recognize across many fields, such as the tipping point or winner takes all, held once and applied across domains. We show this inside the model, Qwen3.8-27B. One set of neurons carries the archetype, say the tipping point; another carries the topic, say politics, ecology or cell biology; a third carries the language, such as English, Spanish or Chinese. Silence the tipping point's neurons, and the model no longer identifies the pattern but still knows what the text is about. Silence the topic's, and it loses the topic but still names the pattern. In the neuron maps the layers organize themselves into a sandwich: the outer layers carry languages, the layers inside them topics, the layers at the heart archetypes. The sandwich emerges spontaneously during pretraining and appears in every model we mapped. Archetypes are the architecture for analogy, and we strongly suggest that this structure of archetypes and topics is the mechanism of a language model's intelligence: we see it self-organize as the model is trained. The neurons, the texts and the code are released with this paper as its reproduction package, so that anyone can repeat the test inside the model.

items.title: RouteAlign: Aligning Task Requirements with Model Profiles for LLM Service Selection
items.description: arXiv:2611.08162v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLM service selection requires performance evidence that reflects the demands of the current task. Aggregate scores obscure differences in capability and difficulty, while semantically related examples can involve different combinations of skills. We present RouteAlign, which uses task requirements to structure both the measurement of model performance and the selection of services. Task requirements describe capability demand and difficulty, enabling alignment with corresponding model performance measurements. Historical requirements determine how outcomes contribute to global profiles and local capability estimates; incoming requirements determine how those measurements inform the current decision. A shared scorer integrates the evidence, and a generation-cost preference controls selection among eligible services. Evaluation across diverse tasks and heterogeneous LLM services shows that RouteAlign extends the empirical quality-cost frontier toward higher task quality. Comparisons with open Jev-style decision backends show consistent quality gains, with lower generation cost than their strongest tested configuration. Ablations support the contribution of local performance evidence, while catalog-update experiments demonstrate effective reuse of the fitted scorer with refreshed model measurements.

items.title: CuriousTogether: Implications of Curiosity and Cultural Grounding in Multi-Agent LLM Interactions
items.description: arXiv:2611.01301v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent settings, exhibiting emergent collective behaviors, yet the role of curiosity as a driver of such dynamics remains understudied. We introduce CuriousTogether, a framework evaluating curiosity-driven multi-agent LLM interactions across three complementary dimensions: novelty-seeking, epistemic and social curiosity. Across eight tasks spanning reasoning, creative generation, and social bias mitigation, curiosity-guided multi-agent settings yield improvements over non-curious ones on seven out of eight tasks, with gains of up to 20.6% in story generation (semantic diversity) and a 14.9 pp reduction in stereotype rates. Furthermore, country-conditioned cultural grounding show benefits for story generation and social tasks, but can hurt precision-oriented reasoning. Finally, we show that inference-time multi-agent curiosity-based approach offers favorable quality-token trade-offs, compared with single-agent baselines. Together, these findings support curiosity-guided interaction as a practical mechanism for improving multi-agent collaboration, with downstream benefits for reasoning, creative, and societal tasks.

items.title: Maswao: An automatically collected, prepared, and benchmarked dataset for South African Sign Language
items.description: arXiv:2611.02903v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent advancements in sign language processing can be attributed to developments in both large-scale dataset collection and algorithmic complexity in areas such as pose estimation techniques, signal processing through Transformer models, and model optimization. However, only a handful of sign languages, such as the American, British, and German, from over 200 globally recognized sign languages, reap the benefits of such advancements, while the rest lag behind. In this study, we aim to address this technological disparity by proposing a framework for the automatic collection and preparation of sign language datasets, with very minimal human-labour intervention, using the South African Sign Language (SASL) as a testbed. Specifically, we automatically collect SASL video content using public resources such as news broadcasts. Additionally, we convert their accompanying audio streams into text using available Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) tools. Furthermore, we crop the sign language area in the videos and use gradient descent to locate valleys of non-motion to determine end-of-sentence points within long videos to create our weakly sentence-aligned parallel corpora -- the Maswao (Signs) dataset. Finally, we benchmark the weakly aligned dataset on the task of Sign-to-text Translation using Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformer models to compare their individual intricacies. Our results show that Transformer models proposed in the literature outperform recurrent baselines, with the best-performing Transformer achieving BLEU-1 to BLEU-4 scores of 13.78, 5.21, 2.52, and 1.54, respectively, as well as ChrF = 18.09 and ROUGE-L = 10.51. These results indicate that the task remains promising and warrants further investigations.

items.title: PixelBench: Can LLMs Understand and Generate Images Pixel by Pixel?
items.description: arXiv:2611.02540v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate visual assets through text-based formats such as SVG and CAD, but these symbolic representations describe images using high-level primitives rather than explicit raster values. We ask whether LLMs can instead generate pixel images directly through their existing vocabulary, without a learned image tokenizer or decoder. We introduce PixelBench, a benchmark for text-to-pixel (T2P) and image-to-pixel (I2P) generation across multiple resolutions, together with a complementary pixel-understanding evaluation. Models generate an RGB color palette followed by a grid of indices specifying the palette color of each output pixel. In T2P, the strongest models produce recognizable images directly from text. In I2P, the strongest models outperform palette-matched downsampling and specialized pixelization algorithms at low resolutions. Pixel-understanding performance correlates strongly with generation performance. A resolution-scaling study shows that pixel-generation performance often improves initially before declining at high resolutions. Finally, we introduce Pixel Reconstruction Tuning (PRT), which augments visual instruction tuning with caption-palette-grid trajectories. We post-train Molmo2-4B from its pretraining checkpoint by mixing general instruction data with our curated PRT data, improving performance across 16 visual-centric benchmarks, indicating that explicit pixel reconstruction can provide useful auxiliary supervision.

items.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
items.description: arXiv:2610.32955v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, its type and urgency and whether to draft a reply, create a task or ignore it. In production these decisions are delegated to a generative LLM or to rules, and their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We describe Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent, and a measurement protocol -- stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, secret redaction, human labels in the review loop -- that produces ground truth before any training. On 231 emails in Italian and English we compare eleven systems: the production rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local and hosted typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble, Jeva, Jev) and generative LLMs (Qwen2.5, Gemma 4). Four results. The production rules for message type score 28% against a 57% majority class. With about two hundred labels a logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90) at a latency three orders of magnitude lower, though it never predicts the two rarest types; the best zero-shot system reaches 0.74 on type. The sender's relationship to the owner is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy on the 63% of emails whose sender was seen before: it belongs in the contact graph, not in the prompt. Per-email accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the baseline ignores 18% of the emails that needed a reply or a task, against 4% for the best generative model; a cost-chosen threshold cuts that to 6% and makes the classifier the cheapest system at every price. An adversarial third round (722 emails) with eleven pre-registered hypotheses confirms seven and refutes four. Two blind annotators agree with the reference at kappa 0.81 and 0.86 on type. We release the protocol and the harness; the emails stay private.

items.title: Forcing a Letter Suppresses Refusal: Mechanistic Evidence from WMDP
items.description: arXiv:2611.08639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety benchmarks for large language models (LLMs) commonly use multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. However, prior studies documented that MCQ format reduces refusal rates, which may significantly affect the safety behavior of the model. We provide a first mechanistic explanation of this effect on the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset across two models - Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B. First, we use the tuned lens technique to show that when processing MCQ the model commits to an answer-letter token very quickly, which is in contrast to the gradual refusal build-up in open-ended formats. Additionally, we observe that activations on the MCQ format lie roughly 3x further from the refusal direction, compared with their open-ended counterparts. Moreover, ablating the attention heads that carry the MCQ format answer increases the refusal, which is a direct evidence that the MCQ answer-selection competes with refusal. These findings indicate that MCQ safety scores primarily measure knowledge capabilities and do not assess the safety-mechanisms.

items.title: FinEvolveKG: Controlled and Attributable Prompt Evolution for Financial Knowledge Graph Construction
items.description: arXiv:2611.08643v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial institutions construct knowledge graphs (KGs) from shared SEC 10-Ks to serve risk analysis, portfolio management, and investment research, whose analytical needs differ. Extraction must adapt without fragmenting shared grounding, typing, and temporal rules. Hand-authored persona prompts and fine-tuning add cost. Weight-free prompt optimization offers an alternative, but unconstrained evolution of a monolithic prompt can rewrite shared rules alongside persona guidance, obscuring changes and complicating review. We introduce FinEvolveKG, a KG-construction harness separating reusable general and persona-policy blocks and mechanically confining GEPA, a reflective prompt optimizer, to the designated block. During persona adaptation, the approved general block remains byte-stable and every optimizer edit is localized to a separately versioned persona policy. A dual objective balances generic temporal-KG quality with persona-relevant facts, motifs, and multi-hop connectivity. We evaluate five mutation scopes on ticker-disjoint 10-K splits, with three seeds for the persona-conditioned arms (v3-v5) across three personas. On the three-seed mean, the complete two-stage block-constrained workflow (v4) improves over the frozen prompt baseline (v1) by 19.4-30.9% and over the tested unconstrained full-prompt workflow (v5) by 2.2-6.4%, leading v5 on both objective components and winning all nine paired-seed comparisons with the lowest seed variance in every persona. Without further optimization, v4 also exceeds v5 across all evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts. An SME audit supports using the generated triplets as ground truth; a blinded two-SME audit favors v4 over v5 in 70.1% of contrast-enriched judgments. These results show that mechanically attributable evolution can coexist with strong empirical performance, without attributing the gains causally to the boundary.

items.title: Compression of Emotion in Language Model Representations
items.description: arXiv:2611.08683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been evaluated on their ability to identify emotions expressed in text and produce fluent emotional language.
