items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
items.description: Today, we’re announcing that NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart. You can deploy it with a few steps in SageMaker Studio or with a few lines of the SageMaker Python SDK. Super VL is the vision-language model (VLM) in the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 family. It accepts images, video, and text as input and generates text. The model pairs a 120B-parameter hybrid Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language backbone with 12B active parameters and a C-RADIO vision encoder. It supports context lengths of up to 1 million tokens and includes a built-in Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head that supports speculative decoding. You can configure reasoning per request. NVIDIA built Super VL for document intelligence, GUI understanding for computer-use agents, video question answering, and multimodal agentic applications. JumpStart offers two variants: NVFP4, quantized from BF16 with quantization-aware distillation for optimized inference, and the BF16 full-precision reference weights. In this post, we walk through the model’s capabilities and the JumpStart deployment configurations. We then show the measured inference performance and demonstrate text, image, and video inference. Model overview Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a 120B-parameter model with 12B active parameters per token. It combines a hybrid language backbone with a dedicated vision encoder. Language backbone : 88 layers that interleave Mamba-2 and MoE layers (512 routed experts, 22 active per token) with 8 attention layers, plus a shared MTP head. The backbone is initialized from Nemotron 3 Super Base and distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra Base. Vision encoder : A C-RADIO vision encoder encodes images and sampled video frames, and a vision-language connector maps them into the language backbone’s embedding space. The encoder and connector stay in BF16 in both variants. Training : The model first goes through continued pre-training, long-context and software-engineering mid-training, and vision-language training. It then goes through two-stage multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on vision, reasoning, code, tool, chat, safety, and long-context data. Next come reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards and human feedback in NeMo RL and NeMo Gym, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and a final stage that further trains the MTP head. The NVFP4 checkpoint is produced from BF16 with NVIDIA Model Optimizer and quantization-aware distillation. It keeps the vision encoder, connector, Mamba convolutions, and embeddings in BF16 and the MoE router in FP32. It runs with 4-bit weights and activations (W4A4) on Blackwell GPUs. The following table compares the specifications of the two variants available in JumpStart. Specification NVFP4 BF16 Parameters 120B total, 12B active 120B total, 12B active Intended for Optimized inference (latency and throughput) Full-precision reference weights for customization: SFT, RL, distillation, domain adaptation, and custom quantization Inputs / output Image, video, text / text Image, video, text / text Context length Up to 1M tokens (JumpStart serving configurations use 520 to 15,600 tokens) Same Checkpoint size About 75 GB About 249 GB JumpStart instances ml.g7.24xlarge (default), ml.g7.48xlarge ml.p5en.48xlarge Speculative decoding Built-in MTP head. Not enabled in the JumpStart serving configuration Same LoRA adapter serving No No Languages English, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Spanish, Chinese Same Reasoning On by default. Configurable with enable_thinking Same Outputs Tool calling, JSON schema output, configurable reasoning Same License OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1 Same Key use cases Super VL is aimed at agentic workloads that must see and read. It targets vision-language agents that combine reasoning, coding, tool use, document understanding, and video understanding. Document intelligence : Optical character recognition (OCR), charts, tables, and multipage documents. Each 1,536 x 1,024 page image costs about 1,536 tokens of context. The JumpStart serving configuration accepts one image and one video per request. GUI understanding : Screen grounding and reasoning for computer-use agents that navigate applications. Video understanding : Analyze and summarize short MP4 video clips, including answering questions about visual content. You can provide videos inline as base64-encoded content, subject to the endpoint’s request payload size limits. Multimodal agents : Tool calling, JSON schema output through response_format , and configurable reasoning support multimodal agent workflows. Customization (BF16) : Download the BF16 reference weights for SFT, RL, distillation, domain adaptation, or creating your own quantized variants. The JumpStart endpoint serves the base weights only and does not load LoRA adapters. Model-quality benchmarks The NVIDIA model cards report results for both checkpoints across reasoning, coding, agentic, long-context, and multimodal benchmarks, with evaluation settings held constant so that only the checkpoint differs. The following table highlights the multimodal benchmarks most relevant to vision-language workloads (reasoning on). Benchmark Capability BF16 NVFP4 MMLongBench-Doc Long-document multimodal understanding 62.82 62.82 OCRBench v2, EN OCR and document understanding 68.12 68.34 CharXiv reasoning Chart and figure reasoning 80.82 79.88 Video-MME v2 Video understanding 32.85 32.54 OSWorld-Verified Visual computer use and agentic tasks 51.14 52.30 NVFP4, the JumpStart default, matches BF16 on MMLongBench-Doc and stays within about one point on the others, scoring slightly higher on OCRBench v2 and OSWorld-Verified. For the full comparison against other publicly available models and the evaluation settings, see the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning Technical Report . items.title: The backlash about data centers might really just be about electricity
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here . As voters went to the polls across the US last week, I was in Ashburn, Virginia, part of what’s known as Data Center Alley—the world’s largest data center hub. It’s also where the backlash now sweeping the country arguably first began taking shape. Driving through it is surreal. Concrete monolithic buildings loom along every major road, with names like Skybox and CloudHQ. It’s accepted wisdom in Big Tech that the war against data centers must be about something bigger than just data centers themselves. Two days after the midterms, OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, wrote that data centers “have become a proxy for public unease about affordability, corporate power, and people losing control over their futures.” It’s a culture war, in other words. But spending a few days in Data Center Alley left me wondering if it’s really the proxy that Lehane describes. I came away convinced that the data center backlash is more about electricity than Big Tech admits. The industry can improve its image, but it can’t escape the physical consequences of its enormous appetite for electricity. Here’s why. There are two ways to power the sort of data center that AI companies want: connecting to the grid, or generating electricity onsite. In Virginia’s Loudoun County, where data centers are ubiquitous but have been built at a steadier pace than the breakneck expansion now underway elsewhere in the country, most are connected to the existing grid. One facility I went inside, operated by Equinix, has massive diesel generators onsite for backup but gets its power from the local utility, Dominion Energy. Much of Dominion’s electricity is generated by natural gas (which is cleaner than coal or oil, but worse than renewables). The average data center operating in this part of Virginia today has a power capacity of 54 megawatts. That’s more than the power draw of the Denver International Airport . Elena Schlossberg, a prominent activist against data centers in Virginia, told me she’s “always banging my head against the wall” when the industry paints the fight as a culture war. “It was always about power,” she says—that is, electricity. Some Virginia protesters appear more animated by a broader anti-tech populism than Schlossberg, to be fair. But it’s the particular consequences of drawing so much power from the grid that have done the most to shape how the backlash has played out. Recent protests have led to new rules from the state that data centers must pay fully for the cost of new transmission lines to the grid and make sure they’re not spread among everyone else. Data center developers told me they’re preparing for new rules that would cut them off from grid power during peak demand. Schlossberg also worries about the downstream effects of a strained grid—for example, that data centers will run more diesel generators or that Dominion Energy will expand fossil fuel inputs rather than renewables to meet demand. The overwhelming majority of AI data centers being built elsewhere in the country are not designed this way. The scale desired is so massive that companies are setting up in rural areas where there is virtually no grid infrastructure to connect to. Building there means bringing your own power (so-called “behind the meter” power), in the form of natural-gas-powered turbines. Companies also build diesel generators for backup. Anthropic, for example, has reportedly agreed to pay $3.4 billion for gas turbines in what’s described as the largest power generation purchase by an AI company. Even if grids were nearby, they’d be unlikely to serve the amount of power demanded. The smallest data centers attractive for AI training are 300 megawatts. It’s a lot of power for one industrial site, but not unprecedented: One data center developer told me he’s eyeing a former steel mill already equipped to draw that much electricity from the grid. But the ideal facilities are more like 6,000 megawatts. That’s the estimated draw of the city of Chicago, which is powered by more than 20 power plants within the city alone (and dozens farther out). The notion of data center companies’ bringing their own power might seem attractive at first, because they wouldn’t be straining the grid. But generating electricity at this scale inevitably affects surrounding communities, and when public utilities build infrastructure of this magnitude, communities have traditionally expected a say in where it goes. Now, private companies are undertaking projects on a similar scale. Natural-gas turbines of any scale release air pollutants. When diesel generators are used, it’s even worse. And in the unprecedented rush to get these facilities operating, companies have become horrible neighbors (recall that Elon Musk violated air quality laws when he set up dozens of turbines to power a data center in Memphis, according to the Environmental Protection Agency). Big Tech’s tendency to chalk the backlash up to a culture war obfuscates one simple fact: There’s only so pleasant you can make a small city of computers to live around. Sure, companies can pursue better deals that raise tax revenues, hire local workers, and get more community involvement, as the protests are leading them to do . But if a small town is asked to welcome a Walt Disney World, an international airport, a steel plant, and the power plants to run them all, should we be surprised by its trepidation? Again, that’s not to say this is the sole reason for opposition to data centers. Fears of job losses, existential risks, and concentrated corporate power all fuel the backlash, as does misinformation (most facilities use far less water than many people think). Nor is consuming enormous amounts of electricity inherently bad: Many of the advances that have improved modern life have required just that. But as one developer recently told me,

items.title: Pluggable Agentic AI Framework: A seven-layer composable enterprise agentic AI reference architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: “How do we run our AI agents in production at scale?” is the question every customer eventually asks. It comes bundled with several questions. How do we handle thousands of concurrent user requests securely and confidently? How do we make sure the agents stay reliable under real traffic instead of failing silently? How do we know if an agent still meets the quality and safety standards it passed during testing? What are agent security best practices? Should that be deterministic or non-deterministic? And many more. A proof-of-concept answers none of these, because it is built to show the agent model can do the task, not to survive production traffic, cost pressure, and security review. That gap between a working prototype and a system that runs reliably, securely, frugally and responsibly at scale, is where most agentic AI initiatives stall, and it is rarely the model’s fault. Every team building an agent tends to rebuild the same scaffolding from scratch: its own routing logic, its own guardrails, its own observability, all applied after the fact rather than built in from the start. The teams need a shared, production-ready architecture that every agent can build on. This post walks through a seven-layer composable reference architecture designed to take multi-agent AI applications from prototype to production scale. Composable architecture The Pluggable Agentic AI Framework is a reference architecture for multi-agent applications organized into seven layers , each with a distinct responsibility and a stable contract. The services and technologies shown in each layer reflect the reference implementation, not mandatory choices. Organizations can substitute alternatives that align with their existing infrastructure and requirements. Together, these layers offer a blueprint for building, securing, and operating agentic AI applications at production scale. Figure 1: The seven layers of the Pluggable Agentic AI Framework Data and Knowledge is the foundation of Agentic AI. An agent is only as good as the data it can access. Whether an agent is checking out a healthcare formulary, tracking inventory, or interpreting a compliance rule, it needs relevant, up-to-date information to answer correctly. This layer owns retrieval, embeddings, and access to structured and unstructured data through a clear contract and protocol: accept a query and return the most relevant information that acts as context for an agent. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Base , Vector Engine for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless , Amazon S3 Vectors and Amazon DynamoDB are example building blocks for this foundation. Model and Inference choices should be driven by configuration, not hardwired into agent or application logic. Use smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger models for requests that require more nuanced reasoning. It is important to conduct a thorough model evaluation for the use case you are building with realistic and representative business data. A model routing layer keeps AI agents decoupled from the model hosting environment and provider-specific APIs by relying on a consistent request-and-response contract. A proxy such as LiteLLM provides a common interface across providers, so you can switch models based on your evaluations without rewriting application logic. Orchestration determines how work is distributed, and choosing the right approach is critical. For straightforward tasks, use a single agent to handle the work from end to end. For complex, cross-domain workflows, use a supervisor to delegate specialist agents, each scoped to a specific capability and tied to a specific set of tools. Avoid building one agent that does everything. As tools, instructions, and context accumulate, the context window grows, latency increases, and accuracy can suffer. Tool sprawl sets in, which can push agents beyond their intended boundaries, leading to unintended actions and security breaches. Splitting responsibilities keeps each agent’s context focused and makes latency more predictable. You can also test each agent’s behavior, scale it, and define its security model independently. Enforce bounded autonomy: specialists should execute strictly within the tools they have been granted, and nothing more. In addition to decomposing into specific specialists and setting its boundary, decouple the specialist agents from the supervisor agents. Allow the supervisor to discover the specialists from a centralized agent registry and invoke them through a standardized protocol like MCP (Model Context Protocol) and A2A (Agent to Agent). Maintain a centralized agent registry that catalogs every agent’s tools, skills, and owner. This gives your organization the visibility it needs for governance at scale, increases the velocity of AI agent implementation through reusability, and avoids the cost of repetitive development. Consider using Strands Agents for specialists, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the orchestrator, AWS Agent Registry and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway for centralized discovery and routing. Security and Guardrails should be a primary concern, built into the design from day one. Agentic AI exposes organizations to a new class of risks that conventional security frameworks were not built to address, from prompt injection and tool misuse to memory and data poisoning. Treat all external content as untrusted by default. Authenticate every request, whether it comes from a user, another agent, or an automated workflow, through a service like Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity . Then use fine-grained access control to determine whether each tool call is permitted before execution. Grant agents temporary, scoped credentials instead of persistent secrets. On the data-protection side, mask sensitive data like PHI (Personal Health Information) and PII (Personally Identifiable Information) in agent and tool requests and responses, so that sensitive customer information does not appear in agent outputs or lingers in memory. items.title: How CrossnoKaye grounds physical AI with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Industrial operations present AI challenges that don’t show up in typical enterprise software. In most facilities, plant data and control logic are spread across separate systems from different vendors: programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and distributed control systems (DCS) run the equipment logic, historians record time-series tags under site-specific naming schemes, supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems drive operator screens, and standalone optimization tools or alarm loggers sit on the side. Bolting an external AI agent onto that stack rarely works well in practice. Each system uses its own naming conventions. The logic that actually governs how equipment behaves (the control sequences, state machines, and safety interlocks) is locked inside proprietary controller code that an external tool can’t inspect. Giving a bolt-on agent access across multiple operational technology (OT) systems also means distributing credentials across the plant network. CrossnoKaye took a different approach to bring physical AI to heavy industry using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore . Its software-defined automation platform, ATLAS, connects live plant data and AI reasoning to closed-loop control of the equipment running food and beverage plants, industrial refrigeration facilities, aggregates quarries, and manufacturing sites. Across more than 100 industrial facilities and 13,000 controlled assets, CrossnoKaye stores over 22 trillion machine data points, ingests more than 50 billion new readings every day, and runs over 1,000 live advanced process control (APC) applications; CrossnoKaye reports that these applications improve production throughput by 11–17 percent while reducing total facility energy costs by an average of 21 percent. Because ATLAS already manages the facility model, the base control software, the historian, and the optimization applications in one platform on AWS, CrossnoKaye’s agentic intelligence system, AURA, has native access to the full operational state of the plant within a single security boundary. Having the plant context is only half the problem, though. Large language models (LLMs) are good at interpreting engineering context and planning an investigation, but they cannot reliably compute statistics or physical balances over millions of sensor readings in a prompt. To back every numerical answer with real math, AURA uses the code interpreter capability in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to write and run Python workloads at runtime inside isolated, AWS managed microVM sandboxes, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails and local edge safety controls. This post covers how CrossnoKaye architected ATLAS and AURA on AWS, how AURA uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore across interactive Chats, repeatable Tasks, and automated Routines, and what the team learned running physical AI in production. Solution overview ATLAS controls industrial processes across existing PLC and DCS infrastructure, from kilns, crushers, drying rooms, ovens, and spiral freezers to chillers, turbines, valves, and compressors, without requiring customers to rip and replace plant hardware. Figure 1 illustrates how on-premises ATLAS edge clusters, continuous cloud optimization, and AURA work together on AWS. Figure 1: CrossnoKaye AURA and ATLAS physical AI architecture with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore ATLAS and AURA are built around three core layers: First, the plant is defined in software from the edge up. At each facility, an on-premises ATLAS control panel with redundant computers, power supplies, and network switches (so local control continues uninterrupted while a failed hardware component is replaced) runs a local Kubernetes cluster that uses contract-first microservices, extending the ATLAS cloud platform on AWS to the plant floor. In the cloud, ATLAS authors, validates, and versions the facility’s base control narratives (defining equipment state machines, sequences, operating bounds, interlocks, and alarm rules), which are downloaded to the edge appliances and run locally against existing equipment and controllers. CrossnoKaye reports over 9,000 control software deployments per year and more than 1 million run hours with zero safety incidents. Each edge appliance also acts as an outbound-only information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) gateway that opens zero inbound firewall ports inside the plant, streaming high-frequency telemetry to AWS through Amazon VPC Lattice and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) . If cloud connectivity drops, the plant continues running safely on the base control narratives on the local edge cluster. Second, derived engineering signals and closed-loop optimization applications run on top of base control using the same shared plant model. In the cloud, CrossnoKaye’s Scheduling system runs two continuous pipelines from versioned Python packages in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , operating on configurable per-instance cadences and event-driven triggers when plant settings change. Synthetic reading algorithms compute derived engineering metrics, such as heat-flow distributions, asset health indices, energy intensity, and mass-balance deviations, and write them back to the historian alongside physical I/O. Closed-loop optimization applications run on top of the base control layer, combining those derived synthetic readings with physics models, model predictive control (MPC), reinforcement learning, utility tariffs, and weather forecasts to compute optimal setpoint schedules. Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) FIFO queues order every schedule and state update by facility before dispatching setpoints to the local base control narrative on the edge cluster, which CrossnoKaye reports runs 650,000 closed-loop control actions per day. Third, AURA runs inside the platform boundary on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) as microservices and durable Temporal workflows. items.title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
items.description: (Thanks to @Goutham Nalagatla for discussion and for sitting with me and talking about it while I wrote it.) METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post ), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff). That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago. Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report). If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon. And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can . For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration. I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this? Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have. This might be the case. Obviously, Redwood researchers extensively use AI agents for their research, mostly using Claude Code and recently Claude Tag. We also have an in-house scaffold for autonomous AI research, which has produced results that we've published in the past (e.g. here , here ), though we haven't put a lot of work into using or improving this scaffold in the last few months. We found that this research scaffold is pretty good at doing empirical research, but Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings; these weaknesses substantially reduced how quickly we could use it to produce useful research outputs. If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products? Maybe they get a lot of uplift from Anthropic-specific infra for their AIs? Maybe they don’t release scaffold features that are specifically useful for ML research? Overall, I think this is maybe a partial explanation, but it seems sort of surprising for our uplift to be way smaller than Anthropic’s. It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us. To some extent, our work is probably less accelerated by AI than Anthropic capabilities research is. I think most of our empirical research is similarly well-suited to AI speedup to most published ML capabilities research. Maybe Anthropic capabilities research is particularly well suited to AI speedup compared to most ML research? Some of the pretraining work may rely more on the AI's strengths. This could be the case if, for example, a big blocker on running experiments on new architectures is implementing them efficiently. One person from Anthropic told me recently that they think that capabilities research is notably more sped up than most of their short-term alignment work. Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed? A lot of the research we do is conducted by interns or relatively junior staff who work fairly closely with their manager to prioritize future experiments. Maybe it's the case that our IC researchers are, in fact, going way faster, but this just means they're much more bottlenecked by their managers' time to understand what they're up to. And maybe this is more true of us vs Anthropic because more of their ICs are more senior/self-reliant, or their research requires less tricky judgement? There are some cases where huge speedup happened. E.g. my guess is that Ryan’s work in the Hugging Face investigation was made wildly faster through his intense use of AI agents; this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows. Whatever the case is, I feel like we are imminently going to learn a lot about how feasible it is to accelerate AI safety research using AI labor. If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon. At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong. See also AI speeds up 3rd party safety researchers by ~1.6x (via self-reports) Discuss

items.title: Claude Code is accidentally exposing secrets all over GitHub
items.description: Claude Code is leaking sensitive information on public GitHub instances thanks to a partial oversight in the way its settings files are handled. That's the finding of AI security researchers at Apiiro, who discovered thousands of secrets , including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, amid Claude Code settings files embedded in GitHub repositories. The leak stems from the way Claude Code handles user approval for automated shell commands. When a user chooses the "Yes, and don't ask again" option to approve running a command, that choice gets stored as part of a rule in the local ".claude/settings.local.json" file on the user's computer. That rule is sometimes coded as a pattern, but the command itself is often written to that settings file as is, including any sensitive information that may be embedded within it. This isn't really a significant security issue if the settings file stays on the user's local machine (assuming that machine doesn't become compromised itself, of course). And Anthropic notes in its Claude Code documentation that this particular settings file gets added to the developer's global .gitignore list , which usually prevents it from being shared publicly. items.title: Nancy Pelosi’s replacement is ready to regulate AI
items.description: As a California state senator, Scott Wiener authored legislation aimed at curbing the risks of advanced AI. Now, after winning a tight congressional race for former Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi’s open San Francisco seat, he could play a key role in setting federal AI policy. I spoke with Wiener on Friday, only a few hours after he had been declared the victor. But he was already thinking about AI risk. The previous day, the AI nonprofit METR had released a report that had been widely interpreted as evidence that Anthropic had achieved recursive self-improvement, a phenomenon in which AI meaningfully contributes to its own advancement and AI progress potentially spins out of control. “It’s very concerning,” Wiener said, citing the report as evidence that we are quickly running out of time to regulate AI. “It was my hope that Congress would take decisive action before [the end of] this year,” he said. “That does not appear to be happening.” Wiener has been increasingly focused on AI in recent years, and he’s made many of the AI safety movement’s concerns his own: During our 20-minute conversation, he used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” half a dozen times, for example.“We need to slow this down,” he says. “Because it’s moving very quickly, and we could sleepwalk into a disaster.” Wiener has already had real influence on AI policy. SB 1047, a bill that he authored in 2024, was set to become the first real piece of frontier AI legislation in the country before it was vetoed by California governor Gavin Newsom; he then sponsored SB 53, a lighter-touch bill that Newsom signed. Both bills have inspired proposed federal legislation. Wiener’s congressional campaign received over $3 million from Public First Action, a nonprofit in favor of AI regulation that receives substantial funding from Anthropic. That contribution led opponents to criticize him for being too close to the AI industry , but Wiener says that couldn’t be further from the truth. “Public First supported me because I was the first lawmaker in the country to introduce AI regulation and the first to pass it and get it implemented,” he wrote in a message after our interview. “The attacks on me for [Public First’s] support were shockingly cynical—literally attacking a candidate who actually regulated AI over Big Tech’s objection and falsely claiming the candidate is somehow too close to Big Tech.” Wiener says that if Congress forms a select committee on artificial intelligence—something that Democrats have discussed since September—he’d be eager to serve. And he’s enthusiastic about many of the policy ideas floating around Congress. “I think it’s really important to have a strong, empowered, nimble federal regulator,” he says, noting that Representative Ro Khanna, a fellow Democrat from California, has proposed legislation to establish such a regulator. He also highlights the importance of whistleblower protections, testing and auditing requirements, and a kill switch requirement, and he wants to see Congress leverage its oversight powers to hold the AI labs to account. “This is about the future of humanity, and we want to make sure that the public has a say and that the public knows what’s going on,” he says. And as a longtime state legislator, he is opposed to broad federal preemption of state AI laws, which some of the proposed federal legislation would require. “States are, as Brandeis says , laboratories,” he notes. “You want the states to be able to continue to be nimble in ways that Congress sometimes is not.” Above all, Wiener says, he wants Congress to pass policies with real teeth. “It’s critically important that when Congress acts, that we do so in a way that is truly meaningful and that meets the moment,” he says. That means taking seriously the possibility of AI catastrophe, something he discusses in the sort of language typically used by AI safety experts. “We’re in a moment that is very dangerous in terms of the risk of loss of control over AI,” he told me. “We need to deal with recursive self-improvement. Once you’re in that realm, that really is potentially a recipe for total loss of control.” He’ll have some allies in the fight against catastrophic AI risk. Senator Bernie Sanders, for instance, has met with many of the AI safety movement’s most influential figures and has spoken repeatedly about AI and existential risk. But there’s still a large gap between Wiener’s Bay Area, AGI-pilled perspective and the national mood on AI, which is anchored by opposition to data centers. The fact that voters approved 40 out of 41 anti-data-center ballot measures on Tuesday might seem to be a good sign for Wiener and others who support AI regulation, but Wiener says he sees this movement as far more tied to local concerns than to bigger questions about AI risk. “Peoople who are really opposed to where AI is going—this is an area where they can actually do something about it,” he says. “But the data center revolt—to me, I think it’s more so that people are upset that there could be something like this in their community, with all the impacts near people’s homes, driving up electric bills and using water. I think that’s the bigger issue for most people, from what I can tell.” Wiener describes himself as only “cautiously optimistic” about Congress’s ability to rein in AI, given its poor track record on regulating the tech industry. He also has concerns about the ability to get legislation past President Donald Trump, who called concerns about catastrophic AI risk a “hoax” in September and has demonstrated a stark unwillingness to collaborate with China, something that Wiener sees as essential to preventing the worst consequences of AI. But he says Trump’s unpredictability provides some measure of hope, though it’s a fraught kind of hope. “So far what we’ve seen are some problematic things, but not complete disasters,” Wiener says. “I hope that it doesn’t take a disaster to spur the president into acting. items.title: AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security
items.description: This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast . Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance. However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof? There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP? Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces. This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution. Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust. How quickly can de-authentication attacks occur? An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system. There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals? Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform. Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration. The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents. Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. items.title: Import AI 480: Self-sustaining space economies; AI for science progress, and Meta builds perfect hands for a superintelligence
items.description: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now AI Science startup converts a quantum conjecture into a theorem: …An evocative taste of the singularity… In the same way a few years ago it went from remarkable to unremarkable to see computers gain the ability to identify objects in images, we’re now in an era where it’s rapidly going from remarkable to unremarkable for computers to extend the bounds of human knowledge. The latest example comes from Physical Superintelligence, an AI science startup which has proved a longstanding quantum computing conjecture. What they did: “Open since 2008, the conjecture of Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis concerns when quantum computers can be exponentially faster than ordinary ones. Now, a research system developed internally at Physical Superintelligence (PSI), running a non-public Anthropic model, found a proof for it, settling one of the most fundamental questions in quantum computing,” the startup writes. “The system had a complete proof of the conjecture during the third day of the run, and Lean, a proof assistant in which a computer checks every step, accepted it. We then set the system to work on related open problems. Along the way, the system improved the result twice, and Lean accepted the final version.” Why this matters – we are in the singularity : As I said in my speech at the IMF ( #477 ), I believe we’re in the early stages of the singularity, defined as the period when the rate of technological and scientific progress exceeds the rate at which we humans can parse out and make sense of it. Research like this is a taste of what that means; mostly automated synthetic researchers extending the frontier of knowledge, spitting out results which need to then be understood by humans. Read more: A proof of the Aaronson‑Ambainis conjecture (Physical Superintelligence, blog) . *** Meta builds the hands that a superintelligence needs to take over the world: …Combine Tactus with an autonomous agent and you have the makings of a scifi takeover… Meta Reality Labs Research has published details on Tactus, “a textile-integrated tactile and pose sensing glove designed from the ground up for naturalistic manipulation data collection”. The cool thing about this glove is that it helps record fine-grained detail from hands as they’re manipulating objects – this is the kind of thing that cameras can visually report but often leads to sub-par data due to occlusion during manipulation. It’s also interesting because this is exactly the kind of hardware an autonomous AI system might want to pay humans to wear so it could gather data and get feedback from the world. More details on Tactus: The gloves have three design pillars: “(1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies”, Meta writes. “Tactus provides calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a textile-integrated form factor that preserves natural grasp behavior.” “(3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable.” Why this matters – hand-by-wire: Picture some takeoff scenario where an AI system has carved out an independent niche for itself running on some stolen compute, perhaps even using a form of distributed inference and training. The AI now has a few goals, some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the digital world, and some of which can be satisfied by doing things in the physical world. For the physical world stuff, it either needs to be able to get robots to do the thing, or figure out a way to get people to work for it – the Tactus gloves are the kind of hardware you might imagine a rogue AI paying people to wear so they could both a) perform tasks for it and it could give live feedback, and b) become a source of data generation for the AI itself. Of course, I am not endorsing this particular future! But I have begun to find it helpful to view research papers through the lens of “how would an AI use this”, similar to how it is often helpful to view papers through the lens of “how would an intelligence agency use the insights shared here”. Read more : Tactus: Tactile & Pose Sensing Glove for Natural Dexterity Data Collection (arXiv) . *** Building a self-sustaining space economy is cheaper than you think – especially with Starship: …A 2016 NASA paper contains some exciting ideas for off-Earth industrialization… Here’s a fascinating paper from researchers with the NASA Kennedy Space Center in 2016 about what it’d take to bootstrap a self-sustaining industry on the moon. “Once successfully bootstrapped, a robotic network can access, process, transport, and utilize the solar system’s resources for mankind’s benefit,” the researchers write. Moon manufacturing – cheaper than you think: The big idea in the paper is how little mass is required to kickstart a manufacturing ecosystem. The key is to start with a relatively basic set of things and then build up from there, eventually fabricating chips on the moon. “In the baseline case with maximum manufacturing rate, a total of 41 MT is launched to the Moon. In the reduced rate case, only 12 MT is launched to the Moon but the scale of industry is two orders of magnitude smaller so the benefits of the industry are relatively delayed by eight years”. items.title: Innovating with AI in the special chemicals industry
items.description: As companies look to accelerate innovation with artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and advanced modeling, the primary challenge is connecting new technologies to reliable data, scientific expertise, and the practical realities of bringing products to market. For specialty chemicals manufacturer Lubrizol, digital transformation is all about giving researchers the tools to test ideas faster, make better-informed decisions, and develop more sustainable materials without compromising performance. Girish Rao, vice president of information technology at Lubrizol, says the company is building a digital foundation that connects business processes, modern data platforms, and cloud infrastructure to support its research and development (R&D) teams. Their goal is to combine decades of accumulated technical data with the deep expertise of chemists and engineers who understand customer needs as well as the physical constraints of their work. Data scientists can help identify patterns, test new hypotheses, and model possibilities before researchers conduct physical experiments. But, Rao emphasizes, “it’s not about replacing scientific judgment; it is about giving our scientists better tools.” Scientists, data scientists, and IT teams approach problems from different perspectives, prioritizing experimental validity, model performance, and platform security and scalability, respectively. By bringing these groups together in “fusion teams,” Lubrizol aligns them around shared objectives, starting with small pilots to build trust. “Once the trust is built between the team members and they know what value they’re about to create,” Rao says, “things go a lot better.” Cloud infrastructure also gives the company flexibility to access computing resources and modern tools without making the substantial investments required to build and maintain its own data centers. These capabilities could prove especially valuable in advancing sustainability. Digital modeling can help researchers evaluate more formulations, explore materials such as starch and corn-based alternatives, and assess trade-offs across a product’s life cycle. Promising a material in a laboratory is only the first step. Scaling production while meeting performance expectations, regulatory requirements, and financial constraints is still a tightrope walk, but AI’s ability to model multiple variables could help teams navigate those competing demands. Looking to the future, Rao expects AI, automation, advanced modeling, digital twins, and connected data to converge as laboratories become more intelligent and manufacturing plants more efficient. The opportunity, he suggests, lies in bringing these capabilities together responsibly and at scale. “It’s not just a single technology. I think it’s the combination of all of these, and it’ll be the ability to connect all these processes that are going to generate tremendous amounts of data.” This webcast is produced in partnership with Infosys. items.title: NVIDIA Announces New Planned Investments in Korean Startups at the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum
items.description: Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT and NVIDIA hosted the MSIT -NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX. Ryu Je-myung, vice minister of science and ICT , joined NVIDIA leaders to meet with over 20 Korean startups across foundation models, physical AI, AI infrastructure and AI semiconductors. NVIDIA also announced an investment in Korean startup Point2 , with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies , RLWRLD and Upstage. Point2 Technology, an AI interconnect company, builds scalable, radio frequency-based interconnects that move data between chips and racks in AI factories, offering an innovative alternative to conventional copper and optical interconnect solutions for AI cluster scale-up, delivering the reach, performance and efficiency needed for next-generation AI infrastructure. Motif Technologies , a Seoul-based AI lab, develops foundation models for building AI agents that carry out complex tasks, including Motif-3, a large language model released with open weights. RLWRLD, a physical AI startup based in San Francisco, Seoul and Tokyo, develops robotics foundation models that enable humanoid and industrial robots to perform complex real-world tasks that require five-finger dexterity, such as precisely inserting components, threading nuts onto bolts and kitting parts from moving conveyors. Upstage , a Korean enterprise AI company, develops Solar language models and document AI tools that help businesses extract information from complex documents, streamline workflows and build AI applications for everyday operations. The companies represent work across the full AI stack , from infrastructure to models to robotics applications. The planned investments build on NVIDIA’s work with Korea’s startup and venture community, including more than 1,000 Korea-based members of NVIDIA Inception , a program that helps startups grow with access to preferred pricing, technical expertise and opportunities for investor introductions.

items.title: Korea’s AI Ecosystem Advances and Secures Agentic AI With NVIDIA
items.description: As AI agents take on more work, they need capable open models and security that advances alongside them. Hyundai Motor Group is exploring NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and the NVIDIA OpenShell runtime, while AIM Intelligence is integrating its Starfort platform with NVIDIA OpenShell to support secure AI agents for employee productivity and enterprise workflows . A key component of the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform, OpenShell provides a secure runtime with sandboxed execution and policy-based controls to safeguard sensitive data, manage access to enterprise tools and govern autonomous agent actions. AIM Intelligence , a Korean AI security company, is integrating its Starfort agent control platform with NVIDIA OpenShell. The goal is to combine OpenShell’s runtime access controls with Starfort’s detection of malicious instructions and data leakage. The company is also considering a preliminary proof of concept for the public energy sector, with potential applications across enterprise, industrial and robotics environments. On the model side, LG AI Research is opening application programming interface access for K-EXAONE-2.5, developed using NVIDIA Nemotron datasets, including Nemotron-Personas-Korea . Nemotron-Personas-Korea is an open dataset of 7 million fully synthetic Korean personas, grounded in official Korean statistics, that model builders use to ground training data and evaluation in Korean contexts. NVIDIA Nemotron is a family of open models, datasets and techniques that help developers build specialized, efficient AI agents. Learn more about NVIDIA Nemotron open models and get started building secure agents with NVIDIA OpenShell .

items.title: From Chips to Skills, NVIDIA and Korea Expand Sovereign AI Collaboration
items.description: NVIDIA and Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) are expanding their collaboration across the country’s sovereign AI ecosystem, from AI semiconductors and data center infrastructure to talent, startups, models, agents and security. The collaboration lays the groundwork for Korean NPU and XPU companies to explore participation in the NVIDIA NVLink Fusion ecosystem, and includes NVIDIA training and certification programs, hackathons and technical seminars to strengthen GPU utilization. Through Korea’s AI for All initiative, NVIDIA will collaborate with three selected consortia and four leading Korean foundation model builders, using NVIDIA Dynamo software to optimize and scale AI inference. In addition, NVIDIA today announced a collaboration with SK Telecom and Rebellions, supported by MSIT, to advance sovereign AI infrastructure for Korean models and workloads with NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. Read more in the press release .

items.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Recipes Bring Korea’s Leading Open Models to Production
items.description: NVIDIA is releasing Dynamo-optimized deployment recipes for Korea’s leading open models: A.X K2 from SK Telecom , K-EXAONE 2.0 from LG AI Research , Solar Open 2 from Upstage and Motif-3 from Motif Technologies . As models grow beyond the capacity of a single GPU, they must be split across multiple GPUs, requiring careful coordination of request routing and communication to maintain performance. NVIDIA Dynamo is an open source, distributed inference-serving framework built to deploy models in multi-node environments at data center scale. It handles this routing and communication to maximize inference performance. Optimized for NVIDIA B200 GPUs, these recipes take the guesswork out of deployment, delivering up to 2x performance out of the box. They help developers bring Korea’s open models into production faster and turn them into broadly accessible AI for All services. Learn more about NVIDIA Dynamo .

items.title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
items.description: arXiv:2611.08506v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor. We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).

items.title: The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford
items.description: My comment on The Web Is More Than Enough, by Paul Ford — Hacker News. OK, this comment convinced me to give that a shot. Here's a thing I made in Three.js this morning - a Nudibranch themed Faberge Egg: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (77KB) I just asked Claude (Opus 5.5 Medium running in regular Claude Chat) to port that to Vanilla JS, in the same thread where it had built it, and got this: https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/Hidden-Reef-Egg... (98KB) They aren't identical - you can see what Claude said about that in the transcript (I don't fully understand why it differed): https://claude.ai/share/e56d163e-2793-4677-aa11-191d5058b414 But yeah, it turns out Claude Opus 5.5 is perfectly capable of 3D modeling in Vanilla JS + WebGL without Three.js. In eyeballing the code I find the Three.js slightly easier to understand myself, but I rarely look at the code for these 3D projects so that isn't a particularly big deal. items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.description: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: Claude Opus 5.5 The hook Plugins implement register_agent_reference_types(datasette) ... When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow. I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests. The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed. I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature. The full agent-written essay then follows in a . I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example. My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details. I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time. Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used: datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot) datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot) datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - " edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)." datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above. llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml , so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output. The mnemonic I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it or ? Here are two tricks that helped me. First, and most obviously, the is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the element must then wrap everything else. An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary". "details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details". Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again. (I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.) Tags: github , html , markdown , ai , datasette , generative-ai , llms , ai-assisted-programming , llm , coding-agents

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.description: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did, using "Clinger's fast path": Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . Tags: research , c , rust , sqlite , claude

items.title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
items.description: Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026) , say this threshold will be met when: They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs. For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed. The report authors found that: Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative." While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted. This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack . Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team ) have projected. Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that. The rest of the post: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai Tweet thread: https://x.com/ajeya_cotra/status/2118802809814708533 Discuss

items.title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
items.description: I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later. Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context . I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll likely be Substack only ; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate. Take-off Speed: In Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me , Ajeya describes three scenarios: Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018): “There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)“. At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall). Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: “An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips” How should we characterise progress up until now? Eliezer writes : If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience. Tom Davidson responded : If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”. “Bumpy” intelligence explosions Forethought defines an additional scenario . For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs. (Modified version of Forethought diagram.) In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology ) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”. Elsewhere they’ve framed this as jaggedness applying not just to capabilities, but also to rate of change. (Modified version of Forethought diagram.) Delving into the weeds Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speeds is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible. Complicating matters further, if someone talks about short-timelines to AGI, it matters hugely whether they mean human-level intelligence (like some researchers have argued that we have already achieved ) or whether they mean a system that is strongly capable of autonomously learning and improving itself. As Ajeya notes , someone might have short-timelines to AGI and then a slow-take off from there, or they might believe that things will move very fast once we’ve achieved the AGI milestone. A fast take-off post-AGI is much more likely if we mean the latter definition. Of course, whether a “take-off” is fast or slow may depend on when we start counting from. Do we start counting from ChatGPT/GPT4 or only when we hit a particular AGI milestone? I think it’s useful to have the concept of a take-off that is slow then fast (argument in favour: perhaps there’s a phase transition when AI starts to feed back into its own development, argument against: improvements in AI-assisted development might be continuous and required simply to maintain the previous pace in light of decreasing marginal returns). Feedback loops The previous section focused primarily on what RSI might look like in terms of outputs , this section focuses on what kind of feedback loop might be driving this. Types of “Intelligence Explosion”: Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops : Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion: software only recursive self-improvement AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design, full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips. The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff. items.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
items.description: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: ; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette

items.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
items.description: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett

items.title: State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away
items.description: Nous Research retrained Alibaba's Qwen3.8-27B to produce Arete-27B, largely stripping out its pro-Chinese bias. The propaganda rate dropped from 22 percent to less than one percent, while general capabilities remained intact in tests. The method relied on 53 million tokens of supervised fine-tuning. The political bias is "applied late, it is applied thin," the team writes. The article State propaganda in some Chinese AI models is only "a thin layer" that fine-tuning can strip away appeared first on The Decoder .
