items.title: Beyond code generation: A developer’s guide to agentic engineering
items.description: This October, GitHub saw more than 1.2 billion commits in one week—over 400% more than a year earlier. This is more commits than GitHub received in all of 2025. Chances are, you’re generating more code than you were a year ago. But ask yourself: do you feel 400% more productive than you were last year? Building software takes more than a good prompt. As AI speeds up implementation, software developers are feeling more pressure in other places: a Faros AI study found that pull requests spent 441% longer in review when teams went from low to high AI adoption. As a software developer, you gather requirements and steer implementation, review changes and evaluate test results, then investigate what happens in production. Agents can help you work more efficiently across all of these stages: Plan, Build, Verify, and Observe. We’ll walk through what an effective agentic engineering workflow looks like on GitHub. Plan: Get everyone and every agent on the same page See if this sounds familiar. You’re planning an API change. The design is in one tool, a compatibility requirement is buried in Slack, and an old pull request explains why the current implementation works this way. Before you can write a useful plan, you need to connect those details, compare approaches, and agree on how existing clients will keep working. What looked like a straightforward planning task has become hours of searching, cross-checking, and chasing answers. You’re exhausted before implementation even begins. You can use Copilot to pull that scattered context into one place, work through the tradeoffs, and turn the decisions into an implementation plan. Plan together where your team already works. Use Copilot in Slack or Teams to collaborate with everyone involved—from product managers and designers to analysts and business stakeholders. Bring in context from connected tools so your team can check assumptions, contribute ideas, and refine requirements together. Turn agreed-upon requirements into actionable work. Ask Copilot to create GitHub Issues with the context and acceptance criteria needed for implementation, breaking out tasks that can be handled separately. Keep routine triage from consuming planning time. Use GitHub Agentic Workflows to label your issues and estimate task complexity. Assign low-complexity tasks directly to Copilot, then spend your time focusing on harder decisions. Give complex work the planning it needs. Use Plan Mode in your preferred Copilot surface to compare approaches and refine an implementation plan. Review and approve the plan before handing it off to Copilot to begin implementation. What took days of searching and context gathering now produces a reviewable plan, explicit acceptance criteria, and scoped issues, with your time spent on the decisions instead of the retrieval. Then, once you settle on an approach, you’ve already set yourself and your agents up to implement your plan. Build: Move more than one task forward at a time You’re ready to turn that plan into code. But life has other ideas. Your agent is halfway through a task, your next meeting starts in five minutes, and your dog has been staring at the door for twenty. Then someone in the meeting points out an edge case the implementation needs to handle. Everyone needs something from you at once. You’d like to keep making progress, but you can’t be in three places at the same time. You can keep your work moving without being tied to the computer where you started it. Continue your conversation from another device. Session continuity lets you pick up the same Copilot session across clients, so you can work wherever it’s most convenient for you. Let work continue after you close your laptop. Copilot runs tasks in cloud sandboxes , keeping execution off your machine and allowing you to leave and return to a session later. Work on separate tasks without mixing their edits. The Copilot app gives sessions isolated copies of the repository, so an implementation task and a documentation update don’t share an unfinished working tree. Carry project knowledge into each task. Repository instructions capture conventions and validation commands, while shared memory stores useful facts Copilot can reuse across a repository. Copilot Dreaming reviews eligible sessions and pull request feedback to keep memories current and propose instruction or skill updates. That means less time re-explaining how your team works and more consistent help from Copilot across tasks. Match the models to the work. Select Copilot Fusion to choose models and reasoning depth for the task, bringing in additional models to review a solution when needed. You set the effort level to balance quality, cost, and response time. Follow company rules wherever you work. Enterprise managed settings carry your company’s policies and configured tools across Copilot surfaces, reducing setup differences as you move between clients. Writing code is more than shooting off a single prompt to your LLM and seeing what you get back. And with more work on your plate than ever, it can be difficult to maintain your coding standards and deliver your projects on time. Copilot helps tasks progress independently with shared project knowledge, while letting you pick up a session where you left off across devices. That gives you more room to work through implementation decisions and handle changes as they come up. And as your work finishes, you have focused changes ready to review. Verify: Spend your attention where it counts After spending an hour wrangling your agents to get them moving in the right direction, you think you’ve all landed in a good spot. So you open a pull request labeled “small refactor.” It changes 47 files. You wanted feedback on shared validation logic, but it’s buried among updates to every endpoint that calls it, formatting changes, and several hundred lines of generated tests.

items.title: AIエージェントのROIの算出方法を解説！計算式とKPI設計から試算例まで
items.description: AIエージェントの導入効果を問われ、削減できた時間を金額に換算できず困っている担当者は多いでしょう。 ROIは、導入で得た効果から総コストを引き、総コストで割れば算出できます。ただしAIエージェントは実行ごとにコストが変わるため、従来のSaaSと同じ見積もりでは数字がずれます。 導入前の数値を測らないまま進めると、効果を示せず予算を打ち切られる事態を招きます。 計算式とコストの内訳を押さえれば、稟議にそのまま使える試算を作れます。 本記事では、エージェント特有の変動コストを含めたROIの計算式と、導入前後の測り方、業務別の試算例を中心に解説します。 自社の数字を当てはめながら、最後までお読みください。 AIエージェントのROIを算出する計算式 ROIの算出に必要な考え方は、以下の3つです。 基本の計算式 効果に含める4つの軸 ハードROIとソフトROIの違い 3つを押さえておけば、数字の根拠を問われても説明できる試算になります。 基本の計算式 ROIは、投資に対してどれだけの利益が出たかを示す割合です。AIエージェントでも、式そのものは一般的なROIと変わりません。 ROI（%）＝（効果の金額－総コスト）÷総コスト×100 総コストに、初期費用だけでなく運用費まで含める点 が算出のポイントです。運用費を除くと、ROIが実態より高く出てしまいます。 たとえば効果が480万円、総コストが300万円なら、ROIは60%です。 式を固定しておけば、部署や業務が変わっても同じ基準で比較できます。経営層への説明も一貫します。 効果に含める4つの軸 AIエージェントの効果は、以下の4つの軸に分けて金額へ換算します。 軸 効果の例 金額への換算方法 時間削減 問い合わせ対応や資料作成の工数減 削減時間×時間単価 コスト削減 外注費や派遣費の減少 導入前の支払額－導入後の支払額 売上向上 商談数や受注率の増加 増加した受注額×粗利率 品質・リスク低減 ミスや手戻りの減少 減った件数×1件あたりの損失額 業務に合う軸を選び、重複しないように合算します。 時間削減は、実際に別の業務へ振り向けた時間だけを数える のが原則です。 浮いた時間を使い切れていなければ、金額としての効果は発生していません。 ハードROIとソフトROIの違い 効果は、金額に直結するかどうかでハードROIとソフトROIに分かれます。 項目 ハードROI ソフトROI 対象 金額で測れる効果 金額に直結しにくい効果 例 人件費・外注費の削減、売上の増加 従業員満足度の向上、意思決定の速さ 稟議での扱い 判断の根拠にする 補足として添える 稟議の判断材料にするのはハードROI で、ソフトROIは補足にとどめます。ソフトROIを無理に金額へ置き換えると、試算全体の信頼性が下がります。 両者を切り分けておけば、経営層から金額に換算できない効果を問われても、落ち着いて答えられます。 AIエージェントのROIに含めるコスト項目 総コストは、以下の3種類に分けて集計します。 初期費用 従量課金などの運用費 人の確認・保守工数 従来のSaaS導入と違い、後ろの2つがエージェント特有のコストです。見落とすと総コストが過小になります。 初期費用 初期費用は、導入前に一度だけ発生するコストです。計上する項目は以下のとおりです。 要件定義、開発または設定の費用 既存システムとの連携費用 データ整備の費用 社内研修の費用 研修費とデータ整備費は、計上が漏れやすい項目 です。担当者の作業時間も人件費として換算します。 初期費用を洗い出しておけば、回収までの期間を正しく見積もれます。 従量課金などの運用費 AIエージェントは、1回の実行ごとに生成AIのAPI利用料（トークン課金）が発生します。処理件数が増えると、費用も比例して増えます。 月間運用費＝基本利用料＋（1件あたりの実行費用×月間処理件数） 処理件数の増加を見込み、平均的な月と最も多い月の両方で試算 しておくと安全です。固定ライセンス型のソフトと同じ感覚で見積もると、利用が広がった月に予算を超えます。 変動幅を事前に示しておけば、予算超過の懸念にも先回りして答えられます。 人の確認・保守工数 エージェントの出力を人が確認する工数と、運用を保つための保守工数も総コストに含めます。 出力結果の確認や承認にかかる時間 プロンプトや業務ルールの見直し エラーや障害への対応 確認工数は、確認時間×時間単価で金額に換算 します。確認が多い業務ほど、自動化で浮く時間が減ります。 この工数を含めておけば、導入後に効果が想定を下回る事態を避けられます。 AIエージェントのROIを測る5ステップ ROIの測定は、以下の5ステップで進めます。 ステップ1：対象業務を決める ステップ2：導入前のベースラインを計測する ステップ3：KPIを設定する ステップ4：導入後の効果を計測する ステップ5：ROIを算出して報告する 導入前のステップ2を飛ばすと、後からROIを算出できなくなります。 ステップ1：対象業務を決める 最初に、ROIを測る対象の業務を1つに絞ります。 対象は、処理件数が多く、手順が一定で、成果を数値で取れる業務が適しています。カスタマーサポートの問い合わせ対応や、経理の請求書処理が代表例です。 範囲を絞って小さく始める と、効果と原因を切り分けやすくなります。最初の成功例が、全社展開の説得材料になります。 ステップ2：導入前のベースラインを計測する 導入前の状態を数値で記録します。記録する指標は以下のとおりです。 月間の処理件数 1件あたりの所要時間 エラー率や手戻り率 担当者の時間単価 導入後に計測を始めても、改善幅は比較できません。 最低でも数週間分を記録し、繁閑の差をならしておきます。 この記録が、そのまま稟議資料の比較元になります。 ステップ3：KPIを設定する ROIの根拠になるKPIを、3〜5個に絞って設定します。指標を増やしすぎると、報告のたびに集計が重くなります。 業務自動化率（エージェントだけで完了した割合） 人の確認率（人が確認や修正に介入した割合） 1件あたりの処理時間 エラー率 処理件数や完了数は作業量を示すだけ で、事業への効果は示しません。顧客満足度や受注額など、成果に近い指標も1つ加えます。 ステップ4：導入後の効果を計測する 導入前と同じ指標を、同じ方法で計測します。計測方法が変わると、比較できなくなります。 導入直後は、担当者の習熟やルールの調整が進んでおらず、効果が低く出ます。 数か月単位で推移を見て 、判断するのが現実的です。 可能であれば、エージェントを使うチームと使わないチームを比較します。業務量の季節変動の影響を除けます。 ステップ5：ROIを算出して報告する 最後に、月次で累計の効果と累計のコストを並べ、ROIと損益分岐点を示します。 報告書には、時間単価や有効活用率といった前提条件を明記します。 前提を開示した試算は、数字への信頼を得やすくなります。 前提が見えていれば、経営層が条件を変えた場合の数字も、その場で確認できます。 AIエージェントのROI試算例 以下の3つの業務について、仮定の数値でROIを試算します。 カスタマーサポート 経理 営業 数値はすべて説明用の仮定であり、実在する企業の実績ではありません。 カスタマーサポートの試算例 月間の問い合わせが3,000件のカスタマーサポートで、エージェントが一次対応を担う想定です。前提は以下のとおりです。 エージェントが自己解決する割合：40%（月1,200件） 1件あたりの対応時間：10分 時間単価：3,000円 初期費用：120万円 月間運用費：30万円（利用料と従量課金20万円、確認工数6万円、保守4万円） 月間効果＝1,200件×10分÷60×3,000円＝60万円 年間効果＝60万円×12か月＝720万円 総コスト＝120万円＋30万円×12か月＝480万円 ROI＝（720万円－480万円）÷480万円×100＝50% 初期費用は、月ごとの純効果30万円（60万円－30万円）で4か月目に回収 できる計算です。 経理の試算例 月1,500件の請求書処理で、1件あたり5分の短縮を見込む想定です。前提は以下のとおりです。 月間の処理件数：1,500件 1件あたりの短縮時間：5分 時間単価：3,000円 初期費用：60万円 月間運用費：19万円（利用料12万円、確認工数4.5万円、保守2.5万円） 月間効果＝1,500件×5分÷60×3,000円＝37.5万円 年間効果＝37.5万円×12か月＝450万円 総コスト＝60万円＋19万円×12か月＝288万円 ROI＝（450万円－288万円）÷288万円×100＝約56% 月ごとの純効果は18.5万円（37.5万円－19万円）で、 初期費用は4か月目に回収 できます。1件あたりの短縮が小さくても、件数が多い定型業務ではROIが出やすくなります。 営業の試算例 営業担当10人が、提案資料の作成やリサーチ、議事録作成にエージェントを使う想定です。前提は以下のとおりです。 1人あたりの月間削減時間：12時間 削減時間のうち実際に活用できる割合：50% 時間単価：4,000円 初期費用：50万円 月間運用費：22万円（利用料15万円、確認工数4万円、保守3万円） 活用できる時間＝10人×12時間×50%＝60時間 月間効果＝60時間×4,000円＝24万円 年間効果＝24万円×12か月＝288万円 総コスト＝50万円＋22万円×12か月＝314万円 ROI＝（288万円－314万円）÷314万円×100＝約－8% 時間削減だけでは、ROIがマイナスになる 試算です。商談に回した時間が受注にどれだけ寄与したかを、売上向上の軸として加えて再評価します。 売上への寄与を別の指標で追っておけば、時間削減だけでは赤字に見える施策でも、継続の是非を正しく判断できます。 AIエージェントのROIに関する調査データと読み方 ROIを説明するときに押さえておきたい調査データと、読み方の要点は以下の3つです。 ROIを得ている企業の割合 ROIの評価軸が損益へ移っている動き ベンダー発表の数値を読むときの注意点 数値の意味を取り違えると、稟議で根拠の甘さを指摘されます。 ROIを得ている企業の割合 Google Cloudは2025年9月、生成AIを導入済みの企業の経営層3,466人（24か国）を対象にした調査結果を発表しました。52%の経営層が、自社でAIエージェントを活用していると回答しています。 生成AIのROIについては、74%の経営層が1年以内に達成したと答えました。AI予算の50%以上をエージェントに充てる先行導入企業（回答者の13%）では、88%が少なくとも1つの用途でROIを得ています。 74%と88%は生成AI全般のROIで、AIエージェント単体のROIではありません。 引用するときは、この区別を明記する必要があります。 参考： Google Cloud Study Reveals 52% of Executives Say Their Organizations Have Deployed AI Agents（Google Cloud） ROIの評価軸が生産性から損益へ移っている Futurum Groupの2026年上半期調査（IT意思決定者830人）では、評価軸の変化が示されました。最も重視するROI指標として、売上や利益などの直接的な財務インパクトを挙げた回答が、21.7%とほぼ倍増しています。 一方、生産性向上を挙げた回答は23.8%から18.0%に下がりました。 時間削減だけでなく、損益への影響まで示す 試算が、経営層に求められる傾向です。 参考： Enterprise AI ROI Shifts as Agentic Priorities Surge（Futurum Group） 前述の営業の試算例のように、売上や利益の軸を加えておけば、この動きに沿った説明ができます。 ベンダー発表の数値を読むときの注意点 ベンダーや調査会社が公表するROIの数値は、条件が揃っていません。引用する前に、以下の3点を確認します。 調査の対象が、導入済み企業に限られていないか ROIの定義が、生成AI全般かAIエージェント単体か ブログなどの二次情報ではなく、一次の発表資料に遡れるか 一次の発表資料まで遡り、数値の定義を確認する 習慣が欠かせません。回答者の自己申告にもとづく数値は、自社の実測値とは別物として扱います。 確認を済ませた数値だけを使えば、稟議で出典を問われても説明に詰まりません。 AIエージェントのROIが出ない3つの原因 ROIが出ない原因は、以下の3つに集約できます。 対象業務の処理件数が少ない 導入前のベースラインがない 削減した時間が活用されていない 自社のROIが低い場合は、どの原因に当てはまるかを切り分けると、改善策が絞れます。 対象業務の処理件数が少ない 処理件数が少ない業務では、初期費用と運用費を回収できません。運用費の一部は件数に関係なく発生するためです。 月間の処理件数が少ない業務は、対象から外すか、複数の業務を同じエージェントにまとめます。 固定費を件数で割った1件あたりのコスト を、手作業の1件あたりのコストと比べると判断できます。 この比較をしておけば、導入前に見送るべき業務を見極められます。 導入前のベースラインがない 導入前の数値がないと、改善幅を示せず、ROIを算出できません。 導入後に慌てて過去の記録を探しても、集計方法が違い比較に使えないことが多くなります。 導入前の計測を、導入作業の一部として予定に組み込む のが確実です。 すでに導入済みの場合は、エージェントを使わないチームの数値を比較元にします。 削減した時間が活用されていない 削減時間を金額として計上できるのは、その時間が別の価値ある業務に使われた場合だけです。 営業の試算例のように、活用できる割合を見込んでいないと、効果が過大に出ます。 浮いた時間の使い道を、導入前に決めておく と、効果が実際の損益に表れます。 使い道が決まっていれば、ステップ3で設定した成果指標とも結び付き、報告の説得力が増します。 AIエージェントのROIに関するよくある質問 AIエージ

items.title: Building the next generation of multimodal AI experiences with fal in Microsoft Foundry
items.description: Microsoft and fal partner to expand video generation in Microsoft Foundry, helping developers bring creative ideas into enterprise applications. Video workloads do not all start with the same input or aim for the same result. A creative team might explore several interpretations of a written brief. A retailer might turn an approved product image into a short motion concept. An application developer might combine image generation and video generation into a workflow that takes an idea from description to frame to scene. Each scenario brings different requirements for visual quality, motion, creative control, turnaround time, and cost. All of this means that a multi-model solution is necessary to realize a full vision. Today, Microsoft and fal are helping developers find the right tools for their workloads. We are excited to announce that Kling, LTX, and MiniMax video models are rolling out to in public preview in Microsoft Foundry through our new partnership with fal. Available as a first-party Azure service, these text-to-video and image-to-video options give creators and developers more ways to utilize video generation with the experiences they want to build. The partnership expands the choices available in Microsoft Foundry while bringing video into the broader platform developers use to build AI applications. The goal is to let developers pick the right model for each step of an experience, then connect those steps into a working application. “fal has seen incredible adoption this year alone with generative media across all industries from advertising to marketing to gaming. Partnering with Microsoft allows both of us to truly enable the wide creative ecosystem and ensure that all AI solutions that lean on generative media, becomes a multi-model one.” – Burkay Gur, Cofounder Bringing fal’s generative media focus to enterprise builders fal is the full stack for generative media, built for creators and developers, with APIs for over 1500 models across image, video, audio, 3D, and generative worlds. As a truly encapsulating platform, fal provides inference, training, and infrastructure to run generative media workloads in production, while also providing innovative post trained models that pushes the boundaries on speed and quality. That specialization matters because generative media is both a creative and an engineering workload. A compelling demo is only the start. Production applications also need to handle real traffic, scale with demand, and balance output quality, latency, and cost. Through this partnership, developers will be able to access a selected set of video models in Microsoft Foundry, served by fal and sourced from the companies that build them. The initial portfolio gives teams a choice of models for different creative requirements instead of relying on one model for every task, with more models planned over time. A portfolio for different video experiences The initial portfolio spans Kling v3 Pro, LTX-2.5 Fast, LTX-2.5 Pro, MiniMax H3 Max, and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo. These models give developers different starting points for generating video from text and animating existing images. A team rapidly exploring creative concepts may prioritize speed and cost, while a team producing fewer, higher-fidelity assets may weigh output quality more heavily. Whether an application starts from text or an existing image, and what it needs in output quality and cost, also shapes the choice. Kling: From a still image to a directed scene Kling v3 Pro combines cinematic visuals and fluid motion with native audio generation and custom element support. Its image-to-video capabilities give developers control over how a starting image becomes a moving scene, a fit for applications that prioritize visual direction and motion. LTX: One model for fast drafts, one for final output For rapid iteration and previews, LTX-2.5 Fast is the speed-optimized option; for high-fidelity final output, LTX-2.5 Pro is the quality-optimized option. Both support text-to-video and image-to-video generation with synchronized audio. MiniMax: Another approach to video generation MiniMax H3 Max and MiniMax H3 Max Turbo are post-trained variants of MiniMax H3 focused on prompt adherence, aesthetics, and inference performance. For developers, they provide additional options to evaluate against an application’s creative brief, quality requirements, and performance needs. “When building with video models, the details matter: how closely the output follows your prompt, how well it preserves your reference images/videos/audios and how quickly you can try another idea. Kling gives developers control over detailed reference to video generation. LTX offers fast iteration and high-quality output through its Fast and Pro variants. H3 Max brings fal’s post-training and inference optimizations to improve quality and speed. Having these models available through Microsoft Foundry gives developers more flexibility to choose what works best for the application they are building.” – Gökay Aydoğan, Creative Engineer Built for enterprise video workloads Bringing video generation into an enterprise application requires more than choosing the right model. Teams need a platform where they can evaluate different options, build with the models that fit their requirements, and operate those experiences alongside the rest of their applications. The initial portfolio of video models is hosted in the US, and Microsoft Foundry is the first provider to offer a US-hosted Kling endpoint. Key considerations for enterprise teams: Data residency: For organizations with data residency requirements, hosting location is one factor to weigh. Review each model’s documented data processing and storage terms to confirm it meets your requirements. Model evaluation: Teams can assess quality, performance, and cost, then connect video generation with the other models and capabilities their applications need. items.title: AIエージェントの例10選！身近なツールから業務別の動きまで解説
items.description: 「AIエージェント」の意味は理解できても、自社の業務でどう動くのかが想像できず、提案資料に書けずに困っていませんか。 AIエージェントの例は、ChatGPT WorkやClaude Codeなどの身近なツールと、営業や経理などの業務別の動きという2方向から見ると整理できます。例を「すごい事例」として眺めるだけでは任せる範囲を誤り、確認を省いた運用で失敗するでしょう。 本記事では、各例を「依頼」「エージェントの動き」「人が確認する点」の順で解説します。企業名ではなくタスクの流れを追うため、自社の業務に置き換えて読めます。 読み終える頃には、自社のどの業務をAIエージェントに任せ、どこを人が確認すべきかを、例を引いて説明できるようになります。 まずは、AIエージェントの例と呼べる条件から確認しましょう。 AIエージェントと呼べる例の3条件 本記事でAIエージェントの例として扱うのは、次の3条件をすべて満たすものです。 目標を渡すだけで手順を自分で組む 外部ツールを操作して実行する 結果を確かめて自分で修正する この3条件に当てはまらない1問1答型のAIは、次章以降の例に含めていません。 目標を渡すだけで手順を自分で組む AIエージェントは、 達成したい目標だけを渡せば、必要な手順を自分で組み立てます 。 チャットAIは、人が手順を分解して1つずつ質問する前提です。一方でAIエージェントは、分解の作業そのものを引き受けます。 たとえば「今月の請求書を発注データと突き合わせて」と依頼すると、読み取り、照合、差異の抽出という順序を自分で決めます。 手順の設計を任せられるため、依頼する人は「何を達成したいか」の整理に集中できます。 外部ツールを操作して実行する AIエージェントは、ブラウザ、ファイル、コマンドなどの 外部ツールを実際に操作して作業を進めます 。 文章を返すだけのAIは、結果を人が手作業で反映しなければなりません。AIエージェントは、反映までを自分で行います。 Claude Codeは、Anthropicの公式ドキュメントでコードベースを読み、ファイルを編集し、コマンドを実行するツールと説明されています。 反映の手間が減る分、人が見るべき点は「何を操作したか」の記録に移ります。 結果を確かめて自分で修正する AIエージェントは、 実行した結果を自分で確認し、足りなければやり直します 。 Claude Codeの公式ドキュメントでは、情報を集め、行動し、結果を検証する流れを繰り返すと説明されています。人はこの途中でいつでも割り込めます。 たとえば、コードを変更してテストが失敗した場合は、エラーを読んで修正案を作り、テストを再度実行します。 自己修正があっても結果が完全とは限りません。人が最終結果を確認する工程を残す前提で、運用を設計できます。 身近なAIエージェントの例4選 身近な例は、2026年11月時点で提供されている次の4つです。 ChatGPT Work Claude Cowork Manus Claude Code 提供元の仕様変更が速い分野のため、各例の末尾にある公式ページで最新の条件を確認してください。 ChatGPT Work：連携アプリとファイルから成果物を作成 ChatGPT Workは、 複数ステップの作業を任せられるOpenAIのAIエージェント です。2026年7月に提供が始まったと報じられています。 OpenAIのヘルプセンターでは、前身のChatGPT agentは提供終了とされています。長い複数ステップの作業や成果物の作成には、ChatGPT Workが案内されています。 依頼の例は「競合3社の価格を調べて比較表にまとめて」です。解説記事では、接続したアプリとファイルを使い、表、スライド、文書などを作成すると紹介されています。 ブラウザ操作の機能は名称や提供範囲が変わっています。旧来の操作手順をそのまま探さず、OpenAIのヘルプで現在の仕様を確認すれば迷いません。 Claude Cowork：ファイルとツールをまたぐ知的作業を完了 Claude Coworkは、 コーディング以外の知的作業を目標だけで任せられる Anthropicのエージェント機能です。 Anthropicの公式ページでは、調査、分析、文書作成などの複数ステップの作業が想定されています。 読み書きできるのは、利用者が接続したフォルダの中だけです。ファイルを完全に削除する前には、許可を求められます。 依頼の例は「このフォルダの議事録を読み、決定事項を一覧にまとめて」です。Anthropicは通常のチャットへの統合を進めており、名称や画面は変わる可能性があります。 範囲を絞って任せる設計のため、ファイルを誤って消す不安を抑えながら試せます。 Manus：調査から成果物までを一括で進める Manusは、目標を渡すと計画から実行までを進める 汎用型のAIエージェント です。 公式ドキュメントでは、調査、Webサイト作成、データ分析、プレゼン資料作成などが用途に挙げられています。 作業は、インターネットに接続できるサンドボックスと呼ばれる隔離環境で進みます。依頼の例は「国内の競合動向を調べ、10枚のスライドにまとめて」です。 ManusはMetaへの参画を公式ブログで発表しています。提供条件が変わる可能性があるため、利用前に公式サイトで確認してください。 Claude Code：ファイル操作とコード実行で作業を完了 Claude Codeは、コードベースを読み、ファイルを編集し、コマンドを実行する エージェント型のコーディングツール です。 ターミナル、IDE、デスクトップアプリ、ブラウザで使えます。既定では、ファイルの変更やコマンドの実行の前に許可を求めます。 依頼の例は「このリポジトリのテストが失敗する原因を調べて直して」です。開発業務が中心の例といえます。 変更前に人の許可が入るため、チームの開発フローにも組み込みやすい例です。 業務別のAIエージェントの例6選 業務別の例は、次の6つです。 営業 マーケティング カスタマーサポート 経理 人事 開発 各例は「依頼」「動き」「人が確認する点」の順で読むと、自社の業務に置き換えられます。 営業：見込み客の調査からメール下書きまで 営業では、 見込み客の調査からメールの下書きまでをAIエージェントが進められます 。 依頼の例は次のとおりです。 A社の事業内容と最近のニュースを調べ、課題の仮説を3つ挙げて、初回メールの下書きを作成してください。 AIエージェントは、次の順で動きます。 企業サイトとニュースを収集する 課題の仮説を整理する 仮説を踏まえてメールの下書きを作る 送信前の宛先と内容は、人が確認します。調査結果に誤りがあれば、そのまま先方に届くためです。 調査にかけていた時間が下書きの確認に変わり、担当者は商談の準備に時間を回せます。 マーケティング：競合調査からレポート作成まで マーケティングでは、 競合調査から比較レポートの作成までを任せられます 。 依頼の例は次のとおりです。 競合3社の料金と機能を調べ、自社との比較表と要点3つのレポートにまとめてください。 AIエージェントは、次の順で動きます。 競合の公式サイトとプレスリリースを収集する 項目ごとに比較表を作る 要点を要約してレポートにする 出典のURLと数値の正確さは、人が確認します。古い料金表を拾っていないかも見ておく必要があります。 収集と整理の工数が減り、担当者は施策の判断に時間を使えます。 カスタマーサポート：問い合わせの分類から回答案まで カスタマーサポートでは、 問い合わせの分類と回答案の作成を任せられます 。 依頼の例は次のとおりです。 届いた問い合わせを内容で分類し、FAQにある内容には回答案を作成してください。FAQにない内容は担当者に回してください。 AIエージェントは、次の順で動きます。 問い合わせを内容で分類する ナレッジを検索して回答案を作る FAQにない内容を担当者に引き継ぐ 返金やクレームを伴う対応は、人が持ちます。回答案の最終的な送信も、人の確認を挟む運用が安全です。 定型の問い合わせが減るため、担当者は判断が必要な対応に集中できます。 経理：請求書の読み取りから照合まで 経理では、 請求書の読み取りから発注データとの照合までを任せられます 。 依頼の例は次のとおりです。 今月届いた請求書のPDFを読み取り、発注データと金額を照合して、差異のある請求書を一覧にしてください。 AIエージェントは、次の順で動きます。 PDFから金額と取引先を読み取る 発注データと突き合わせる 差異のある請求書を一覧にする 支払いの承認は、人が行います。読み取りの誤りが残っていないか、差異の一覧を見て確かめます。 全件の目視確認が差異のある請求書の確認に絞られ、月次の締め作業が軽くなります。 人事：応募書類の整理から面接調整まで 人事では、 応募書類の整理と面接日程の調整を任せられます 。 依頼の例は次のとおりです。 応募書類を募集要件の観点で整理し、面接日程の候補を3つ提示してください。 AIエージェントは、次の順で動きます。 書類を要件の項目に沿って要約する 面接官の空き時間を確認する 候補日を一覧にする 合否の判断は、人が行います。要約が応募者の評価を左右するため、要約に偏りがないかも確認します。 書類整理と日程調整の手間が減り、面接や候補者への連絡に時間を回せます。 開発：コードレビューから修正案の提示まで 開発では、 コードレビューから修正案の提示までを任せられます 。 依頼の例は次のとおりです。 このプルリクエストの差分を確認し、バグの可能性がある箇所を指摘して、修正案を提示してください。 AIエージェントは、次の順で動きます。 差分と周辺のコードを読む 指摘点を整理する 修正案を提示する 変更を取り込むかどうかの判断は、人が行います。修正案がほかの機能に影響しないかも確かめます。 一次レビューを任せられるため、レビュアーは設計の妥当性のような判断に集中できます。 AIエージェントに向かない例も押さえる AIエージェントに任せると失敗しやすい例は、次の3つです。 最終判断を伴う業務 誤りが許されない処理 権限を渡しにくい業務 任せる範囲を誤ると、確認を省いた運用で問題が起きます。向かない例を先に知っておけば、導入の判断を誤りにくくなります。 最終判断を伴う業務 採用の合否や契約の可否のように、 責任を伴う最終判断は人が持つべきです 。 AIエージェントは、判断の材料を集めて整理するところまでが得意な領域です。判断そのものを任せると、誤りが起きたときに責任の所在が曖昧になります。 たとえば採用では、応募書類の要約まではAIエージェントに任せ、合否は面接官が決める運用が現実的です。 材料の整理と判断を分けておけば、判断の質を保ったまま、準備の時間だけを減らせます。 誤りが許されない処理 支払いや本番環境の変更のように、 取り消しにくい操作には承認の工程を必ず挟みます 。 AIエージェントの結果が完全とは限らないためです。誤った操作がそのまま反映されると、被害が広がります。 Claude Codeは、既定でファイルの変更やコマンドの実行の前に許可を求めます。この仕組みを外さずに使えば、実行前に人が止められます。 承認の工程を残せば、速度を保ちながら、取り返しのつかない誤りを防げます。 権限を渡しにくい業務 個人情報や機密データを扱う業務は、 AIエージェントに渡す権限を絞ることが前提 です。 AIエージェントは、渡された権限の範囲で操作します。広い権限を渡すほど、誤操作や情報の取り扱いのリスクも広がります。 Claude Coworkは、利用者が接続したフォルダの中だけを読み書きします。このように、操作できる範囲を限定する設計が基本です。 範囲を限定しておけば、機密を含む業務でも、任せてよい部分だけを切り出して試せます。 AIエージェントの例に関するよくある質問 AIエージェントの例に関する質問は以下の3つです。 ChatGPTはAIエージェントですか 無料で試せる例はありますか 最初に試すならどの例ですか 質問に対する回答を確認して、自社で最初に試す例を選ぶ参考にしてみてください。 ChatGPTはAIエージェントですか 通常のチャットだけであれば、AIエージェントとは呼べません。1問1答で、手順の設計や外部ツールの操作を伴わないためです。 一方で、ChatGPT Workのように複数ステップの作業を任せる機能は、3条件を満たすためAIエージェントの例に当たります。 無料で試せる例はありますか 無料で使える範囲は、提供元とプランごとに異なり、変更も頻繁です。各ツールの公式料金ページで現在の条件を確認してください。 無料の範囲で試す場合は、機密情報を含まない作業から始めると安全です。 最初に試すならどの例ですか 送信や支払いを伴わない、調査と資料作成から試すのがおすすめです。結果を人が目で見て確認でき、誤りがあっても影響が小さいためです。 業務別の例では、マーケティングの競合調査が該当します。 AIエージェントの例は「任せる範囲」で選ぶ AIエージェントの例は、ChatGPT WorkやClaude Codeなどの身近なツールと、営業や経理などの業務別の動きに分けて整理できます。どの例にも共通するのは、目標を渡し、手順の実行を任せ、結果は人が確認するという流れです。 例を選ぶ基準は、任せる範囲と人が確認する点です 。 まずは、自社の業務を1つ選び、依頼の文章と人が確認する点を書き出してみましょう。調査や資料作成のように、結果をすぐ目で確認できる業務が始めやすい対象です。 ただし、例を選べても、任せる範囲と確認の工程を設計し、運用できる人材がいなければ成果は定着しません。導入の判断とあわせて、推進役となる人材をどう育てるかも検討しておきましょう。 The post AIエージェントの例10選！身近なツールから業務別の動きまで解説 first appeared on AI専門ニュースメディア AINOW .

items.title: SageMaker Inference now supports Multi-Instance GPU to maximize GPU utilization for model endpoints
items.description: When you deploy a model to a GPU endpoint, the smallest unit of GPU you can request is one whole accelerator. This constraint can cost you twice. First, you can’t host more models on an instance than it has accelerators. An ml.p4d.24xlarge has eight A100s, so it holds eight models, whether each one needs 40 GB or 14 GB. Second, and less obvious, it makes every deployment come down to a choice of which full GPU to deploy to. As your concurrency and prompt lengths grow, a full GPU on an older instance stops being enough, but a full GPU on a newer one is more than your model can use. You end up either under-served or paying for capability you never reach. Today, Amazon SageMaker Inference supports GPU partitioning, which uses NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) to divide a physical GPU into independent partitions. Each partition receives a fixed share of the GPU’s compute units and a dedicated block of its memory, with isolation enforced in hardware. That changes both constraints: you can place a different model in each partition, and you can choose a fraction of a newer accelerator instead of a whole one of either generation. This post covers both. The first part is the direct benefit: deploy more models than you have GPUs, with isolation between them. The second is the one customers ask about when the question turns to cost: how the granularity of partitioning helps you pick the right-sized unit, and what we measured when we did. One thing to know before you read further: GPU partitioning works on endpoints that use inference components , the construct you use to deploy several models to one endpoint and set the compute each model gets. Partitioning builds directly on it. A partition is a resource a component asks for, in the same place it already asks for CPU and memory. If you haven’t used inference components, this post introduces them. Single-model endpoints, serverless endpoints, and heterogeneous instance pools cannot be partitioned. What customers do today, and why each option falls short If you have more models than accelerators, you have had three choices. Run fewer, larger endpoints and batch harder – This raises utilization, but only when the models are interchangeable. A portfolio of fine-tuned variants or per-tenant models is not. Use multi-model endpoints – These load and unload models from a shared GPU on demand, which fits sparse, bursty traffic. But models share the device without isolation, so a heavy request for one model affects the others. A model that isn’t loaded also pays a load penalty on first use. Move to self-managed Kubernetes – This is where customers who need real GPU partitioning have gone. MIG works there, but you take on driver versioning, partition configuration, a device plugin, scheduling, and keeping it all consistent across a fleet. That’s a lot of work for a hardware capability your instances already have. Why MIG NVIDIA Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) splits one GPU into as many as seven instances, depending on the GPU. Each instance has its own compute, cache, memory and memory bandwidth. Because the split is in hardware rather than software, you get guarantees that other sharing methods can’t give: Predictable latency – Each partition has dedicated memory bandwidth, so one model’s traffic spike doesn’t show up in another model’s p99. Fault isolation – A crash or memory error stays inside its partition instead of taking down every model on the GPU. Right-sized capacity – Small and mid-sized models get a slice that fits them instead of a whole GPU. You can mix slice sizes on one device. No cold starts – Every model keeps its own partition and stays loaded, with no load penalty and no eviction. Tenant isolation – Memory protection between partitions is enforced in hardware, which makes security and compliance reviews simpler. Reliable planning and chargeback – A partition performs the same way regardless of its neighbors, so load tests predict production. GPU cost also maps cleanly to a model, team or tenant. Partitioning has boundaries worth knowing up front. The maximum number of partitions depends on the accelerator and never exceeds seven. MIG itself only allows a layout to change while its partitions are idle, and on SageMaker AI that means choosing a layout when you create the endpoint. A model that needs more than one GPU still needs whole devices. Within those boundaries, you get the isolation of separate GPUs without dedicating one to each model. Partitioning without the platform work Until now, getting MIG meant running the Kubernetes stack yourself. GPU partitioning on Amazon SageMaker AI removes that step: you pick a partition profile for your model, and SageMaker AI handles GPU configuration, placement and scaling. You get hardware-isolated GPU sharing on a managed endpoint, without having to run the platform underneath it. Salesforce has been part of this work from the start, helping define the requirements and validating the initial implementation. “NVIDIA MIG partitions a single GPU into multiple isolated instances, each with dedicated compute and memory resources. Salesforce sees this as an important capability because many inference workloads do not require an entire GPU. MIG would allow us to consolidate workloads safely, significantly improve GPU utilization, reduce inference costs, and maintain predictable performance and strong isolation. This capability would help us scale AI Inference more efficiently across different use cases. Salesforce has helped define requirements, validated the initial solution. We are now preparing to validate the solution with representative production workload and demonstrate strong customer demand with AWS. items.title: Taxonomy of agentic primitives in AWS Quick
items.description: Over the past year, as we built AWS Quick, our agents went from answering questions to taking actions: scheduling meetings, running research, generating reports. As the system evolved, one problem kept resurfacing: there was no shared definition of the primitives that agentic work is built from. The same few ideas kept getting rebuilt under different names: an actor that does the work, a signal that starts it, a packaged procedure, and a memory that carries lessons forward. This repetition leaked into product design and onto the user. Take the user who says “ monitor my Slack channel and send me a daily digest ”. Is that a new agent, a scheduled instruction to an existing one, a workflow, or a skill? These are different questions, but without a shared vocabulary they collapse into one confusing choice. This post shares the taxonomy we converged on: one set of primitives found by decomposing agentic work into four plain questions: When? , What? , Who? , and How? Most of the framework stays invisible to end users by design, but a shared vocabulary makes the system easier to reason about for anyone building beneath it. The framework at a glance Figure 1: How triggers, agents, and capabilities relate, with learning feeding back from the session runtime A trigger starts the work and carries the task ( When and What ), an agent takes it on ( Who ) and uses its capabilities (tools, skills, and workflows) to perform the task ( How ). This post describes these primitives and how they relate to one another. It’s the first post in a series, and upcoming posts cover our agentic operating system, background learning, proactive feeds, and much more. Triggers: What causes work to begin Triggers are the activation mechanism for getting work done, but they also carry instructions: a human message is both the moment of activation and the description of what to do. They are both the When? and the What? of a task. Human-initiated: A person opens a conversation and asks the agent to do something. Interactive, synchronous, conversational. Agent-delegated: One agent, mid-task, invokes another to handle a sub-problem. Programmatic, composable, potentially recursive. Scheduled: Time-based activation, like “run financial research every Monday at 9am.” Deterministic, with the same standing instructions applied across runs. Event-driven: A signal from an external system, such as a new email, a Slack mention, a file change, or a webhook. The type of trigger conditions the execution: a scheduled background task might stay conservative (for example, do nothing if uncertain), while a human-initiated one would be responsive (for example, ask rather than stop). Agents We define an agent as a persistent, learning actor . It’s the Who? in any execution, and the anchor against which learning accrues. Two agents given identical input can differ, because they carry different instructions, capabilities, and histories. The agent isn’t the instructions it follows. It’s the entity that interprets them. It consists of three things: Instructions: Standing guidance defining persona, role, context files, and operating principles. A Finance Agent behaves differently from a general assistant primarily because of this. Capabilities: The tools, skills, workflows, and sub-agents available for use, updated dynamically. A charting library can be added in one session and removed the next. Learned context: Memory that accumulates through use: the queries that work for a tool, the formatting users prefer, the edge cases they care about. This is how the tenth execution beats the first without anyone changing the instructions. Everything else is extrinsic: the large language model (LLM) underlying the agent is a swappable model parameter, conversation history is per-session state, and triggers belong to the platform. A consequence of this definition is that a user request “ I want an agent that monitors my Slack and sends a digest every morning ” is usually a trigger added to an existing agent , not a new agent or workflow. With this framing, we can merge chat, scheduled, and “autonomous” agents into one actor that you can converse with, schedule, and that can orchestrate and inspect its own past work. Capabilities Capabilities are How an agent acts, spanning a spectrum from fully agentic to fully deterministic. That axis is really a confidence contract : how much latitude the agent keeps versus how much the user fixes in advance. Tools are atomic operations with a typed schema: send an email, query a database, read a file. Whether a local function, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or another agent behind a protocol boundary, the caller sees the same interface: name, description, parameters, result. Skills are structured guidance with room for judgment: instructions bundled with resources (templates, scripts, examples) that describe an approach rather than a rigid sequence. They load through progressive disclosure , so the agent sees only names and short descriptions until one becomes relevant, then reads the full instructions in. A skill can therefore bundle arbitrary depth of expertise without a constant cost. Workflows are deterministic coordination: declared steps, control flow, branching, and error handling that execute in fixed order, with decision logic in code rather than model inference. Think of a purchase-approval route: budget check, manager sign-off, then finance, each recorded. The route is fixed, but the judgment inside a step is still the agent’s. Figure 2: Skills versus workflows, which differ in whether the agent or the code decides the step order Why skills and workflows outlast model improvements A natural question arises: if models keep improving, won’t skills and workflows become unnecessary? We don’t think so, because each holds value independent of model capability. Skills are the unit for capturing, versioning, and sharing institutional expertise, while workflows deliver auditability, step-wise visibility, and dete

items.title: Serverless MCP server for AI agent data lake access on Amazon ECS Fargate
items.description: Organizations building applications powered by artificial intelligence (AI) face a recurring challenge: giving large language model (LLM) agents access to enterprise data lakes without duplicating integration logic across every agent and application. Most teams begin by wiring agents directly to databases and APIs, with no shared gateway such as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in between. Each new dataset demands custom code, and each agent reimplements its own access control. As the number of datasets or agents grows, permission enforcement drifts, and onboarding a new data source becomes a multi-day engineering effort. Our team supports Amazon’s North America Sort Center (NASC) network, where planning teams rely on operational data to manage capacity, labor, and package flow. To give those teams conversational access to that data, we built a serverless Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) with AWS Fargate to address this problem for planning teams in NASC. The server acts as a centralized, agent-agnostic gateway between AI agents and our enterprise data lake. Exposing a new dataset requires only a JSON metadata file that the server discovers automatically on the next pipeline sync. In this post, we describe the architecture, show how a metadata-driven approach removes the need for per-dataset integration code, and explain how the serverless infrastructure supports multiple agents and applications in a multi-tenant environment. Problem statement and design goals Two interrelated challenges shaped how we designed this system: fragmented data access patterns and an unsustainable onboarding model. Integration challenge at scale Our data lake contains thousands of datasets spanning operational metrics, business analytics, and domain-specific data. Multiple teams wanted AI assistants that could query this data conversationally, but each built its own integration from scratch. Each agent embedded its own SQL generation logic, schema knowledge, and connection handling, so a schema change meant patching every agent individually. Access control was fragmented, with no single audit point for data access decisions. Onboarding a new dataset required custom tool code, query validation, and redeployment, typically a multi-day effort per table. Design goals We established four requirements: Configuration-driven data lake access. Adding a dataset requires only a metadata file, not code. Agent-agnostic tool interfaces. Any MCP-compatible client can invoke the same tools. Centralized permission enforcement. Access control is enforced at the MCP server layer. Elastic infrastructure. The system scales with bursty AI workload patterns. Solution overview The architecture separates concerns into four layers (client, MCP server, tools, and knowledge-base refresh), each independently scalable and deployable. A metadata catalog underpins the tools layer, storing schema descriptions, column-level semantics, and table relationships that the AI agent references when generating SQL. Because the agent derives schema knowledge from the catalog at query time, there is no need to hardcode table structures or redeploy when schemas change. The knowledge-base refresh layer keeps that catalog current, indexing new dataset metadata as it arrives. The following sections describe each layer in detail. Architecture walkthrough The following diagram shows the request flow from user query to data layer across all four layers. A user submits a query from a client application (web chat, Slack, an IDE plugin, or an external agent). The request resolves through Amazon Route 53 for DNS and reaches an Application Load Balancer in a public subnet, configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF. The load balancer routes to Amazon Cognito, which authenticates the user and enriches the request. Authenticated traffic then enters the private subnet, where the client layer runs on Amazon ECS Fargate. This layer handles session state in Amazon DynamoDB and forwards requests through an internal Application Load Balancer to the MCP server layer, also on Amazon ECS Fargate. In the MCP server layer, an AI agent powered by Amazon Bedrock orchestrates tools built with FastMCP (a Python framework for building MCP servers). Amazon Bedrock Guardrails is applied to every model interaction. On the right, the data layer holds the tool backends. Amazon Athena and Amazon Redshift run SQL queries against the data lake, and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handles semantic search. Data ingestion into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and the knowledge bases is handled by AWS Lambda. Each layer is described in detail in the sections that follow. Figure 1: Request flow through the serverless MCP server, from client applications to the data layer MCP client layer: Authentication and session management A request flows from the client application through Amazon Route 53 for DNS resolution to an Application Load Balancer configured with HTTPS and AWS WAF . The load balancer forwards traffic to the Amazon ECS Fargate client service, which integrates with Amazon Cognito for JSON Web Token (JWT) authentication and Amazon DynamoDB for session storage. A context mapping configuration drives this enrichment, scoping each query to only the relevant tables. In our testing, this scoping keeps end-to-end interaction latency in the 15–20 second range. The following example shows a context mapping configuration: { "package_data": { "description": "Package tracking and delivery information", "tables": ["analytics_db.regional_order_summary", "operations_gold.load_summary"], "sources": {"wiki": [], "quip": []} }, "labor_planning": { "description": "Workforce management and capacity planning", "tables": ["workforce.capacity_details"], "sources": {"wiki": [], "quip": []} } } When a context specifies tables, the MCP server narrows its search of the metadata catalog to t

items.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 2
items.description: In Part 1 , you built a task agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and acts for signed-in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA). Okta decided which agent might act for which user, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeemed Okta’s grant inside the agent. That proves the governance mechanism, and it runs on a deliberately small topology: one agent, two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and the authorization check written into each server. The mechanism scales. The topology doesn’t. Three things that are fine for one agent and two tools become the work in an enterprise with hundreds of agents and thousands of tools: What Part 1 does Why it stops scaling What Part 2 does instead The agent holds each MCP server’s runtime ARN and calls it directly N agents against M servers is a wiring matrix, and every new tool touches every agent that needs it Agents reach one Gateway endpoint, and the Gateway holds the target registry The agent’s role holds the token-exchange permission and reads the provider’s secret Every agent that acts for users gets a credential path to every resource it might reach The Gateway redeems the grant, and the agent’s role holds no token-exchange or secret permissions Each MCP server carries the same groups check in its own code The same rule, copied into thousands of servers, drifts and can’t be audited or changed in one place One default-deny Cedar policy set, evaluated at the Gateway before tools run In this post, you make that change on the Part 1 solution. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, becomes the single front door and redeems Okta’s grant for each target. Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies that bind each tool to the agent and the scope Okta delegated. A second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) joins under its own Okta identity, to show that the front door doesn’t care where an agent runs. And Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Amazon CloudWatch gives you one place to read every decision, including Okta’s. We also compare XAA with per-user OAuth consent for applications that can’t accept Okta’s grant. What changes from Part 1 The Okta configuration, the AgentCore Identity credential provider, and the MCP servers from Part 1 stay as they are. Figure 1 shows the architecture with the additions. Figure 1: The Part 1 solution with AgentCore Gateway, Policy, and Observability, a second agent on Amazon EKS, and the audit path, with numbers matching the steps that follow The user signs in, and the backend for frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) issued to the task agent, agent A, as in Part 1. The BFF invokes agent A on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG. Agent A forwards the ID-JAG to its Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session. The Gateway’s inbound authorizer accepts only agent A’s ID-JAGs. Policy in AgentCore evaluates Cedar policies for each tool listing and each tool call, before the Gateway invokes a target. For calls that Cedar permits, the Gateway has AgentCore Identity redeem the ID-JAG for each target at Okta’s custom authorization server through the Part 1 credential provider. A call that Cedar denies doesn’t redeem the ID-JAG. The MCP server checks the user’s groups and scope, as in Part 1, and records each decision as an authz.check span. Every hop emits OpenTelemetry spans to AgentCore Observability, which CloudWatch Transaction Search collects, and Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge. The reporting agent, agent B, runs on Amazon EKS and follows the same path through its own Gateway. Prerequisites In addition to the Part 1 solution, you need the following: Prerequisite Needed for eksctl, kubectl, and Docker The second agent on Amazon EKS Okta Log Streaming Okta’s System Log in CloudWatch AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions AgentCore Gateways and policy engines, Amazon EKS clusters, CloudWatch log groups, and Amazon EventBridge rules The additions take about 90 minutes. The EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus nodes and the Amazon EKS Auto Mode management fee, and the AgentCore features charge for what you use. See Amazon EKS pricing and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . As in Part 1, the base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain on GitHub, and you can build the Part 2 additions on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it. Create a Gateway that accepts the ID-JAG The Gateway’s inbound authorizer works like the runtime authorizer from Part 1. Its issuer is Okta’s org authorization server, its audience is the custom authorization server, and allowedClients pins it to one agent: authorizer = {"customJWTAuthorizer": { "discoveryUrl": f"{OKTA_ORG}/.well-known/openid-configuration", # the ID-JAG's issuer "allowedAudience": [f"{OKTA_ORG}/oauth2/{CUSTOM_AS_ID}"], # the resource's authorization server "allowedClients": [AGENT_CLIENT_ID], # only this agent's ID-JAGs "allowedScopes": ["xaa:read", "xaa:write"], }} Figure 2 shows the resulting inbound authorizer. Figure 2: The Gateway accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to the agent for the resource’s authorization server Each MCP server becomes a Gateway target whose outbound authorization uses TOKEN_EXCHANGE through the Part 1 credential provider, so the Gateway performs the second exchange: "credential

items.title: Govern AI agent access with Okta Cross App Access and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – Part 1
items.description: An AI agent that updates a ticket or reads a customer record acts for a person, inside applications that person can reach. Your identity team then has to answer a question that per-app OAuth consent and shared service accounts leave open: which agent might act for which user in which application, and how you stop it. Okta Cross App Access (XAA) answers it in your identity provider (IdP). You register the agent in Okta, an administrator approves the applications it might reach, and Okta evaluates policy each time the agent asks to act for a user. In our tests, after an administrator removed a user’s assignment to the agent, Okta refused the agent’s new requests for that user within about 1 second, and tokens already issued expired within 5 minutes. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses two of its capabilities to carry out Okta’s decision on AWS. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, validates Okta’s grant. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, redeems it for a short-lived access token with credentials your agent code doesn’t see, and keeps that token in its token vault. In our tests, AgentCore Identity added about 0.6 seconds to a request that took about 30 seconds end to end. In this post, the first of two, you build a task agent on AgentCore runtime that acts for signed-in users through XAA and AgentCore Identity. You configure the AgentCore Identity parts it needs, enforce each user’s authority in the tools, and see what we measured: what each check refuses, the practices we settled on, and how fast Okta’s controls take effect. Part 2 then puts the same governance behind Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with Cedar policies, a second agent on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS), and an audit trail in Amazon CloudWatch. Solution overview Okta is the governance plane: it decides which agent might act for which user, against which resource. AgentCore Identity is the execution plane: it holds the agent’s credentials, turns Okta’s decision into a token the resource accepts, and keeps both identities in that token. In Figure 1, the agent and the two Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it calls all run on AgentCore runtime. Figure 1: Solution architecture, with numbers matching the steps that follow Each request carries three tokens, and each records a different decision: the ID token says who the user is, the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG) is Okta’s decision, and the access token is what the resource accepts. One request flows like this: The user signs in to the web front end, a backend for frontend (BFF), with OpenID Connect through the agent’s linked Okta app. For each request, the BFF exchanges the user’s ID token for an ID-JAG at Okta’s org authorization server, authenticated as the agent (RFC 8693 token exchange). Okta checks that the agent is active, that the user is assigned to it, and that an administrator connected it to the target authorization server for the requested scopes. The ID-JAG is single-use and expires in 5 minutes. The BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID-JAG as its bearer token. The runtime’s JWT authorizer accepts only ID-JAGs that Okta issued to this agent. The runtime gets a workload access token from AgentCore Identity that binds the agent’s workload identity to the user, and passes it to the agent code. This workload access token is an AWS-internal binding token: neither Okta nor the resource sees it, so it isn’t one of the three tokens. The agent asks AgentCore Identity for an access token. AgentCore Identity redeems the ID-JAG at the resource’s Okta custom authorization server with the JWT authorization grant (RFC 7523), authenticated as the agent. Okta returns a 5-minute access token that names both the user and the agent and carries the user’s groups. The agent calls the MCP servers with that token. The task manager checks that a registered agent obtained it, and that the user’s group and scope allow the tool. Figure 2 shows the same request as a sequence, with the check that each party makes. Figure 2: The three-token chain and the check each party makes, with the step 4 workload access token staying inside AWS Prerequisites To follow along, you need the following: Prerequisite What we used An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and an Anthropic Claude model in Amazon Bedrock US West (Oregon) An Okta org with Cross App Access for AI agents and API Access Management (custom authorization servers) An Okta Integrator Free Plan org Python, the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), boto3, the AgentCore CLI, and the AgentCore Python SDK, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Python 3.11, AWS CLI version 2, boto3 1.43, AgentCore CLI 0.31.1, and AgentCore Python SDK 1.24.1 AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions Permission to create AgentCore resources and IAM roles The walkthrough takes about 1 hour. AgentCore charges for what you use. See Amazon Bedrock AgentCore pricing . The base for this solution is the AWS sample 08-okta-xaa-delegation-chain in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub, and you can build the solution in this post on top of it. Beyond that sample, the snippets and configurations in this post show the pattern conceptually. They aren’t a complete, deployable solution. The code is sample code for non-production use, so work with your security and legal teams to meet your organization’s security, regulatory, and compliance requirements before you deploy it. Register the agent in Okta Okta needs an authorization server for the resource, the agent, a connection between them, and a policy that admits the agent’s grant. Do all of these steps in the Okta Admin Console: registering the agent creates its linked app, so you don’t need an app integration wizard.

items.title: How Greenlight Financial built an autonomous SOC solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Greenlight Financial resolves more than 90 percent of up to 4,000 security and risk cases each month without human intervention. Greenlight’s Luna uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , infrastructure for building, connecting, and optimizing agents at scale. Specifically, Greenlight uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to host Luna’s agent code. It uses AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to support its tiered multi-agent system. This avoids the need to build and operate these capabilities in-house. Luna triages dark web breach-card alerts, identity anomalies, and financial-risk events in seconds. This post explains how Greenlight Financial built an autonomous security operations center (SOC) solution on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover its multi-tiered supervisor architecture, more than 30 specialized agents, episodic memory for continuous learning, and expansion from SOC use cases into financial risk triage. We share production metrics, infrastructure decisions, and patterns for building autonomous security operations in regulated industries. What Greenlight needed to solve Greenlight Financial provides financial products for families: debit cards, savings tools, and connected devices such as the Family Hub and Pet Tracker. The company processes sensitive financial data at scale under the same regulatory requirements as major banks. Greenlight’s SOC receives 3,000–4,000 security and risk alerts per month from four primary vectors: Dark web breach cards – Card Network and internal threat intel flag Greenlight customer cards found on the dark web. Identity and access anomalies – Unusual login patterns, privilege escalations, and policy violations across Identity Provider (IdP) and internal systems. Infrastructure alerts – Signals from Signals from EDR (Endpoint Detection and Response), SIEM (Security Information and Event Management), Asset Inventory, and other observability tools. Financial risk events – Suspicious transaction patterns, compliance triggers, and fraud indicators from card processing systems. Each alert demands cross-referencing multiple data sources before an analyst can render a verdict. A single dark web breach card notification requires checking whether the card is active, deduplicating against prior notifications, reviewing customer session data, and checking open support tickets. This workflow takes a human analyst 15-30 minutes per case. At 4,000 cases per month, that math breaks. Greenlight needed a system that could: Triage and resolve routine cases autonomously at machine speed. Escalate complex cases with full context to human analysts. Learn from resolution patterns to improve accuracy over time. Operate within financial services compliance guardrails. Architecture: Tiered multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Greenlight built Luna as a hierarchical multi-agent system on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The architecture follows a tiered supervisor pattern that mirrors how human SOC teams operate. L1 handles volume, and L2 handles complexity. Figure 1: Luna’s tiered supervisor architecture on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Tier 1 supervisor: High-volume triage Tier 1 supervisor uses an advanced language model available through Amazon Bedrock running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime within an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). The runtime uses private subnets and direct code deployment through a ZIP file and Amazon Simple Storage Service ( Amazon S3 ). It handles initial triage of incoming cases by orchestrating more than 30 specialized agents: Domain What the agent does Identity and Access Checks login history, MFA status, session anomalies Endpoint Detection Pulls endpoint alerts, process trees, IOC matches Observability Correlates infrastructure metrics with alert timing Asset Inventory Maps affected assets, ownership, exposure surface Data Analytics Queries historical patterns and baseline deviations Payment Processing Verifies card status, transaction history, account state Customer Experience Reviews customer session behavior around incident time Customer Support Checks related open tickets, prior complaints Code and Repositories Traces code changes correlated with alerts Project Tracking Links incidents to recent deployments or known issues Threat Intelligence Enriches IOCs with external threat context Automation (SOAR) Executes approved remediation playbooks The Tier 1 supervisor receives cases through two paths: Amazon API Gateway, which exposes the Luna Queue API and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint, and Tines SOAR for automated alert ingestion. It determines which specialized agents to invoke based on alert type, synthesizes their findings, and renders a verdict. The median triage time for routine cases is single-digit seconds. Tier 2 supervisor: Deep-dive investigation Cases that exceed Tier 1’s confidence threshold escalate to a Tier 2 supervisor using an advanced foundation model on Amazon Bedrock with extended reasoning capabilities. This agent handles the 10 percent of cases that require multi-step reasoning: Re-investigates escalated cases with deeper cross-source correlation. Invokes specialized agents through boto3 with expanded context windows. Chains reasoning across 3–5 data sources to establish causality. Produces detailed investigation reports with evidence chains for human review. The Tier 2 supervisor runs on a scheduled basis, using Amazon EventBridge rate triggers and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) queue completions to batch-process escalated cases, and on demand for urgent Tier 1-escalated cases. Entry points for different personas Different teams engage Luna in different ways, so the application exposes three entry points. These range from fully automated alert ingestion to interactive, on-demand investigation. Each entry point maps to a persona and how their work arrives: Tines SOAR – Primary volume driver. items.title: Taxbit Assist: A grounded, role-aware AI agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
items.description: Taxbit is a digital-asset tax and accounting compliance platform. Founded in 2018, Taxbit helps enterprises such as exchanges, payment services, and brokers calculate gains and losses, collect tax documentation, and file information returns at scale. Now, a cited, permission-aware AI assistant helps compliance teams find answers right inside the product dashboard. But the knowledge needed to use that dashboard well was scattered across the public website, API documentation, and help-center articles, and a meaningful share was never written down at all. When a customer asked “what does this form status mean?”, they either went digging or filed a support ticket. Today more than 55 percent of users who ask Assist a question return to ask another within 24 hours, according to Taxbit’s internal production analytics. In this post, we share how we built Taxbit Assist , the AI assistant now embedded in the Taxbit dashboard, on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. We cover the architecture, the retrieval work that made answers trustworthy enough to ship to regulated customers, how we handle safety and data residency, and how we continuously measure answer quality on live production traffic. What the assistant had to get right A generic chatbot was not an option in this domain. Four constraints shaped what we built: Grounded and cited – Our users make filing decisions. Every answer had to trace back to a source the user could open and read, and when the assistant didn’t know something, it had to say so. Role and organization awareness – The assistant shouldn’t walk a Support User through an admin-only workflow and send them to a page that they can’t open. No tax advice – Explaining how Taxbit computes cost basis (the accounting method used to compute a gain or loss) is product documentation. Telling a user which method to elect is tax advice. The line between the two is narrow. Regional data residency – Supported from a single codebase, with continuous quality measurement in production. Inside our compliance program – Taxbit Assist is developed and operated in line with ISO/IEC 42001, the international standard for AI management systems. Taxbit is also certified to ISO/IEC 27001 and ISO/IEC 27701 and holds a SOC 2 Type II report. Taxbit doesn’t train or fine-tune any model, and Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use prompts or completions to train models. We are also a small team. Rather than build and operate the agent loop, conversation-state store, and session isolation ourselves, we chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for three reasons: its managed agent runtime removed infrastructure operations, built-in AgentCore memory, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, eliminated a separate conversation-state store, and per-session isolation kept each user’s context contained. That let us put most of our effort into the retrieval and safety work that follows. Solution overview Taxbit Assist is a Strands Agents SDK application running on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram illustrates the solution architecture. Figure 1: Request flow from a dashboard question through guardrails screening, knowledge base retrieval, model reasoning, permission checks, and response streaming The workflow consists of the following steps: A user asks a question in the Taxbit dashboard. A streaming chat API forwards it to AgentCore runtime along with the user’s verified identity (email, organization ID, and dashboard roles). The runtime screens the incoming message with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails . Personally identifiable information (PII) is masked in place. If the message is blocked, the model is never invoked. The agent retrieves candidate passages from an Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases knowledge base, and then reranks them server-side. The knowledge base uses the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability of Amazon Bedrock, backed by Amazon S3 Vectors , a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). Amazon Bedrock models reason over the retrieved passages and verify that the user has access to the relevant feature and role before recommending any workflow. For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region . The answer streams back to the dashboard with source links. AgentCore memory carries the conversation across turns. Every request emits OpenTelemetry traces to Amazon CloudWatch , which feeds our evaluation tooling. The agent runtime The agent is a small Python application: a system prompt, a model, and eight tools. It ships as an ARM64 container image that AgentCore runtime pulls from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) and scales on demand. The tools are deliberately narrow: Knowledge base search, the primary tool. Two access checks, one for organization entitlement and one for the user’s dashboard role. Four support ticket tools to create, list, update, and close the caller’s own tickets. Current time, for the rare question that needs sub-day precision. In this version, the agent has no read access to customer tax data. It answers from product knowledge, and the only writes it can perform are the caller’s own support tickets. One security decision underpins all of them: the model never handles identity. The user’s email, organization ID, and roles come from the trusted calling service and are bound into each tool through a closure before the model sees it. The model can decide whether to check permissions but not whose permissions to check, because identity isn’t a parameter it can set. User input is sanitized at the boundary, so a prompt injection cannot imitate the trusted context line. The agent runs a foundation model (FM) through Amazon Bedrock, invoked through cross-Region inference profiles. Geography-aware inference handles data residency. The inference profile ID carries a geography prefix derived from the deployment Region, so EU de

items.title: Extend Claude Code to remote sessions on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with security controls
items.description: You might already run Claude Code locally on your laptop, backed by Amazon Bedrock. This post shows how to go a step further: run it as a remote agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The sample uses AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, so every task runs in its own isolated session inside your AWS account. You offload a coding task, close the laptop, and come back to the result. We first discuss why teams choose Amazon Bedrock for Claude Code and highlight a few key security characteristics. Then, we discuss the remote agent architecture and walk through an accompanying sample, sample-remote-coding-agent , that implements it. The sample runs each task in its own AgentCore runtime session and returns a GitHub pull request for you to review and merge. Along the way, we show how the Amazon Bedrock data controls stay intact when a task runs remotely. Why customers run Claude Code on Amazon Bedrock Customers choose Amazon Bedrock as Claude Code’s model provider for many reasons. These include billing and credits through their existing AWS account with no per-seat licenses, audit logging in AWS CloudTrail, and geographic inference profiles for data residency. Amazon Bedrock also provides three valuable security characteristics: Data protection. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t use your content to train models or share it with model providers, and providers can’t access your prompts, completions, or the Amazon Bedrock service logs. Amazon Bedrock is in scope for SOC, ISO, and FedRAMP Moderate, is HIPAA eligible, and can be used in compliance with the GDPR. See Compliance validation for Amazon Bedrock for details. Access through controls you already govern. Claude Code calls Amazon Bedrock with temporary AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) credentials, and you can sign in through an identity provider such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta by following the Guidance for Claude Code with Amazon Bedrock . AWS PrivateLink gives your Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) a private connection to Amazon Bedrock. Control over retention and operator access. Mantle, the next-generation inference engine for Amazon Bedrock, is designed for zero operator access (ZOA), so AWS operators have no technical means to access customer data such as your prompts or completions. You also control whether the prompts and outputs from your inference requests are retained. You can configure zero data retention (ZDR) to make sure that no request or response data is written to durable storage by AWS or shared with the model provider. See Data retention and Exploring the zero operator access design of Mantle for details. Why teams add a remote coding agent Remote coding agents have become a common pattern because they turn a coding task into a hand-off. You assign the task, close the laptop or move on to other work, and come back to the result. Several tasks can run at once instead of competing for one machine, and each task runs in its own disposable environment, outside of your laptop and the credentials in your shell. The result comes back as a pull request that a teammate can review like any other change. The pattern has trade-offs: you steer less while a task runs, the environment needs some setup, and cost is harder to predict. The solution in this post runs the work in your own AWS account. Every task runs as an AgentCore runtime session that belongs to your account, and every model call goes to Amazon Bedrock, so those calls inherit the security characteristics described in the previous section. The sample suits some tasks better than others: Good fit. Scoped features, bug fixes, and tests on a trusted repository that declares its own setup and test commands. Not a fit. Untrusted code, because the agent runs the repository’s own commands and can’t make them safe, and open-ended work, because each task stops after three attempts. Solution overview The following diagram shows how a task flows from Claude Code or the web console through the control plane to an isolated AgentCore runtime session in your VPC, and back out as a GitHub pull request. Figure 1: Architecture of the sample The workflow consists of the following steps: Submit. From Claude Code, the sample-rca plugin runs a local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, a small helper that gives Claude Code extra tools. The server signs each request with your AWS credentials and calls an IAM-authorized Amazon API Gateway HTTP API. Alternatively, you submit from a web console that Amazon CloudFront serves. You sign in to it with Amazon Cognito, and it calls a Cognito-authorized API. Queue. An AWS Lambda function screens the task prompt with an Amazon Bedrock Guardrails guardrail, then records the task in Amazon DynamoDB and puts it on an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. A dispatcher function then starts one AgentCore runtime session for the task, on the runtime that belongs to that repository. Run in an isolated session. Each registered repository has its own AgentCore runtime, which runs one container image stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). The image carries the Claude Code CLI, the Claude Agent SDK that drives it, git, and make. AgentCore runtime runs every session in its own microVM, a lightweight virtual machine with isolated CPU, memory, and filesystem. The microVM runs inside a VPC with private endpoints to Amazon Bedrock and the other AWS services the agent uses. Check out and plan. In the session, the agent gets a GitHub access token from AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and clones the repository. It then searches AgentCore memory, another AgentCore capability, for lessons that earlier tasks learned about this repository. Next, Claude Code plans the change with Claude Opus on Amazon Bedrock. Now, a former Rockstar tech director says he thinks that exact threat could cause the developer to work faster on the official PC version of its soon-to-release crime/lifestyle simulator. Obbe Vermeij hasn't worked at Rockstar since 2009 , but in a new interview with Rock Paper Shotgun , he recalled how artists for the PC version of the original top-down Grand Theft Auto were incensed when the console version squashed the game's 256-color textures down to 16 colors for the PS1 release. "So it always has been that sort of awkward relationship between PC and the console," Vermeij said. items.title: How NVIDIA Open Source Tools Are Helping Researchers Build Next-Generation 6G Networks
items.description: A year ago, NVIDIA open sourced its Aerial wireless software , joining Sionna and a broader suite of open source tools for accelerating next-generation 6G network development. Together, they give researchers a foundation for testing ideas, comparing results and building on each other’s work — connecting simulation and AI training with experiments on real over-the-air wireless systems. Today, researchers and developers are using these tools to build 6G-ready networks that do more than just transmit data — receiving signals more effectively, keeping robots and autonomous systems connected when it matters most, and adapting in real time as devices move through the world. Over the past year, global developer adoption of NVIDIA AI Aerial and NVIDIA Sionna software has grown 10x, while NVIDIA’s open source 5G/6G tools have surpassed 1 million downloads. More than 8,000 research and academic institutions worldwide are using these platforms. The projects emerging today offer a view of how future networks could look. Each addresses a different challenge, but together point toward a broader ambition for building AI-native 6G networks that deliver connectivity, computing and sensing over a converged software-defined platform for billions of people, machines and agents. Networks That Help Robots React Faster A robot picking up an object needs to understand its surroundings and act before they change. When the AI powering that decision runs on a nearby server or in the cloud, the wireless connection becomes part of the response time. Researchers are exploring a more efficient approach called goal-oriented semantic communications. Instead of sending full images, robots transmit compact descriptions of objects, their positions and their relationships. Transmitting just as much information as needed allows robots to more quickly respond, especially in dynamic environments like workplaces and warehouses. At King’s College London , researchers connected a camera-equipped robot arm to an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin running NVIDIA Sionna, which supports both software-defined 5G network and edge AI processing. In fruit-packing and cube-stacking experiments with deliberately introduced faults, the approach reduced robot task completion time by up to 52.6% and improved task success compared with sending periodic images. In addition to quicker responses and less processing overhead, the system also proved more resilient — detecting dropped objects, recovering from unsuccessful actions and, in configurations using a digital twin, checking planned movements for potential collisions before execution. Networks That Learn to Receive Signals Better For a firefighter receiving live drone footage or a rescue team searching for a missing person, timely images can help guide urgent decisions. But interference and changing radio conditions can make wireless signals harder to decode, causing errors and retransmissions that delay information from the field. AI receivers address this challenge by learning to recover information from incoming signals more effectively. Better reception could help responders maintain a clearer, more current view of a fire scene or search area. SoftBank demonstrated this by integrating a neural receiver into NVIDIA Aerial CUDA-Accelerated RAN (ACAR) and testing it with a commercial 5G smartphone. In controlled tests with interference, the neural receiver delivered higher uplink throughput than a conventional receiver at all 15 tested settings, with a maximum gain of roughly 60% . Another way to improve reception is to teach receivers about the environments where they operate. Using NVIDIA Aerial Testbed, ETH Zurich researchers found that tuning neural receivers using local measurements reduced block error rates by more than one-third compared with selected pretrained versions. Networks That Learn When to Save Power As 6G connects more devices and supports more AI applications, managing energy demand will become increasingly important. For example, a network may need enough capacity to serve a busy stadium, but demand changes when the crowd leaves. AI can help identify when spare capacity can power down — and when it needs to come back online — so operators can reduce electricity use without dropping connections. At the University of Leeds , researchers developed a system that predicts network demand 10 minutes ahead and uses those forecasts to guide base station sleep decisions. Before powering down, it checks that neighboring active stations can continue serving affected devices and monitors for changes that require capacity to be restored. The team tested their approach using a portable, NVIDIA DGX Spark -powered 5G “network-in-a-box” alongside a digital twin for validating decisions against real wireless equipment. The result: researchers reported a 45.6% reduction in RAN power consumption relative to a full-power baseline while maintaining device connectivity. Networks That Can Be Tested Faster — Before They’re Built Before deploying a network, researchers need to know how it will perform when hundreds of devices compete for connections or radio signals run into interference. Simulating these conditions helps teams evaluate designs before committing to costly equipment and field trials. But realistic simulations can take hours, limiting how many ideas researchers can explore. The Centre Tecnològic de Telecomunicacions de Catalunya (CTTC) is accelerating that process by bringing GPU-accelerated radio channel models, running on ACAR, into CTTC’s open source 5G-LENA network simulator. These models calculate how wireless signals travel between antennas and devices — a computation that grows increasingly demanding as simulated networks grow. In an early evaluation, the approach reduced simulation runtime from approximately three hours to 10-20 minutes, depending on the integration, while preserving the expected statistical behavior and network performance.
